abstract: We discuss in this paper architectures for executing probabilistic rule-bases in a par(cid:173) allel manner, using as a theoretical basis recently introduced information-theoretic models. We will begin by describing our (non-neural) learning algorithm and theory of quantitative rule modelling, followed by a discussion on the exact nature of two particular models. Finally we work through an example of our approach, going from database to rules to inference network, and compare the network's performance with the theoretical limits for specific problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to execute probabilistic rule systems in parallel using connectionist architectures. Probabilistic rules express relationships with uncertainty, so the problem involves more than applying rules as absolute statements. The authors use information-theoretic models as the basis for giving these rules a quantitative meaning and building networks that perform inference with them.

The presentation begins with a non-neural learning algorithm and a theory of quantitative rule modeling. It then examines two particular models before turning to the inference architecture. This sequence connects the way rules are learned and interpreted with the way a network executes them, making the underlying rule semantics part of the architectural design.

A worked example follows the entire route from a database to rules and then to an inference network. The authors compare the resulting network's performance with theoretical limits for specific problems. That comparison frames the network as an implementation of a defined probabilistic reasoning procedure, allowing its behavior to be assessed against the theory that motivated it.
summary.tldr: The paper connects information-theoretic rule learning with parallel inference networks and evaluates them against problem-specific theoretical limits.

title: An Information Theoretic Approach to Rule-Based Connectionist Expert Systems

abstract: We describe a framework for real-time tracking of facial expressions that uses neurally-inspired correlation and interpolation methods. A distributed view-based representation is used to characterize facial state, and is computed using a replicated correlation network. The ensemble response of the set of view correlation scores is input to a network based interpolation method, which maps perceptual state to motor control states for a simulated 3-D face model. Activation levels of the motor state correspond to muscle activations in an anatomically derived model. By integrating fast and robust 2-D processing with 3-D models, we obtain a system that is able to quickly track and interpret complex facial motions in real-time.

paragraphs: This paper describes a system that tracks facial expressions and uses them to control a simulated three-dimensional face in real time. It links visual analysis to facial motion through two neural-inspired operations: correlation and interpolation. The aim is to turn an observed facial state into the control signals needed to reproduce its expression.

A replicated correlation network computes a distributed, view-based representation of the face. Facial state is expressed through the combined responses of multiple view-correlation scores. Those scores then enter an interpolation network, which maps the perceptual representation to motor-control states. In the simulated face, the resulting activation levels correspond to muscles in an anatomically derived model.

The architecture connects fast two-dimensional image processing with a structured three-dimensional account of facial movement. Correlation supplies the visual description, and interpolation translates that description into coordinated muscle activations. The authors report that the integrated system can quickly track and interpret complex facial motions in real time, demonstrating a complete path from observed appearance to animated expression.
summary.tldr: Correlation and interpolation networks translate observed facial expressions into muscle controls for a real-time three-dimensional face model.

title: Correlation and Interpolation Networks for Real-time Expression Analysis/Synthesis

abstract: No finite sample is sufficient to determine the density, and therefore the entropy, of a signal directly. Some assumption about either the functional form of the density or about its smoothness is necessary. Both amount to a prior over the space of possible density functions. By far the most common approach is to assume that the density has a parametric form. By contrast we derive a differential learning rule called EMMA that optimizes entropy by way of kernel density estimation. En(cid:173) tropy and its derivative can then be calculated by sampling from this density estimate. The resulting parameter update rule is sur(cid:173) prisingly simple and efficient. We will show how EMMA can be used to detect and correct cor(cid:173) ruption in magnetic resonance images (MRI). This application is beyond the scope of existing parametric entropy models.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to optimize a signal's entropy when only a finite collection of observations is available. Those observations cannot uniquely determine the signal's probability density or its entropy. Estimation therefore requires assumptions, such as a chosen functional form or a degree of smoothness, that favor some possible densities over others.

The authors introduce EMMA, a differential learning rule that uses kernel density estimation instead of committing to a parametric density form. Entropy and its derivative are calculated by sampling from the estimated density. The derivative then supplies information for updating the parameters being learned, producing a rule the authors describe as simple and efficient.

The application is detecting and correcting corruption in magnetic resonance images. The authors position this task beyond the reach of existing parametric entropy models. The approach matters because it connects a more flexible density estimate directly to an optimization procedure. It still relies on assumptions needed for density estimation, but those assumptions need not take the form of a fixed parametric distribution.
summary.tldr: EMMA uses kernel density estimates to optimize entropy, with an application to detecting and correcting MRI corruption.

title: Empirical Entropy Manipulation for Real-World Problems

abstract: By now it is widely accepted that learning a task from scratch, i.e., without any prior knowledge, is a daunting undertaking. Humans, however, rarely at(cid:173) tempt to learn from scratch. They extract initial biases as well as strategies how to approach a learning problem from instructions and/or demonstrations of other humans. For learning control, this paper investigates how learning from demonstration can be applied in the context of reinforcement learning. We consider priming the Q-function, the value function, the policy, and the model of the task dynamics as possible areas where demonstrations can speed up learning. In general nonlinear learning problems, only model-based rein(cid:173) forcement learning shows significant speed-up after a demonstration, while in the special case of linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problems, all methods profit from the demonstration. In an implementation of pole balancing on a complex anthropomorphic robot arm, we demonstrate that, when facing the complexities of real signal processing, model-based reinforcement learning offers the most robustness for LQR problems. Using the suggested methods, the robot learns pole balancing in just a single trial after a 30 second long demonstration of the human instructor.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how demonstrations can give reinforcement learning a useful starting point for control tasks. It considers four places to insert this information: the Q-function, the value function, the policy, and a model of the task’s dynamics. The question is which form of preparation most effectively accelerates subsequent learning.

The answer depends on the problem setting. For general nonlinear learning problems, only model-based reinforcement learning shows a significant speed-up after a demonstration. For linear quadratic regulator problems, all the considered methods benefit. This distinction makes the destination of demonstration information important: different learning components do not gain equally across the two settings.

The authors also implement pole balancing on a complex anthropomorphic robot arm. Under the practical demands of real signal processing, model-based reinforcement learning provides the greatest robustness for the LQR setting. With the proposed methods, the robot learns pole balancing in a single trial following a 30-second human demonstration. The result connects the comparison of learning strategies to a concrete physical control task.
summary.tldr: Demonstrations most consistently help model-based reinforcement learning, enabling a robot to learn pole balancing in one trial after a 30-second demonstration.

title: Learning from Demonstration

abstract: We model the responses of cells in visual area VI during natural vision. Our model consists of a classical energy mechanism whose output is divided by nonclassical gain control and texture contrast mechanisms. We apply this model to review movies, a stimulus sequence that replicates the stimulation a cell receives during free viewing of natural images. Data were collected from three cells using five different review movies, and the model was fit separately to the data from each movie. For the energy mechanism alone we find modest but significant correlations (rE = 0.41, 0.43, 0.59, 0.35) between model and data. These correlations are improved somewhat when we allow for suppressive surround effects (rE+G = 0.42, 0.56, 0.60, 0.37). In one case the inclusion of a delayed suppressive surround dramatically improves the fit to the data by modifying the time course of the model's response.

paragraphs: The paper models visual-cell responses during natural viewing, asking how well a classical energy mechanism explains activity and what additional suppression contributes. The full model divides the energy mechanism's output by terms representing nonclassical gain control and texture contrast. This makes the predicted response depend on more than the energy mechanism alone.

The authors use review movies that reproduce the stimulation a cell receives while freely viewing natural images. They collect data from three cells using five review movies and fit the model separately for each movie. This arrangement evaluates the model against temporally changing input related to natural viewing, while allowing each movie's responses to receive their own fit.

The energy mechanism alone yields modest but significant correlations with recorded activity. Adding suppressive surround effects improves the correlations somewhat. In one case, delayed surround suppression substantially improves the fit by changing the predicted response's time course. That result highlights timing as an important part of suppression: its contribution can involve reshaping when a cell responds, beyond adjusting response strength.
summary.tldr: Adding surround suppression improves models of visual-cell responses, with delayed suppression markedly improving one response time course.

title: Modeling Complex Cells in an Awake Macaque during Natural Image Viewing

abstract: Fishers linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is a classical multivari(cid:173) ate technique both for dimension reduction and classification. The data vectors are transformed into a low dimensional subspace such that the class centroids are spread out as much as possible. In this subspace LDA works as a simple prototype classifier with lin(cid:173) ear decision boundaries. However, in many applications the linear boundaries do not adequately separate the classes. We present a nonlinear generalization of discriminant analysis that uses the ker(cid:173) nel trick of representing dot products by kernel functions. The pre(cid:173) sented algorithm allows a simple formulation of the EM-algorithm in terms of kernel functions which leads to a unique concept for un(cid:173) supervised mixture analysis, supervised discriminant analysis and semi-supervised discriminant analysis with partially unlabelled ob(cid:173) servations in feature spaces.

paragraphs: The paper generalizes linear discriminant analysis to handle nonlinear class separation. Classical LDA finds a lower-dimensional representation in which class centers are spread apart and uses linear decision boundaries. This can be inadequate when the arrangement of the data requires more flexible boundaries to separate the classes.

The proposed approach uses kernel functions in place of dot products. This kernel formulation allows discriminant analysis to operate in a feature space and supports a nonlinear generalization of the original method. The central change is in the representation and its associated computations, extending the kinds of class structure that discriminant analysis can address.

The authors also formulate the expectation-maximization algorithm in terms of kernel functions. This provides a common framework for unsupervised mixture analysis, supervised discriminant analysis, and semi-supervised analysis with some observations left unlabeled. The contribution therefore joins nonlinear representation with different levels of label availability, allowing these learning settings to be expressed through a shared feature-space approach.
summary.tldr: Kernel-based discriminant analysis extends linear class separation and unifies supervised, unsupervised, and partially labeled learning through an EM formulation.

title: Nonlinear Discriminant Analysis Using Kernel Functions

abstract: A central issue in principal component analysis (PCA) is choosing the number of principal components to be retained. By interpreting PCA as density estimation, we show how to use Bayesian model selection to es(cid:173) timate the true dimensionality of the data. The resulting estimate is sim(cid:173) ple to compute yet guaranteed to pick the correct dimensionality, given enough data. The estimate involves an integral over the Steifel manifold of k-frames, which is difficult to compute exactly. But after choosing an appropriate parameterization and applying Laplace's method, an accu(cid:173) rate and practical estimator is obtained. In simulations, it is convincingly better than cross-validation and other proposed algorithms, plus it runs much faster.

The estimate involves an integral over the Steifel manifold of k-frames, which is difficult to compute exactly. paragraphs: Principal component analysis requires deciding how many components to keep. This paper approaches that decision by treating PCA as a model of the data's probability distribution. That interpretation makes the number of retained components a Bayesian model-selection problem, allowing dimensionality to be estimated through a common probabilistic framework.

The calculation involves integrating over possible collections of orthogonal directions, represented mathematically by a Stiefel manifold. Computing that integral exactly is difficult. The authors choose a suitable parameterization and apply Laplace's method to obtain a practical approximation. This step turns the Bayesian formulation into an estimator described as both accurate and simple to compute.

The paper states that the estimate selects the correct dimensionality given enough data. That is a large-data guarantee, not a promise of correctness for every finite dataset. In the reported simulations, the estimator performs substantially better than cross-validation and other proposed algorithms while running much faster. Together, these results support both its statistical motivation and its practical usefulness for choosing PCA dimensionality.
summary.tldr: A practical Bayesian estimator chooses PCA dimensionality, with a stated large-data correctness guarantee and strong simulation results.

title: Automatic Choice of Dimensionality for PCA

abstract: The Temporal Coding Hypothesis of Miller and colleagues [7] sug(cid:173) gests that animals integrate related temporal patterns of stimuli into single memory representations. We formalize this concept using quasi-Bayes estimation to update the parameters of a con(cid:173) strained hidden Markov model. This approach allows us to account for some surprising temporal effects in the second order condition(cid:173) ing experiments of Miller et al. [1 , 2, 3], which other models are unable to explain.

This approach allows us to account for some surprising temporal effects in the second order condition(cid:173) ing experiments of Miller et al. [1 , 2, 3], which other models are unable to explain.

paragraphs: This paper develops a computational account of how animals combine information about the timing of stimuli during conditioning. Its starting point is the Temporal Coding Hypothesis, which proposes that related temporal patterns are integrated into a single memory representation. The emphasis is therefore on the organization of events in time, beyond simply recording that events are related.

The authors formalize this idea with a constrained hidden Markov model. They use quasi-Bayesian estimation to update the model's parameters as information is acquired. This turns a hypothesis about integrated temporal memory into a specified probabilistic learning approach whose behavior can be compared with conditioning results.

The approach accounts for some surprising temporal effects in the cited second-order conditioning experiments that other models cannot explain. The stated achievement concerns those effects, rather than every phenomenon in conditioning. Its importance is that explicitly representing and updating temporal structure gives the memory-integration hypothesis explanatory force in cases where the alternative models discussed fall short.
summary.tldr: A constrained hidden Markov model formalizes integrated temporal memory and explains selected second-order conditioning effects.

title: Modeling Temporal Structure in Classical Conditioning

abstract: A new distance measure between probability density functions (pdfs) is introduced, which we refer to as the Laplacian pdf distance. The Laplacian pdf distance exhibits a remarkable connection to Mercer kernel based learning theory via the Parzen window technique for density estimation. In a kernel feature space defined by the eigenspectrum of the Laplacian data matrix, this pdf distance is shown to measure the cosine of the angle between cluster mean vectors. The Laplacian data matrix, and hence its eigenspectrum, can be obtained automatically based on the data at hand, by optimal Parzen window selection. We show that the Laplacian pdf distance has an interesting interpretation as a risk function connected to the probability of error.

paragraphs: Clustering can be studied by comparing probability distributions associated with groups of data. This paper introduces the Laplacian pdf distance, a measure between probability density functions. It connects that measure to kernel learning through Parzen-window density estimation, linking a statistical comparison to a geometric representation.

In a kernel feature space defined by the eigenspectrum of the Laplacian data matrix, the measure corresponds to the cosine of the angle between cluster mean vectors. This gives the density comparison a concrete geometric interpretation: it relates to the directions of group averages in the constructed feature space.

The Laplacian data matrix and its eigenspectrum can be obtained automatically from the available data through optimal Parzen-window selection. The authors also interpret the distance as a risk function connected to error probability. Together, these results tie density estimation, kernel geometry, and statistical risk into one clustering objective. The contribution is this mathematical connection and data-based construction, rather than an empirical claim about outperforming particular clustering algorithms.
summary.tldr: The Laplacian pdf distance links density comparisons to angles between cluster means in a kernel feature space and to a risk interpretation involving error probability.

title: The Laplacian PDF Distance: A Cost Function for Clustering in a Kernel Feature Space

abstract: Spike sorting involves clustering spike trains recorded by a microelectrode according to the source neuron. It is a complicated problem, which requires a lot of human labor, partly due to the non-stationary nature of the data. We propose an automated technique for the clustering of non-stationary Gaussian sources in a Bayesian framework. At a first search stage, data is divided into short time frames and candidate descriptions of the data as a mixture of Gaussians are computed for each frame. At a second stage transition probabilities between candidate mixtures are computed, and a globally optimal clustering is found as the MAP solution of the resulting probabilistic model. Transition probabilities are computed using local stationarity assumptions and are based on a Gaussian version of the Jensen-Shannon divergence. The method was applied to several recordings. The performance appeared almost indistinguishable from humans in a wide range of scenarios, including movement, merges, and splits of clusters.

paragraphs: Spike sorting assigns activity recorded by a microelectrode to its source neurons. The paper focuses on the difficulty caused by recordings whose statistical structure changes over time. It proposes an automated Bayesian method for clustering nonstationary Gaussian sources, addressing a source of the substantial human effort often required for this task.

The method first divides the data into short time frames and generates candidate Gaussian-mixture descriptions for each frame. It then computes transition probabilities between these candidates and finds the globally optimal clustering as a maximum a posteriori solution of the resulting model. Global consistency therefore enters through the probabilistic connections between local candidate descriptions.

Those transition probabilities rely on local stationarity assumptions and a Gaussian form of Jensen-Shannon divergence. Applied to several recordings, the method appeared nearly indistinguishable from human performance across scenarios involving moving, merging, and splitting clusters. This empirical finding supports combining local mixture searches with a global temporal model to track changing sources within the stated modeling framework.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian temporal clustering method tracks changing spike sources and appeared close to human performance on several recordings.

title: Spike Sorting: Bayesian Clustering of Non-Stationary Data

paragraphs: Kernel learning usually starts with a single kernel, which supplies the comparisons used by the learning algorithm. This paper addresses settings where combining several kernels is desirable. It builds on a formulation that learns conic combinations of kernel matrices for classification, making the choice of combination part of the learning problem.

The main computational contribution is to rewrite that formulation as a semi-infinite linear program. This reformulation allows the authors to reuse standard support vector machine implementations to solve the problem efficiently. They also extend both the formulation and the solution method beyond the original classification setting, including regression and one-class classification.

The experiments indicate that the algorithm helps automate model selection and makes learned results easier to interpret. They also demonstrate operation with hundreds of thousands of examples or hundreds of candidate kernels. These findings support the practicality of learning kernel combinations at substantial scale. The broader significance is a shared optimization approach that can draw on existing implementations across several kinds of learning tasks.
summary.tldr: A reformulation of multiple kernel learning reuses standard SVM implementations and extends to regression and one-class classification.

title: A General and Efficient Multiple Kernel Learning Algorithm

abstract: We consider the problem of denoising a noisily sampled submanifold M in Rd, where the submanifold M is a priori unknown and we are only given a noisy point sample. The presented denoising algorithm is based on a graph-based diffusion process of the point sample. We analyze this diffusion process using recent re- sults about the convergence of graph Laplacians. In the experiments we show that our method is capable of dealing with non-trivial high-dimensional noise. More- over using the denoising algorithm as pre-processing method we can improve the results of a semi-supervised learning algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to remove noise from points sampled around an unknown submanifold in a higher-dimensional space. The underlying geometric structure is not supplied to the algorithm. It must work from the noisy points themselves, so denoising and the geometry of the sample are closely connected.

The proposed method uses a graph-based diffusion process on the point sample. The graph provides the structure through which the diffusion acts on the data. The authors analyze that process using results about convergence of graph Laplacians, connecting the graph operation to the geometric setting in which the points were sampled.

Experiments show that the method can handle nontrivial noise in high-dimensional data. The authors also use it as preprocessing for a semi-supervised learning algorithm and obtain improved results. This second finding gives the denoising operation a downstream role: cleaning the sample can help a subsequent learner. Both results support the usefulness of diffusion-based denoising when the underlying manifold must be inferred from noisy observations.
summary.tldr: Graph-based diffusion denoises samples from an unknown manifold and improves a semi-supervised learner when used as preprocessing.

title: Manifold Denoising

abstract: Stress and genetic background regulate different aspects of behavioral learning through the action of stress hormones and neuromodulators. In reinforcement learning (RL) models, meta-parameters such as learning rate, future reward dis- count factor, and exploitation-exploration factor, control learning dynamics and performance. They are hypothesized to be related to neuromodulatory levels in the brain. We found that many aspects of animal learning and performance can be described by simple RL models using dynamic control of the meta-parameters. To study the effects of stress and genotype, we carried out 5-hole-box light condition- ing and Morris water maze experiments with C57BL/6 and DBA/2 mouse strains. The animals were exposed to different kinds of stress to evaluate its effects on immediate performance as well as on long-term memory. Then, we used RL mod- els to simulate their behavior. For each experimental session, we estimated a set of model meta-parameters that produced the best ﬁt between the model and the animal performance. The dynamics of several estimated meta-parameters were qualitatively similar for the two simulated experiments, and with statistically sig- niﬁcant differences between different genetic strains and stress conditions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning models contain settings that govern how quickly learning occurs, how future rewards are valued, and how behavior balances exploration with exploitation. This paper investigates whether changes in these meta-parameters can describe differences in animal learning associated with stress and genetic background. Their relationship to brain neuromodulators is presented as a hypothesis.

The authors studied C57BL/6 and DBA/2 mice in light conditioning using a five-hole box and in the Morris water maze. Different stress conditions allowed them to examine immediate performance and long-term memory. They then simulated behavior with reinforcement learning models, fitting a set of meta-parameters separately for each experimental session.

Several fitted meta-parameters showed qualitatively similar dynamics across the two simulated experiments, alongside statistically significant differences between strains and stress conditions. These findings support the use of dynamically controlled reinforcement learning settings to describe many aspects of the observed behavior. The fitted values provide a computational account of behavioral differences; the abstract does not establish them as direct measurements of neuromodulator levels.
summary.tldr: Changing reinforcement learning meta-parameters describes behavioral differences associated with mouse genotype and stress conditions.

title: Effects of Stress and Genotype on Meta-parameter Dynamics in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Motivated in part by the hierarchical organization of cortex, a number of algorithms have recently been proposed that try to learn hierarchical, or deep,'' structure from unlabeled data. While several authors have formally or informally compared their algorithms to computations performed in visual area V1 (and the cochlea), little attempt has been made thus far to evaluate these algorithms in terms of their fidelity for mimicking computations at deeper levels in the cortical hierarchy. This paper presents an unsupervised learning model that faithfully mimics certain properties of visual area V2. Specifically, we develop a sparse variant of the deep belief networks of Hinton et al. (2006). We learn two layers of nodes in the network, and demonstrate that the first layer, similar to prior work on sparse coding and ICA, results in localized, oriented, edge filters, similar to the Gabor functions known to model V1 cell receptive fields. Further, the second layer in our model encodes correlations of the first layer responses in the data. Specifically, it picks up both collinear ( contour'') features as well as corners and junctions. More interestingly, in a quantitative comparison, the encoding of these more complex ``corner'' features matches well with the results from the Ito & Komatsu's study of biological V2 responses. This suggests that our sparse variant of deep belief networks holds promise for modeling more higher-order features.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a model learned from unlabeled data can reproduce properties of a deeper stage of visual processing. Earlier comparisons often focused on visual area V1. The authors develop a sparse deep belief network with two learned layers and examine whether its representations also resemble particular responses associated with visual area V2.

The first layer learns localized, oriented edge filters resembling the Gabor-like receptive fields used to model V1 cells. The second layer captures correlations among those first-layer responses. It represents aligned contour features as well as corners and junctions, showing how combinations of simpler responses can encode more complex visual structure.

A quantitative comparison finds that the model's corner-feature encoding matches biological V2 results from the study identified in the abstract. This supports the claim that the model mimics certain V2 properties and suggests promise for modeling higher-order features. The biological comparison concerns these specific response properties; its significance is that an unsupervised hierarchical model can reproduce more than first-layer edge selectivity.
summary.tldr: A sparse two-layer deep belief network learns edge combinations whose corner encoding matches certain biological V2 responses.

title: Sparse deep belief net model for visual area V2

abstract: We study an encoding/decoding mechanism accounting for the relative spike timing of the signals propagating from peripheral nerve fibers to second-order somatosensory neurons in the cuneate nucleus (CN). The CN is modeled as a population of spiking neurons receiving as inputs the spatiotemporal responses of real mechanoreceptors obtained via microneurography recordings in humans. The efficiency of the haptic discrimination process is quantified by a novel definition of entropy that takes into full account the metrical properties of the spike train space. This measure proves to be a suitable decoding scheme for generalizing the classical Shannon entropy to spike-based neural codes. It permits an assessment of neurotransmission in the presence of a large output space (i.e. hundreds of spike trains) with 1 ms temporal precision. It is shown that the CN population code performs a complete discrimination of 81 distinct stimuli already within 35 ms of the first afferent spike, whereas a partial discrimination (80% of the maximum information transmission) is possible as rapidly as 15 ms. This study suggests that the CN may not constitute a mere synaptic relay along the somatosensory pathway but, rather, it may convey optimal contextual accounts (in terms of fast and reliable information transfer) of peripheral tactile inputs to downstream structures of the central nervous system.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the timing of touch-related nerve spikes can support rapid discrimination between stimuli. It models neurons in the cuneate nucleus using inputs from real human mechanoreceptors recorded through microneurography. The focus is on how a population of second-order neurons processes the spatial and temporal structure arriving from peripheral nerve fibers.

The authors introduce an entropy measure that accounts for distances between spike trains. This extends the information-theoretic analysis to the timing structure of spike-based codes and supports assessment of hundreds of output spike trains at one-millisecond precision. The measure provides a decoding scheme for evaluating how much stimulus information the modeled population conveys.

The modeled population completely discriminates 81 stimuli within 35 milliseconds of the first incoming spike. It reaches 80% of maximum information transmission within 15 milliseconds. These results suggest that the cuneate nucleus may contribute fast, reliable contextual representations of touch inputs, with a processing role beyond simply passing signals onward through the somatosensory pathway.
summary.tldr: A cuneate-nucleus model driven by human receptor recordings rapidly distinguishes tactile stimuli using a population code sensitive to spike timing.

title: Optimal context separation of spiking haptic signals by second-order somatosensory neurons

abstract: The problem of optimal and automatic design of a detector cascade is considered. A novel mathematical model is introduced for a cascaded detector. This model is analytically tractable, leads to recursive computation, and accounts for both classification and complexity. A boosting algorithm, FCBoost, is proposed for fully automated cascade design. It exploits the new cascade model, minimizes a Lagrangian cost that accounts for both classification risk and complexity. It searches the space of cascade configurations to automatically determine the optimal number of stages and their predictors, and is compatible with bootstrapping of negative examples and cost sensitive learning. Experiments show that the resulting cascades have state-of-the-art performance in various computer vision problems.

paragraphs: A detector cascade organizes prediction into a sequence of stages, making its design a question of both recognition quality and computational cost. Choosing the stages separately can miss how these objectives interact across the whole detector. This paper develops a mathematical model that accounts for classification performance and complexity together, while allowing the necessary calculations to be performed recursively.

The proposed boosting algorithm, FCBoost, uses this model to automate cascade construction. Its objective combines classification risk and complexity through a Lagrangian cost, giving both considerations a role in the search. The algorithm searches cascade configurations to determine the number of stages and the predictors assigned to them. It also accommodates cost-sensitive learning and bootstrapping of negative examples.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across several computer vision problems. The contribution is therefore both a tractable way to describe cascades and a procedure for designing them automatically. The findings support treating computational effort as part of the learning objective when constructing a detector.
summary.tldr: FCBoost automatically designs detector cascades by jointly optimizing classification risk and computational complexity.

title: Boosting Classifier Cascades

abstract: We consider the problem of identifying an activation pattern in a complex, large-scale network that is embedded in very noisy measurements. This problem is relevant to several applications, such as identifying traces of a biochemical spread by a sensor network, expression levels of genes, and anomalous activity or congestion in the Internet. Extracting such patterns is a challenging task specially if the network is large (pattern is very high-dimensional) and the noise is so excessive that it masks the activity at any single node. However, typically there are statistical dependencies in the network activation process that can be leveraged to fuse the measurements of multiple nodes and enable reliable extraction of high-dimensional noisy patterns. In this paper, we analyze an estimator based on the graph Laplacian eigenbasis, and establish the limits of mean square error recovery of noisy patterns arising from a probabilistic (Gaussian or Ising) model based on an arbitrary graph structure. We consider both deterministic and probabilistic network evolution models, and our results indicate that by leveraging the network interaction structure, it is possible to consistently recover high-dimensional patterns even when the noise variance increases with network size.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover activity spread across a large network when measurements are extremely noisy. Individual nodes may provide too little information to reveal whether they are active. However, activity at different nodes can be statistically related, so combining their measurements according to the network structure may expose a pattern hidden at the individual-node level.

The authors analyze an estimator built from the graph Laplacian eigenbasis, a representation tied to the graph's connections. They establish mean-square-error recovery limits for activation patterns generated by Gaussian or Ising probabilistic models on arbitrary graph structures. Their analysis considers both deterministic and probabilistic ways in which the network evolves.

The results indicate that incorporating network interactions can make consistent recovery possible even as noise variance grows with network size. This is a possibility supported by the analyzed models and recovery conditions, rather than a guarantee for every growing noisy network. The contribution explains how structural dependence can supply enough collective information to recover a high-dimensional pattern despite unreliable individual measurements.
summary.tldr: Graph-based estimation can consistently recover noisy network activity under analyzed conditions even when noise variance increases with network size.

title: Identifying graph-structured activation patterns in networks

abstract: Consider a sequence of bits where we are trying to predict the next bit from the previous bits. Assume we are allowed to say `predict 0' or `predict 1', and our payoff is $+1$ if the prediction is correct and $-1$ otherwise. We will say that at each point in time the loss of an algorithm is the number of wrong predictions minus the number of right predictions so far. In this paper we are interested in algorithms that have essentially zero (expected) loss over any string at any point in time and yet have small regret with respect to always predicting $0$ or always predicting $1$. For a sequence of length $T$ our algorithm has regret $14\epsilon T $ and loss $2\sqrt{T}e^{-\epsilon^2 T} $ in expectation for all strings. We show that the tradeoff between loss and regret is optimal up to constant factors. Our techniques extend to the general setting of $N$ experts, where the related problem of trading off regret to the best expert for regret to the 'special' expert has been studied by Even-Dar et al. (COLT'07). We obtain essentially zero loss with respect to the special expert and optimal loss/regret tradeoff, improving upon the results of Even-Dar et al (COLT'07) and settling the main question left open in their paper. The strong loss bounds of the algorithm have some surprising consequences. First, we obtain a parameter free algorithm for the experts problem that has optimal regret bounds with respect to $k$-shifting optima, i.e. bounds with respect to the optimum that is allowed to change arms multiple times. Moreover, for {\em any window of size $n$} the regret of our algorithm to any expert never exceeds $O(\sqrt{n(\log N+\log T)})$, where $N$ is the number of experts and $T$ is the time horizon, while maintaining the essentially zero loss property.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential bit prediction, with a reward for correct guesses and an equal penalty for incorrect ones. It seeks algorithms whose expected cumulative loss stays essentially zero for every sequence while remaining competitive with always predicting either bit. This combines protection against negative performance with low regret against simple comparators.

For a sequence of length T, the stated expected regret is 14 epsilon T and expected loss is 2 sqrt(T) exp(−epsilon² T). The authors prove the tradeoff optimal up to constant factors. These are expectation guarantees, so essentially zero expected loss does not mean that every realized prediction sequence avoids losses.

The techniques extend to N experts, preserving essentially zero loss relative to a designated special expert while obtaining an optimal loss-regret tradeoff. They also yield a parameter-free algorithm competitive with comparators that switch choices. On any window of length n, regret to any expert is bounded by O(sqrt(n(log N + log T))).
summary.tldr: Sequential prediction algorithms achieve essentially zero expected loss while maintaining provably optimal loss-regret tradeoffs up to constants.

title: Prediction strategies without loss

abstract: We consider a general inference setting for discrete probabilistic graphical models where we seek maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates for a subset of the random variables (max nodes), marginalizing over the rest (sum nodes). We present a hybrid message-passing algorithm to accomplish this. The hybrid algorithm passes a mix of sum and max messages depending on the type of source node (sum or max). We derive our algorithm by showing that it falls out as the solution of a particular relaxation of a variational framework. We further show that the Expectation Maximization algorithm can be seen as an approximation to our algorithm. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets, against several baselines, demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed algorithm.

We present a hybrid message-passing algorithm to accomplish this. The hybrid algorithm passes a mix of sum and max messages depending on the type of source node (sum or max). We derive our algorithm by showing that it falls out as the solution of a particular relaxation of a variational framework. paragraphs: In a discrete probabilistic graphical model, an inference task may require choosing values for some variables while averaging over uncertainty in others. This paper studies that combination: it seeks maximum a posteriori estimates for designated variables and marginalizes the remaining variables. The two groups are described as max nodes and sum nodes.

The proposed algorithm passes a mixture of max and sum messages through the model, choosing the message type according to the source node. The authors derive this hybrid procedure from a relaxation of a variational framework. That derivation gives the algorithm an optimization-based foundation and explains how the two forms of inference fit into one procedure.

The paper further shows that Expectation Maximization can be viewed as an approximation to the proposed algorithm. This connects the new method to a familiar approach for inference involving latent variables. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, with several baselines, demonstrate its effectiveness. The result is an approximate inference method built explicitly around the different roles of selected and marginalized variables.
summary.tldr: A variationally derived hybrid message-passing algorithm combines maximization over selected variables with marginalization over latent variables.

title: Message-Passing for Approximate MAP Inference with Latent Variables

abstract: Recent spiking network models of Bayesian inference and unsupervised learning frequently assume either inputs to arrive in a special format or employ complex computations in neuronal activation functions and synaptic plasticity rules. Here we show in a rigorous mathematical treatment how homeostatic processes, which have previously received little attention in this context, can overcome common theoretical limitations and facilitate the neural implementation and performance of existing models. In particular, we show that homeostatic plasticity can be understood as the enforcement of a 'balancing' posterior constraint during probabilistic inference and learning with Expectation Maximization. We link homeostatic dynamics to the theory of variational inference, and show that nontrivial terms, which typically appear during probabilistic inference in a large class of models, drop out. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach in a spiking Winner-Take-All architecture of Bayesian inference and learning. Finally, we sketch how the mathematical framework can be extended to richer recurrent network architectures. Altogether, our theory provides a novel perspective on the interplay of homeostatic processes and synaptic plasticity in cortical microcircuits, and points to an essential role of homeostasis during inference and learning in spiking networks.

paragraphs: Spiking-network models of Bayesian inference and unsupervised learning often depend on specially formatted inputs or complicated neuronal and synaptic computations. This paper investigates whether homeostatic processes can ease those requirements. Its mathematical treatment gives such processes a direct role in implementing probabilistic learning, beyond merely accompanying synaptic change.

The central result interprets homeostatic plasticity as enforcing a balancing constraint on the posterior during inference and Expectation Maximization learning. Connecting these dynamics to variational inference shows that difficult terms appearing in a broad class of probabilistic models disappear under the framework. This explains how balancing activity can simplify the computations required by existing models.

The authors demonstrate feasibility in a spiking Winner-Take-All architecture for Bayesian inference and learning. They also outline how the framework could extend to richer recurrent networks; that extension is presented as a sketch. Overall, the theory links homeostatic dynamics and synaptic plasticity through a shared probabilistic interpretation and points toward an essential role for homeostasis in these spiking-network computations.
summary.tldr: Homeostatic plasticity can enforce posterior balancing constraints that simplify Bayesian inference and learning in spiking networks.

title: Homeostatic plasticity in Bayesian spiking networks as Expectation Maximization with posterior constraints

abstract: We develop and analyze stochastic optimization algorithms for problems in which the expected loss is strongly convex, and the optimum is (approximately) sparse. Previous approaches are able to exploit only one of these two structures, yielding a $\order(\pdim/T)$ convergence rate for strongly convex objectives in $\pdim$ dimensions and $\order(\sqrt{\spindex( \log\pdim)/T})$ convergence rate when the optimum is $\spindex$-sparse. Our algorithm is based on successively solving a series of $\ell_1$-regularized optimization problems using Nesterov's dual averaging algorithm. We establish that the error of our solution after $T$ iterations is at most $\order(\spindex(\log\pdim)/T)$, with natural extensions to approximate sparsity. Our results apply to locally Lipschitz losses including the logistic, exponential, hinge and least-squares losses. By recourse to statistical minimax results, we show that our convergence rates are optimal up to constants. The effectiveness of our approach is also confirmed in numerical simulations where we compare to several baselines on a least-squares regression problem.

paragraphs: The paper studies stochastic optimization when the expected loss is strongly convex and its optimum is sparse or approximately sparse. Previous approaches described in the abstract exploit only one of these properties. The authors instead combine them, aiming to make convergence reflect the number of important coordinates as well as the curvature of the objective.

Their algorithm successively solves l1-regularized problems using Nesterov's dual averaging method. After T iterations, its error is at most order s log(d)/T, where s represents sparsity and d is dimension. This combines the faster dependence on iterations associated with strong convexity with a logarithmic, sparsity-weighted dependence on dimension. The analysis also extends to approximate sparsity.

The results cover locally Lipschitz losses, including logistic, exponential, hinge, and least-squares losses, under the stated problem assumptions. Statistical minimax results establish that the convergence rates are optimal up to constants. Numerical comparisons on least-squares regression also confirm the approach's effectiveness, complementing the theoretical argument for exploiting sparsity and strong convexity together.
summary.tldr: Combining strong convexity and sparsity yields stochastic optimization rates of order s log(d)/T, optimal up to constants.

title: Stochastic optimization and sparse statistical recovery: Optimal algorithms for high dimensions

abstract: Attentional Neural Network is a new framework that integrates top-down cognitive bias and bottom-up feature extraction in one coherent architecture. The top-down influence is especially effective when dealing with high noise or difficult segmentation problems. Our system is modular and extensible. It is also easy to train and cheap to run, and yet can accommodate complex behaviors. We obtain classification accuracy better than or competitive with state of art results on the MNIST variation dataset, and successfully disentangle overlaid digits with high success rates. We view such a general purpose framework as an essential foundation for a larger system emulating the cognitive abilities of the whole brain.
originalAbstract: Attentional Neural Network is a new framework that integrates top-down cognitive bias and bottom-up feature extraction in one coherent architecture. The top-down influence is especially effective when dealing with high noise or difficult segmentation problems. Our system is modular and extensible. It is also easy to train and cheap to run, and yet can accommodate complex behaviors. We obtain classification accuracy better than or competitive with state of art results on the MNIST variation dataset, and successfully disentangle overlaid digits with high success rates. We view such a general purpose framework as an essential foundation for a larger system emulating the cognitive abilities of the whole brain.

paragraphs: The Attentional Neural Network combines two directions of processing in one architecture. Bottom-up processing extracts features from the input, while top-down cognitive feedback influences which features receive attention. The central idea is that feature extraction can benefit from higher-level guidance, especially when noisy or overlapping input makes the relevant evidence difficult to isolate.

This interaction is particularly relevant to segmentation: deciding which parts of an input belong together. When digits overlap, recognizing each digit involves separating evidence that appears in the same image. The framework incorporates feedback into this process. The authors describe the system as modular and extensible, as well as easy to train and inexpensive to run while accommodating complex behavior.

On the MNIST variation dataset, classification accuracy is reported as better than or competitive with leading results. The system also disentangles overlaid digits with high success rates. These findings support the usefulness of cognitive feedback for the tested recognition problems. The authors additionally propose the architecture as a foundation for broader brain-inspired systems; that is a future-facing interpretation of the framework.
summary.tldr: An attentional neural network uses top-down feedback to guide feature extraction and reports strong results on noisy and overlapping digit recognition.

title: Attentional Neural Network: Feature Selection Using Cognitive Feedback

abstract: Maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) has been successfully applied to learn deep generative models for characterizing a joint distribution of variables via kernel mean embedding. In this paper, we present conditional generative moment-matching networks (CGMMN), which learn a conditional distribution given some input variables based on a conditional maximum mean discrepancy (CMMD) criterion. The learning is performed by stochastic gradient descent with the gradient calculated by back-propagation. We evaluate CGMMN on a wide range of tasks, including predictive modeling, contextual generation, and Bayesian dark knowledge, which distills knowledge from a Bayesian model by learning a relatively small CGMMN student network. Our results demonstrate competitive performance in all the tasks.

In this paper, we present conditional generative moment-matching networks (CGMMN), which learn a conditional distribution given some input variables based on a conditional maximum mean discrepancy (CMMD) criterion. The learning is performed by stochastic gradient descent with the gradient calculated by back-propagation. paragraphs: Generative models can describe a joint distribution over variables, but many tasks require a distribution of outputs conditioned on a particular input. This paper introduces conditional generative moment-matching networks to learn that input-dependent distribution. It builds on the use of kernel mean embeddings and maximum mean discrepancy in deep generative modeling.

The proposed training criterion is conditional maximum mean discrepancy. It extends distribution matching to the conditional setting, so the network learns how the output distribution relates to the supplied input variables. Training uses stochastic gradient descent, with gradients computed through backpropagation, connecting the conditional criterion to standard neural network optimization.

The authors evaluate the method on predictive modeling, contextual generation, and Bayesian dark knowledge. In the last application, a relatively small student network learns knowledge from a Bayesian model. Reported performance is competitive across these tasks. The results support the same conditional distribution-learning framework for several purposes, including prediction, generation informed by context, and transferring Bayesian model knowledge into a smaller network.
summary.tldr: Conditional moment matching trains generative networks for input-dependent distributions, with competitive results in prediction, contextual generation, and Bayesian distillation.

title: Conditional Generative Moment-Matching Networks

abstract: We present Cyclades, a general framework for parallelizing stochastic optimization algorithms in a shared memory setting. Cyclades is asynchronous during model updates, and requires no memory locking mechanisms, similar to Hogwild!-type algorithms. Unlike Hogwild!, Cyclades introduces no conflicts during parallel execution, and offers a black-box analysis for provable speedups across a large family of algorithms. Due to its inherent cache locality and conflict-free nature, our multi-core implementation of Cyclades consistently outperforms Hogwild!-type algorithms on sufficiently sparse datasets, leading to up to 40% speedup gains compared to Hogwild!, and up to 5\times gains over asynchronous implementations of variance reduction algorithms.
originalAbstract: We present Cyclades, a general framework for parallelizing stochastic optimization algorithms in a shared memory setting. Cyclades is asynchronous during model updates, and requires no memory locking mechanisms, similar to Hogwild!-type algorithms. Unlike Hogwild!, Cyclades introduces no conflicts during parallel execution, and offers a black-box analysis for provable speedups across a large family of algorithms. Due to its inherent cache locality and conflict-free nature, our multi-core implementation of Cyclades consistently outperforms Hogwild!-type algorithms on sufficiently sparse datasets, leading to up to 40% speedup gains compared to Hogwild!, and up to 5\times gains over asynchronous implementations of variance reduction algorithms.

paragraphs: Parallel stochastic optimization lets multiple workers update a shared model. Asynchronous methods allow workers to proceed without waiting for each other, but concurrent updates can conflict. Cyclades is a general framework for shared-memory optimization that permits asynchronous model updates without memory locks while avoiding conflicts during parallel execution.

The framework also supplies an analysis that can establish speedups across a broad family of algorithms. This matters because its contribution extends beyond one particular optimizer: the authors present a reusable way to obtain conflict-free parallel execution and reason about its benefits. They attribute the implementation's performance to both the absence of conflicts and favorable cache locality.

On sufficiently sparse datasets, the multicore implementation consistently outperforms the Hogwild!-type algorithms considered. The reported gains reach up to 40% compared with Hogwild! and up to fivefold compared with asynchronous variance-reduction implementations. These are empirical improvements under the stated sparsity condition, showing that avoiding update conflicts can accompany strong practical parallel performance.
summary.tldr: Cyclades enables lock-free, conflict-free parallel stochastic optimization, with provable speedups and empirical gains on sufficiently sparse datasets.

title: Cyclades: Conflict-free Asynchronous Machine Learning

abstract: In many applications, it is desirable to extract only the relevant aspects of data. A principled way to do this is the information bottleneck (IB) method, where one seeks a code that maximises information about a relevance variable, Y, while constraining the information encoded about the original data, X. Unfortunately however, the IB method is computationally demanding when data are high-dimensional and/or non-gaussian. Here we propose an approximate variational scheme for maximising a lower bound on the IB objective, analogous to variational EM. Using this method, we derive an IB algorithm to recover features that are both relevant and sparse. Finally, we demonstrate how kernelised versions of the algorithm can be used to address a broad range of problems with non-linear relation between X and Y.

Here we propose an approximate variational scheme for maximising a lower bound on the IB objective, analogous to variational EM. Using this method, we derive an IB algorithm to recover features that are both relevant and sparse. Finally, we demonstrate how kernelised versions of the algorithm can be used to address a broad range of problems with non-linear relation between X and Y.

paragraphs: A useful representation should retain the parts of data that matter for a particular purpose. The information bottleneck formalizes this by seeking a code that preserves information about a relevance variable while limiting how much information it carries about the original input. This balances relevance against the amount of input detail retained.

Applying that principle becomes computationally demanding for high-dimensional or non-Gaussian data. The authors propose an approximate variational procedure that maximizes a lower bound on the information bottleneck objective. Its relationship to variational expectation-maximization provides a route to optimization without claiming to solve the original difficult objective exactly.

From this procedure, the paper derives an algorithm for recovering features that are both relevant and sparse. Sparsity complements the information bottleneck's emphasis on selective representation. The authors further demonstrate kernelized versions for problems where the input and relevance variable have nonlinear relationships. The contribution therefore connects a principled representation objective to an approximate algorithm that supports sparse features and extends beyond linear relationships.
summary.tldr: A variational approximation to the information bottleneck learns relevant sparse features, with kernelized versions addressing nonlinear relationships.

title: Relevant sparse codes with variational information bottleneck

abstract: In this paper, we suggest a novel data-driven approach to active learning (AL). The key idea is to train a regressor that predicts the expected error reduction for a candidate sample in a particular learning state. By formulating the query selection procedure as a regression problem we are not restricted to working with existing AL heuristics; instead, we learn strategies based on experience from previous AL outcomes. We show that a strategy can be learnt either from simple synthetic 2D datasets or from a subset of domain-specific data. Our method yields strategies that work well on real data from a wide range of domains.

paragraphs: Active learning involves choosing which example to request information about next. The usefulness of a candidate depends on the learner’s current state, so a fixed selection rule may not capture every useful situation. This paper treats the selection strategy itself as something that can be learned from previous active-learning experience.

The authors train a regression model to predict how much a candidate sample is expected to reduce error in a particular learning state. Query selection can then use those predictions. Framing selection as regression makes it possible to learn from earlier outcomes instead of restricting the procedure to existing active-learning heuristics.

The paper shows that these strategies can be learned from simple synthetic two-dimensional datasets or from a subset of data from the intended domain. The resulting strategies work well on real datasets across a wide range of domains. This finding supports a practical division of labor: past learning outcomes train the selection model, which then helps decide what information a learner should seek next.
summary.tldr: A learned regressor guides active learning by predicting which candidate example will most reduce the learner’s error.

title: Learning Active Learning from Data

abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding ribonucleic acids (RNAs) which play key roles in post-transcriptional gene regulation. Direct identification of mature miRNAs is infeasible due to their short lengths, and researchers instead aim at identifying precursor miRNAs (pre-miRNAs). Many of the known pre-miRNAs have distinctive stem-loop secondary structure, and structure-based filtering is usually the first step to predict the possibility of a given sequence being a pre-miRNA. To identify new pre-miRNAs that often have non-canonical structure, however, we need to consider additional features other than structure. To obtain such additional characteristics, existing computational methods rely on manual feature extraction, which inevitably limits the efficiency, robustness, and generalization of computational identification. To address the limitations of existing approaches, we propose a pre-miRNA identification method that incorporates (1) a deep recurrent neural network (RNN) for automated feature learning and classification, (2) multimodal architecture for seamless integration of prior knowledge (secondary structure), (3) an attention mechanism for improving long-term dependence modeling, and (4) an RNN-based class activation mapping for highlighting the learned representations that can contrast pre-miRNAs and non-pre-miRNAs. In our experiments with recent benchmarks, the proposed approach outperformed the compared state-of-the-art alternatives in terms of various performance metrics.

Existing computational approaches obtain such signals through manually designed features.

The paper proposes a deep recurrent neural network that learns features and performs classification automatically. A multimodal architecture combines this learned information with prior knowledge about secondary structure. An attention mechanism supports modeling of dependencies across the sequence. Together, these components allow the detector to incorporate structural knowledge while learning additional characteristics relevant to precursor identification.

The method also includes recurrent-network class activation mapping, which highlights learned representations that help distinguish precursors from other sequences. This supplies a way to inspect what supports the classifier's decisions. On the benchmarks used in the experiments, the approach outperforms the compared state-of-the-art alternatives across several performance measures, supporting the usefulness of combining feature learning, structural information, and attention.
summary.tldr: A recurrent neural network combines learned sequence features, structural knowledge, and attention to improve precursor microRNA identification on tested benchmarks.

title: Deep Recurrent Neural Network-Based Identification of Precursor microRNAs

abstract: We use complex-weighted, deep networks to invert the effects of multimode optical fibre distortion of a coherent input image. We generated experimental data based on collections of optical fibre responses to greyscale input images generated with coherent light, by measuring only image amplitude (not amplitude and phase as is typical) at the output of \SI{1}{\metre} and \SI{10}{\metre} long, \SI{105}{\micro\metre} diameter multimode fibre. This data is made available as the {\it Optical fibre inverse problem} Benchmark collection. The experimental data is used to train complex-weighted models with a range of regularisation approaches. A {\it unitary regularisation} approach for complex-weighted networks is proposed which performs well in robustly inverting the fibre transmission matrix, which fits well with the physical theory. A key benefit of the unitary constraint is that it allows us to learn a forward unitary model and analytically invert it to solve the inverse problem. We demonstrate this approach, and show how it can improve performance by incorporating knowledge of the phase shift induced by the spatial light modulator.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to reconstruct a coherent input image after transmission through a multimode optical fibre distorts it. The authors collect experimental responses to grayscale images using fibres one and ten metres long, each 105 micrometres in diameter. Their measurements record output amplitude alone, rather than both amplitude and phase, and become a public benchmark collection.

They train deep networks with complex-valued weights using several regularization approaches. The central proposal is unitary regularization, a constraint that fits the physical theory and performs well at robustly reversing the fibre's transmission effects. Complex-valued modeling provides the setting in which this structural constraint is applied.

A useful consequence is that a learned forward unitary model can be inverted analytically to solve the reconstruction problem. This connects learning how the fibre transforms an image with recovering the original image from its response. The authors demonstrate the approach and show that incorporating knowledge of the spatial light modulator's phase shift can further improve performance.
summary.tldr: Complex-valued networks with unitary regularization learn invertible models for reconstructing images distorted by multimode optical fibres.

title: Deep, complex, invertible networks for inversion of transmission effects in multimode optical fibres

abstract: \textit{Adaptive importance sampling} (AIS) uses past samples to update the \textit{sampling policy} $q_t$ at each stage $t$. Each stage $t$ is formed with two steps : (i) to explore the space with $n_t$ points according to $q_t$ and (ii) to exploit the current amount of information to update the sampling policy. The very fundamental question raised in this paper concerns the behavior of empirical sums based on AIS. Without making any assumption on the \textit{allocation policy} $n_t$, the theory developed involves no restriction on the split of computational resources between the explore (i) and the exploit (ii) step. It is shown that AIS is asymptotically optimal : the asymptotic behavior of AIS is the same as some ``oracle'' strategy that knows the targeted sampling policy from the beginning. From a practical perspective, weighted AIS is introduced, a new method that allows to forget poor samples from early stages.

paragraphs: Adaptive importance sampling repeatedly changes where it draws samples using information collected so far. Each stage combines exploration, which generates points under the current sampling policy, with an update that uses accumulated information to improve that policy. The paper studies the behavior of empirical sums built from this changing sequence of sampling distributions.

The central theoretical result is asymptotic optimality: as sampling continues, the method has the same asymptotic behavior as an oracle strategy that knew the targeted sampling policy from the start. The analysis places no assumptions on the allocation of sample counts across stages. Consequently, its treatment does not require a prescribed division of computational resources between drawing samples and updating the policy.

The paper also introduces weighted adaptive importance sampling, which allows poor samples from early stages to be forgotten. This addresses the practical fact that early sampling policies can be less useful than later ones. Together, the contributions connect a long-run optimality result with a mechanism for reducing the influence of an initially weak sampling strategy.
summary.tldr: Adaptive importance sampling can asymptotically match an oracle sampling strategy without a prescribed allocation of samples across stages.

title: Asymptotic optimality of adaptive importance sampling

abstract: We study the computational tractability of PAC reinforcement learning with rich observations. We present new provably sample-efficient algorithms for environments with deterministic hidden state dynamics and stochastic rich observations. These methods operate in an oracle model of computation -- accessing policy and value function classes exclusively through standard optimization primitives -- and therefore represent computationally efficient alternatives to prior algorithms that require enumeration. With stochastic hidden state dynamics, we prove that the only known sample-efficient algorithm, OLIVE, cannot be implemented in the oracle model. We also present several examples that illustrate fundamental challenges of tractable PAC reinforcement learning in such general settings.

With stochastic hidden state dynamics, we prove that the only known sample-efficient algorithm, OLIVE, cannot be implemented in the oracle model. We also present several examples that illustrate fundamental challenges of tractable PAC reinforcement learning in such general settings.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning algorithm can use few samples yet still require impractical computation. This paper studies that distinction for learning with rich observations. It asks whether sample-efficient learning can also be computationally tractable when access to policy and value-function classes is restricted to standard optimization primitives.

The authors provide provably sample-efficient algorithms for environments whose hidden-state dynamics are deterministic, even though their rich observations are stochastic. The algorithms operate through optimization oracles instead of enumerating the policy or value-function classes. In this oracle model, they offer computationally efficient alternatives to earlier enumeration-based approaches.

The picture changes when the hidden-state dynamics are stochastic. The paper proves that OLIVE, described as the only known sample-efficient algorithm in that setting, cannot be implemented within the oracle model. This result concerns that algorithm and computational model, rather than ruling out every possible learning approach. Additional examples illustrate fundamental obstacles in the more general setting. Together, the results clarify how assumptions about hidden dynamics affect the prospects for combining sample efficiency with tractable computation.
summary.tldr: Oracle-based algorithms make sample-efficient learning tractable with deterministic hidden dynamics, while stochastic dynamics expose stronger computational obstacles.

title: On Oracle-Efficient PAC RL with Rich Observations

abstract: Nonlinear kernels can be approximated using finite-dimensional feature maps for efficient risk minimization. Due to the inherent trade-off between the dimension of the (mapped) feature space and the approximation accuracy, the key problem is to identify promising (explicit) features leading to a satisfactory out-of-sample performance. In this work, we tackle this problem by efficiently choosing such features from multiple kernels in a greedy fashion. Our method sequentially selects these explicit features from a set of candidate features using a correlation metric. We establish an out-of-sample error bound capturing the trade-off between the error in terms of explicit features (approximation error) and the error due to spectral properties of the best model in the Hilbert space associated to the combined kernel (spectral error). The result verifies that when the (best) underlying data model is sparse enough, i.e., the spectral error is negligible, one can control the test error with a small number of explicit features, that can scale poly-logarithmically with data. Our empirical results show that given a fixed number of explicit features, the method can achieve a lower test error with a smaller time cost, compared to the state-of-the-art in data-dependent random features.

paragraphs: Finite feature maps make nonlinear kernel methods more computationally manageable, but reducing the number of features can sacrifice approximation quality. This paper asks how to choose a small, useful set of explicit features from multiple kernels. Its method builds that set sequentially, selecting candidates greedily according to a correlation measure.

The authors establish a test-error bound separating two contributions. One reflects approximation using the selected explicit features; the other depends on spectral properties of the best model in the combined kernel's Hilbert space. This distinction explains why the usefulness of a compact feature representation depends on the structure of the underlying model as well as on feature selection.

When the best underlying model is sufficiently sparse that spectral error is negligible, the bound permits test-error control with a small feature set whose size can grow polylogarithmically with the data. This is a conditional result, not a guarantee for every dataset. Empirically, at a fixed feature count, the method can obtain lower test error with less computation time than leading data-dependent random-feature methods.
summary.tldr: Greedy feature selection across kernels offers compact approximations with test-error guarantees when the underlying model is sufficiently sparse.

title: Learning Bounds for Greedy Approximation with Explicit Feature Maps from Multiple Kernels

abstract: Humans have a remarkable capacity to understand the physical dynamics of objects in their environment, flexibly capturing complex structures and interactions at multiple levels of detail. Inspired by this ability, we propose a hierarchical particle-based object representation that covers a wide variety of types of three-dimensional objects, including both arbitrary rigid geometrical shapes and deformable materials. We then describe the Hierarchical Relation Network (HRN), an end-to-end differentiable neural network based on hierarchical graph convolution, that learns to predict physical dynamics in this representation. Compared to other neural network baselines, the HRN accurately handles complex collisions and nonrigid deformations, generating plausible dynamics predictions at long time scales in novel settings, and scaling to large scene configurations. These results demonstrate an architecture with the potential to form the basis of next-generation physics predictors for use in computer vision, robotics, and quantitative cognitive science.
