paragraphs: Predicting physical behavior requires representing both an object's structure and its interactions with other objects. This paper proposes a hierarchical particle representation that accommodates a broad range of three-dimensional objects. The representation covers rigid objects with arbitrary geometry as well as deformable materials, allowing different kinds of physical structure to share a common framework.

The authors pair this representation with the Hierarchical Relation Network, or HRN. It uses graph convolution across the hierarchy to learn physical dynamics and is differentiable from end to end. The representation and network are connected design choices: the hierarchy organizes the objects, while the network learns relationships within that organization to predict their behavior.

Compared with other neural network baselines, HRN handles complex collisions and nonrigid deformation accurately in the reported results. It also produces plausible long-term predictions in new settings and scales to large scene configurations. These findings support the architecture's potential as a foundation for future physics predictors in vision, robotics, and cognitive science; the proposed applications are possibilities motivated by the demonstrated predictive behavior.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical particle representation and graph network predict collisions and deformations across varied three-dimensional objects and scenes.

title: Flexible neural representation for physics prediction

abstract: Natural gradient descent has proven very effective at mitigating the catastrophic effects of pathological curvature in the objective function, but little is known theoretically about its convergence properties, especially for \emph{non-linear} networks. In this work, we analyze for the first time the speed of convergence to global optimum for natural gradient descent on non-linear neural networks with the squared error loss. We identify two conditions which guarantee the global convergence: (1) the Jacobian matrix (of network's output for all training cases w.r.t the parameters) is full row rank and (2) the Jacobian matrix is stable for small perturbations around the initialization. For two-layer ReLU neural networks (i.e. with one hidden layer), we prove that these two conditions do hold throughout the training under the assumptions that the inputs do not degenerate and the network is over-parameterized. We further extend our analysis to more general loss function with similar convergence property. Lastly, we show that K-FAC, an approximate natural gradient descent method, also converges to global minima under the same assumptions.

paragraphs: Natural gradient descent can help optimization when the objective has difficult curvature, but its convergence in nonlinear neural networks has been less understood. This paper analyzes convergence to a global optimum for nonlinear networks trained with squared error, providing conditions under which that behavior is guaranteed.

The two conditions concern the network’s Jacobian, which describes how outputs on the training examples change with the parameters. It must have full row rank and remain stable under small perturbations around initialization. The authors prove that both conditions hold throughout training for two-layer ReLU networks under assumptions of nondegenerate inputs and sufficient overparameterization.

The analysis also extends to more general loss functions with similar convergence behavior. Additionally, the authors establish global-minimum convergence for K-FAC, an approximate natural gradient method, under the same assumptions. The significance is a theoretical connection between network structure, local output sensitivity, and successful optimization. These are conditional guarantees, rather than claims that natural gradient or K-FAC globally solves every neural-network training problem.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sufficient Jacobian conditions for global convergence of natural gradient and proves relevant guarantees for overparameterized two-layer ReLU networks.

title: Fast Convergence of Natural Gradient Descent for Over-Parameterized Neural Networks

abstract: Semantic image synthesis aims at generating photorealistic images from semantic layouts. Previous approaches with conditional generative adversarial networks (GAN) show state-of-the-art performance on this task, which either feed the semantic label maps as inputs to the generator, or use them to modulate the activations in normalization layers via affine transformations. We argue that convolutional kernels in the generator should be aware of the distinct semantic labels at different locations when generating images. In order to better exploit the semantic layout for the image generator, we propose to predict convolutional kernels conditioned on the semantic label map to generate the intermediate feature maps from the noise maps and eventually generate the images. Moreover, we propose a feature pyramid semantics-embedding discriminator, which is more effective in enhancing fine details and semantic alignments between the generated images and the input semantic layouts than previous multi-scale discriminators. We achieve state-of-the-art results on both quantitative metrics and subjective evaluation on various semantic segmentation datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Semantic image synthesis turns a layout of labeled regions into a photorealistic image. The layout specifies what belongs at each location, and the generator must turn that spatial information into image content. This paper argues that the generator's convolutional kernels should themselves depend on the semantic labels they are processing.

The proposed approach predicts convolutional kernels from the semantic label map. Those kernels transform noise maps into intermediate features and ultimately into an image. This makes the operations that construct the image responsive to the layout, extending conditioning beyond supplying labels as inputs or using them to adjust normalized activations.

The authors also introduce a discriminator that embeds semantic information in a feature pyramid. They report that it improves fine detail and alignment between generated images and input layouts compared with previous multi-scale discriminators. Across several semantic segmentation datasets, the overall approach achieves state-of-the-art quantitative and subjective evaluation results. The findings support conditioning both image construction and image assessment more directly on the requested semantic structure.
summary.tldr: Predicting convolutional kernels from semantic layouts improves image synthesis, supported by a discriminator designed for detail and semantic alignment.

title: Learning to Predict Layout-to-image Conditional Convolutions for Semantic Image Synthesis

abstract: Inspired by recent work in attention models for image captioning and question answering, we present a soft attention model for the reinforcement learning domain. This model bottlenecks the view of an agent by a soft, top-down attention mechanism, forcing the agent to focus on task-relevant information by sequentially querying its view of the environment. The output of the attention mechanism allows direct observation of the information used by the agent to select its actions, enabling easier interpretation of this model than of traditional models. We analyze the different strategies the agents learn and show that a handful of strategies arise repeatedly across different games. We also show that the model learns to query separately about space and content ( where'' vs. what''). We demonstrate that an agent using this mechanism can achieve performance competitive with state-of-the-art models on ATARI tasks while still being interpretable.

This model bottlenecks the view of an agent by a soft, top-down attention mechanism, forcing the agent to focus on task-relevant information by sequentially querying its view of the environment. The output of the attention mechanism allows direct observation of the information used by the agent to select its actions, enabling easier interpretation of this model than of traditional models. paragraphs: Understanding a reinforcement-learning agent is easier when its use of visual information is visible. This paper introduces a soft attention mechanism that restricts the agent's view through successive, task-directed queries. Inspired by attention in image captioning and question answering, the design makes selective information gathering part of how the agent chooses actions.

The attention output exposes the information being used for action selection, giving researchers a more direct way to inspect behavior than traditional models provide. The authors analyze the strategies that emerge and find a small set recurring across different games. They also observe that the model learns to ask separately about spatial location and content, corresponding to where something is and what it is.

On Atari tasks, an agent using this mechanism achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art models while retaining the proposed interpretability benefit. The result shows that the attention bottleneck can coexist with strong task performance. Its explanatory value comes specifically from observing the agent's information selection and recurring query strategies, making those aspects of its decision process easier to examine.
summary.tldr: A soft attention bottleneck reveals what reinforcement-learning agents query while preserving competitive Atari performance.

title: Towards Interpretable Reinforcement Learning Using Attention Augmented Agents

abstract: Curriculum reinforcement learning (CRL) improves the learning speed and stability of an agent by exposing it to a tailored series of tasks throughout learning. Despite empirical successes, an open question in CRL is how to automatically generate a curriculum for a given reinforcement learning (RL) agent, avoiding manual design. In this paper, we propose an answer by interpreting the curriculum generation as an inference problem, where distributions over tasks are progressively learned to approach the target task. This approach leads to an automatic curriculum generation, whose pace is controlled by the agent, with solid theoretical motivation and easily integrated with deep RL algorithms. In the conducted experiments, the curricula generated with the proposed algorithm significantly improve learning performance across several environments and deep RL algorithms, matching or outperforming state-of-the-art existing CRL algorithms.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning curriculum changes the tasks an agent encounters during training to support learning speed and stability. Designing that progression by hand is difficult. This paper proposes an automatic method that makes curriculum generation depend on the learner, allowing the pace of progression to reflect the agent being trained.

The approach treats curriculum construction as an inference problem. It progressively learns distributions over tasks that move toward the target task. The object being adapted is therefore the distribution of training experiences across tasks. The authors give this formulation a theoretical motivation and describe it as easy to integrate with deep reinforcement learning algorithms.

In experiments spanning several environments and deep reinforcement learning methods, the generated curricula significantly improve learning performance. They match or outperform existing state-of-the-art curriculum methods in those comparisons. The results support automatically adapting the sequence of training tasks as a useful component of deep reinforcement learning, with the agent's progress controlling how quickly the curriculum approaches its target.
summary.tldr: An inference-based curriculum gradually adapts task distributions toward the target at a pace controlled by the reinforcement learning agent.

title: Self-Paced Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose an estimator and confidence interval for computing the value of a policy from off-policy data in the contextual bandit setting. To this end we apply empirical likelihood techniques to formulate our estimator and confidence interval as simple convex optimization problems. Using the lower bound of our confidence interval, we then propose an off-policy policy optimization algorithm that searches for policies with large reward lower bound. We empirically find that both our estimator and confidence interval improve over previous proposals in finite sample regimes. Finally, the policy optimization algorithm we propose outperforms a strong baseline system for learning from off-policy data.

To this end we apply empirical likelihood techniques to formulate our estimator and confidence interval as simple convex optimization problems. Using the lower bound of our confidence interval, we then propose an off-policy policy optimization algorithm that searches for policies with large reward lower bound. We empirically find that both our estimator and confidence interval improve over previous proposals in finite sample regimes. Finally, the policy optimization algorithm we propose outperforms a strong baseline system for learning from off-policy data.

paragraphs: In contextual bandits, a policy chooses actions based on the current context. Off-policy evaluation asks how well a policy would perform using data gathered under a different policy. This paper addresses both estimating that value and expressing uncertainty about the estimate, so that existing data can also guide the search for better policies.

The authors apply empirical likelihood to construct a policy-value estimator and a confidence interval. Both are formulated as simple convex optimization problems. They then use the interval's lower endpoint as the objective for policy optimization, searching for policies with high reward lower bounds. This makes uncertainty part of the selection criterion instead of relying only on a point estimate.

Empirically, the estimator and confidence interval improve over earlier proposals when data are finite. The resulting policy-learning algorithm also outperforms a strong off-policy learning baseline. The contribution ties evaluation and optimization together: the same uncertainty-aware framework both assesses a candidate policy and supplies the quantity used to search for promising alternatives.
summary.tldr: Empirical likelihood supports policy-value estimation, confidence intervals, and policy learning that maximizes a reward lower bound from off-policy data.

title: Empirical Likelihood for Contextual Bandits

abstract: In continual learning (CL), a learner is faced with a sequence of tasks, arriving one after the other, and the goal is to remember all the tasks once the continual learning experience is finished. The prior art in CL uses episodic memory, parameter regularization or extensible network structures to reduce interference among tasks, but in the end, all the approaches learn different tasks in a joint vector space. We believe this invariably leads to interference among different tasks. We propose to learn tasks in different (low-rank) vector subspaces that are kept orthogonal to each other in order to minimize interference. Further, to keep the gradients of different tasks coming from these subspaces orthogonal to each other, we learn isometric mappings by posing network training as an optimization problem over the Stiefel manifold. To the best of our understanding, we report, for the first time, strong results over experience-replay baseline with and without memory on standard classification benchmarks in continual learning.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to learn tasks one after another while retaining what it learned previously. The authors argue that placing different tasks in a shared vector space creates interference, even when methods use stored examples, parameter penalties, or expanding networks to reduce forgetting. Their proposal changes the geometry in which tasks are represented.

Each task is learned in a separate low-rank subspace, and these subspaces are kept orthogonal to one another. The aim is to reduce interference by separating the directions associated with different tasks. The method also learns isometric mappings so that gradients coming from those subspaces remain orthogonal. It formulates network training as optimization over the Stiefel manifold to impose this geometric structure.

The authors report strong results relative to an experience-replay baseline on standard continual-learning classification benchmarks, including settings with and without memory. These findings support orthogonal task representations as a useful approach to reducing interference. The stated goal is to minimize interference while preserving learning across the task sequence.
summary.tldr: The method separates sequential tasks into low-rank orthogonal subspaces and preserves gradient orthogonality to reduce interference.

title: Continual Learning in Low-rank Orthogonal Subspaces

abstract: We propose a new methodology to design first-order methods for unconstrained strongly convex problems. Specifically, instead of tackling the original objective directly, we construct a shifted objective function that has the same minimizer as the original objective and encodes both the smoothness and strong convexity of the original objective in an interpolation condition. We then propose an algorithmic template for tackling the shifted objective, which can exploit such a condition. Following this template, we derive several new accelerated schemes for problems that are equipped with various first-order oracles and show that the interpolation condition allows us to vastly simplify and tighten the analysis of the derived methods. In particular, all the derived methods have faster worst-case convergence rates than their existing counterparts. Experiments on machine learning tasks are conducted to evaluate the new methods.

paragraphs: This paper presents a way to design faster optimization algorithms for unconstrained, strongly convex problems. Its starting point is to change the objective being optimized while preserving its minimizer. Because the location of the best solution remains the same, progress on the transformed problem can still serve the original optimization goal.

The shifted objective expresses the original function’s smoothness and strong convexity through an interpolation condition. The authors construct an algorithmic template that explicitly exploits this condition. From that template, they derive several accelerated methods for settings with different first-order oracles, meaning different forms of access to first-order information about the objective.

For every derived method, the authors establish a faster worst-case convergence rate than the corresponding existing method. They also report that the interpolation condition makes the analysis both simpler and tighter, and evaluate the methods on machine learning tasks. The main contribution is therefore a reusable design principle: restructuring an objective can expose useful mathematical properties without changing the solution being sought.
summary.tldr: Shifting an objective without changing its minimizer yields accelerated first-order methods with improved worst-case convergence guarantees.

title: Boosting First-Order Methods by Shifting Objective: New Schemes with Faster Worst-Case Rates

abstract: Verifiable training is a promising research direction for training a robust network. However, most verifiable training methods are slow or lack scalability. In this study, we propose a fast and scalable certifiable training algorithm based on Lipschitz analysis and interval arithmetic. Our certifiable training algorithm provides a tight propagated outer bound by introducing the box constraint propagation (BCP), and it efficiently computes the worst logit over the outer bound. In the experiments, we show that BCP achieves a tighter outer bound than the global Lipschitz-based outer bound. Moreover, our certifiable training algorithm is over 12 times faster than the state-of-the-art dual relaxation-based method; however, it achieves comparable or better verification performance, improving natural accuracy. Our fast certifiable training algorithm with the tight outer bound can scale to Tiny ImageNet with verification accuracy of 20.1\% ($\ell_2$-perturbation of $\epsilon=36/255$). Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/sungyoon-lee/bcp}.

paragraphs: Certifiable training aims to produce networks whose robustness can be verified, but existing approaches can be slow or difficult to scale. This paper develops a training algorithm combining Lipschitz analysis with interval arithmetic. Its central device is box constraint propagation, or BCP, which produces a tight outer bound during propagation through the network.

The algorithm efficiently computes the worst logit over this outer bound, making the bound useful during training. Experiments find that BCP gives a tighter bound than the global Lipschitz-based alternative. A tighter bound matters because the certification calculation depends on the set of possibilities enclosed by that bound.

The authors report training more than twelve times faster than the state-of-the-art dual relaxation-based method considered, with comparable or better verification performance and improved natural accuracy. They also scale to Tiny ImageNet, obtaining 20.1% verification accuracy for an l2 perturbation radius of 36/255. These results connect the proposed bounding procedure to both computational efficiency and demonstrated certification performance.
summary.tldr: Box constraint propagation enables faster certifiable training with tighter bounds and competitive verification performance in the reported experiments.

title: Lipschitz-Certifiable Training with a Tight Outer Bound

abstract: Shapley values provide model agnostic feature attributions for model outcome at a particular instance by simulating feature absence under a global population distribution. The use of a global population can lead to potentially misleading results when local model behaviour is of interest. Hence we consider the formulation of neighbourhood reference distributions that improve the local interpretability of Shapley values. By doing so, we find that the Nadaraya-Watson estimator, a well-studied kernel regressor, can be expressed as a self-normalised importance sampling estimator. Empirically, we observe that Neighbourhood Shapley values identify meaningful sparse feature relevance attributions that provide insight into local model behaviour, complimenting conventional Shapley analysis. They also increase on-manifold explainability and robustness to the construction of adversarial classifiers.

The use of a global population can lead to potentially misleading results when local model behaviour is of interest. Hence we consider the formulation of neighbourhood reference distributions that improve the local interpretability of Shapley values. By doing so, we find that the Nadaraya-Watson estimator, a well-studied kernel regressor, can be expressed as a self-normalised importance sampling estimator. paragraphs: A feature attribution explains how individual inputs contribute to a model’s prediction for one example. Shapley-based explanations simulate missing features using a reference population. This paper points out that using a global population can produce potentially misleading explanations when the question concerns how the model behaves near the particular example.

The authors formulate neighborhood reference distributions to make Shapley explanations more locally interpretable. The reference distribution matters because it determines the comparisons used to assign importance to features. In developing this approach, they also show that the Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression estimator can be written as a self-normalized importance sampling estimator.

Empirically, the resulting Neighbourhood Shapley values identify meaningful, sparse feature attributions that illuminate local model behavior and complement conventional Shapley analysis. The experiments also show improved on-manifold explainability and robustness against the construction of adversarial classifiers. These findings make locality a property of the explanation’s reference distribution, rather than assuming that an explanation is local simply because it describes one prediction. They support using neighborhood-based comparisons when local behavior is the object of interest.
summary.tldr: Neighbourhood Shapley values use local reference distributions to provide empirically more informative and robust explanations of nearby model behavior.

title: On Locality of Local Explanation Models

abstract: Bayesian optimization is a sample-efficient black-box optimization procedure that is typically applied to a small number of independent objectives. However, in practice we often wish to optimize objectives defined over many correlated outcomes (or “tasks”). For example, scientists may want to optimize the coverage of a cell tower network across a dense grid of locations. Similarly, engineers may seek to balance the performance of a robot across dozens of different environments via constrained or robust optimization. However, the Gaussian Process (GP) models typically used as probabilistic surrogates for multi-task Bayesian optimization scale poorly with the number of outcomes, greatly limiting applicability. We devise an efficient technique for exact multi-task GP sampling that combines exploiting Kronecker structure in the covariance matrices with Matheron’s identity, allowing us to perform Bayesian optimization using exact multi-task GP models with tens of thousands of correlated outputs. In doing so, we achieve substantial improvements in sample efficiency compared to existing approaches that model solely the outcome metrics. We demonstrate how this unlocks a new class of applications for Bayesian optimization across a range of tasks in science and engineering, including optimizing interference patterns of an optical interferometer with 65,000 outputs.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good settings while limiting expensive evaluations. Its objectives can depend on many correlated outcomes, such as network coverage at many locations or robot performance across environments. Modeling those outcomes individually can provide useful information, but the multi-task Gaussian processes commonly used for this purpose scale poorly as the number of outputs grows.

The paper develops an efficient method for exact sampling from multi-task Gaussian processes. It combines structured covariance matrices, specifically Kronecker structure, with Matheron's identity. This enables Bayesian optimization with exact multi-task models containing tens of thousands of correlated outputs, making much larger output spaces computationally accessible.

The authors report substantial gains in sample efficiency over approaches that model only the outcome metrics. This means the richer output model helps the optimization procedure make more effective use of evaluations in the studied tasks. Demonstrations span science and engineering, including optimization of an optical interferometer's interference patterns with 65,000 outputs. The contribution concerns high-dimensional outcomes, which are the many measurements returned by an evaluation.
summary.tldr: Efficient exact multi-task Gaussian-process sampling enables Bayesian optimization over tens of thousands of correlated outputs with improved sample efficiency.

title: Bayesian Optimization with High-Dimensional Outputs

abstract: Training multiple deep neural networks (DNNs) and averaging their outputs is a simple way to improve the predictive performance. Nevertheless, the multiplied training cost prevents this ensemble method to be practical and efficient. Several recent works attempt to save and ensemble the checkpoints of DNNs, which only requires the same computational cost as training a single network. However, these methods suffer from either marginal accuracy improvements due to the low diversity of checkpoints or high risk of divergence due to the cyclical learning rates they adopted. In this paper, we propose a novel method to ensemble the checkpoints, where a boosting scheme is utilized to accelerate model convergence and maximize the checkpoint diversity. We theoretically prove that it converges by reducing exponential loss. The empirical evaluation also indicates our proposed ensemble outperforms single model and existing ensembles in terms of accuracy and efficiency. With the same training budget, our method achieves 4.16% lower error on Cifar-100 and 6.96% on Tiny-ImageNet with ResNet-110 architecture. Moreover, the adaptive sample weights in our method make it an effective solution to address the imbalanced class distribution. In the experiments, it yields up to 5.02% higher accuracy over single EfficientNet-B0 on the imbalanced datasets.

paragraphs: Combining several neural networks can improve predictions, but training each network separately multiplies the cost. An alternative is to combine checkpoints saved during one training run. The difficulty is making those checkpoints different enough to contribute useful information. Earlier approaches can produce only small accuracy gains or introduce a risk of training divergence through cyclical learning rates.

This paper uses a boosting scheme to build a checkpoint ensemble, aiming to accelerate convergence while increasing checkpoint diversity. The method also assigns adaptive weights to training examples. The authors prove convergence through a reduction in exponential loss, connecting the ensemble construction to a specific mathematical training objective.

Experiments report better accuracy and efficiency than single models and existing ensembles. With the same training budget, the method achieves reported error reductions of 4.16% on Cifar-100 and 6.96% on Tiny-ImageNet using ResNet-110. Adaptive sample weighting also helps with class imbalance: experiments show accuracy gains of up to 5.02% over a single EfficientNet-B0 on imbalanced datasets.
summary.tldr: A boosting scheme turns saved neural-network checkpoints into a more diverse ensemble, improving accuracy within the same training budget in reported experiments.

title: Boost Neural Networks by Checkpoints

abstract: The problem of (point) forecasting univariate time series is considered. Most approaches, ranging from traditional statistical methods to recent learning-based techniques with neural networks, directly operate on raw time series observations. As an extension, we study whether local topological properties, as captured via persistent homology, can serve as a reliable signal that provides complementary information for learning to forecast. To this end, we propose topological attention, which allows attending to local topological features within a time horizon of historical data. Our approach easily integrates into existing end-to-end trainable forecasting models, such as N-BEATS, and, in combination with the latter exhibits state-of-the-art performance on the large-scale M4 benchmark dataset of 100,000 diverse time series from different domains. Ablation experiments, as well as a comparison to recent techniques in a setting where only a single time series is available for training, corroborate the beneficial nature of including local topological information through an attention mechanism.

paragraphs: The paper studies point forecasting for a single time series, where the goal is to predict future values from historical observations. It asks whether local topological structure can provide useful information alongside the raw measurements. Persistent homology supplies these topological features, giving the forecasting model another description of patterns in its recent history.

The proposed topological attention mechanism lets a model attend to local topological features within a historical time window. It can be integrated into existing forecasting architectures and trained end to end. This makes topology an additional signal that the forecasting system can use selectively as part of its prediction process.

Combined with N-BEATS, the approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on M4, a benchmark containing 100,000 diverse time series. Ablation experiments and comparisons in a setting with only one time series available for training also support the benefit of including these features through attention. The evidence therefore links the added structural information to improved forecasts in several evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Topological attention adds local persistent-homology features to forecasting models and achieves state-of-the-art M4 results when combined with N-BEATS.

title: Topological Attention for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: For different parameterizations (mappings from parameters to predictors), we study the regularization cost in predictor space induced by $l_2$ regularization on the parameters (weights). We focus on linear neural networks as parameterizations of linear predictors. We identify the representation cost of certain sparse linear ConvNets and residual networks. In order to get a better understanding of how the architecture and parameterization affect the representation cost, we also study the reverse problem, identifying which regularizers on linear predictors (e.g., $l_p$ norms, group norms, the $k$-support-norm, elastic net) can be the representation cost induced by simple $l_2$ regularization, and designing the parameterizations that do so.
originalAbstract: For different parameterizations (mappings from parameters to predictors), we study the regularization cost in predictor space induced by $l_2$ regularization on the parameters (weights). We focus on linear neural networks as parameterizations of linear predictors. We identify the representation cost of certain sparse linear ConvNets and residual networks. In order to get a better understanding of how the architecture and parameterization affect the representation cost, we also study the reverse problem, identifying which regularizers on linear predictors (e.g., $l_p$ norms, group norms, the $k$-support-norm, elastic net) can be the representation cost induced by simple $l_2$ regularization, and designing the parameterizations that do so.

paragraphs: A penalty on network weights also influences which predictors are inexpensive for the network to represent. This paper studies that relationship for linear neural networks, where the mapping from parameters to a linear predictor depends on the architecture. Its central object is representation cost: the regularization cost in predictor space induced by an l2 penalty on the underlying weights.

The authors identify these costs for certain sparse linear convolutional networks and residual networks. This analysis separates the form of the weight penalty from its effect on the represented predictor. Even when training uses the same simple l2 regularization, different parameterizations can translate that penalty into different preferences over linear predictors.

The paper also reverses the question by asking which desired predictor-space regularizers can arise through a suitable parameterization. It considers examples including lp norms, group norms, the k-support norm, and elastic net, and designs parameterizations that induce such costs. This turns representation-cost analysis into a design tool: architecture can be chosen partly for the regularization effect it creates under a simple weight penalty.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes how linear-network parameterizations turn l2 weight penalties into predictor regularizers and designs parameterizations for desired costs.

title: Representation Costs of Linear Neural Networks: Analysis and Design

abstract: The machine learning (ML) toolbox for estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects from observational data is expanding rapidly, yet many of its algorithms have been evaluated only on a very limited set of semi-synthetic benchmark datasets. In this paper, we investigate current benchmarking practices for ML-based conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimators, with special focus on empirical evaluation based on the popular semi-synthetic IHDP benchmark. We identify problems with current practice and highlight that semi-synthetic benchmark datasets, which (unlike real-world benchmarks used elsewhere in ML) do not necessarily reflect properties of real data, can systematically favor some algorithms over others -- a fact that is rarely acknowledged but of immense relevance for interpretation of empirical results. Further, we argue that current evaluation metrics evaluate performance only for a small subset of possible use cases of CATE estimators, and discuss alternative metrics relevant for applications in personalized medicine. Additionally, we discuss alternatives for current benchmark datasets, and implications of our findings for benchmarking in CATE estimation.

paragraphs: Conditional average treatment effect estimation studies how treatment effects differ across groups characterized by observed information. Many machine-learning methods for this problem have been tested on only a narrow set of semi-synthetic datasets. This paper examines what those evaluations establish, focusing particularly on the widely used IHDP benchmark.

The authors argue that semi-synthetic datasets do not necessarily preserve the properties of real data and can systematically favor some algorithms. Consequently, a strong result may partly reflect how a benchmark was constructed. This matters for interpreting empirical rankings because success under a particular generated setup does not by itself establish suitability across real applications.

The paper also questions whether commonly used metrics cover the purposes for which treatment-effect estimates are needed. The authors argue that current metrics address only a small subset of possible uses and discuss alternatives relevant to personalized medicine. Alongside alternative datasets, these considerations frame evaluation as a choice that should reflect both the data setting and the intended application.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how semi-synthetic benchmark design and narrow metrics can distort comparisons of treatment-effect estimators.

title: Really Doing Great at Estimating CATE? A Critical Look at ML Benchmarking Practices in Treatment Effect Estimation

abstract: In recent years, the neural stochastic differential equation (NSDE) has gained attention for modeling stochastic representations with great success in various types of applications. However, it typically loses expressivity when the data representation is manifold-valued. To address this issue, we suggest a principled method for expressing the stochastic representation with the Riemannian neural SDE (RNSDE), which extends the conventional Euclidean NSDE. Empirical results for various tasks demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms baseline methods.
originalAbstract: In recent years, the neural stochastic differential equation (NSDE) has gained attention for modeling stochastic representations with great success in various types of applications. However, it typically loses expressivity when the data representation is manifold-valued. To address this issue, we suggest a principled method for expressing the stochastic representation with the Riemannian neural SDE (RNSDE), which extends the conventional Euclidean NSDE. Empirical results for various tasks demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms baseline methods.

paragraphs: Neural stochastic differential equations model representations that evolve with randomness. The paper identifies a difficulty when those representations take values on a manifold, a space with geometric structure that need not behave like ordinary Euclidean space. In that setting, conventional neural SDEs typically lose expressive power.

The proposed Riemannian neural SDE extends the conventional Euclidean formulation to express stochastic representations on manifolds. The central design choice is to make the geometry of the representation space part of the modeling framework. This directly addresses the mismatch identified by the authors between a manifold-valued representation and the usual Euclidean model.

Empirical evaluations across various tasks show significant improvements over the baseline methods. These results support the proposed extension as a way to model stochastic representations more effectively when their geometry matters. The contribution concerns the combination of randomness and manifold structure: the model retains the neural SDE approach while extending the space in which its representations are expressed. The reported performance gains provide empirical support for that geometric adaptation.
summary.tldr: Riemannian neural SDEs extend stochastic representation learning to manifolds and significantly outperform compared baselines in the reported tasks.

title: Riemannian Neural SDE: Learning Stochastic Representations on Manifolds

abstract: Symmetry has been a fundamental tool in the exploration of a broad range of complex systems. In machine learning, symmetry has been explored in both models and data. In this paper we seek to connect the symmetries arising from the architecture of a family of models with the symmetries of that family’s internal representation of data. We do this by calculating a set of fundamental symmetry groups, which we call the intertwiner groups of the model. Each of these arises from a particular nonlinear layer of the model and different nonlinearities result in different symmetry groups. These groups change the weights of a model in such a way that the underlying function that the model represents remains constant but the internal representations of data inside the model may change. We connect intertwiner groups to a model’s internal representations of data through a range of experiments that probe similarities between hidden states across models with the same architecture. Our work suggests that the symmetries of a network are propagated into the symmetries in that network’s representation of data, providing us with a better understanding of how architecture affects the learning and prediction process. Finally, we speculate that for ReLU networks, the intertwiner groups may provide a justification for the common practice of concentrating model interpretability exploration on the activation basis in hidden layers rather than arbitrary linear combinations thereof.

paragraphs: A neural network’s weights can sometimes change while the function it computes stays the same. Its internal representations may nevertheless change. This paper investigates how such architectural symmetries relate to the ways networks represent data, connecting properties of the model’s construction with similarities and differences in its hidden states.

The authors calculate symmetry groups called intertwiner groups. Each arises from a particular nonlinear layer, and different nonlinearities produce different groups. These groups describe weight transformations that preserve the network’s overall function. They therefore provide a structured way to study changes inside a network that leave its input-output behavior intact.

Experiments compare hidden representations across models with the same architecture. The results suggest that network symmetries carry through into symmetries of the learned representations, clarifying how architecture influences internal organization. For ReLU networks, the authors further speculate that intertwiner groups may help justify interpreting individual activation directions instead of arbitrary linear combinations. That interpretability connection is presented as a possible explanation rather than an established conclusion.
summary.tldr: Intertwiner groups connect function-preserving neural-network symmetries with the organization of internal representations.

title: On the Symmetries of Deep Learning Models and their Internal Representations

abstract: We consider a high-dimensional mean estimation problem over a binary hidden Markov model, which illuminates the interplay between memory in data, sample size, dimension, and signal strength in statistical inference. In this model, an estimator observes $n$ samples of a $d$-dimensional parameter vector $\theta_{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, multiplied by a random sign $ S_i $ ($1\le i\le n$), and corrupted by isotropic standard Gaussian noise. The sequence of signs $\{S_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}\in\{-1,1\}^{n}$ is drawn from a stationary homogeneous Markov chain with flip probability $\delta\in[0,1/2]$. As $\delta$ varies, this model smoothly interpolates two well-studied models: the Gaussian Location Model for which $\delta=0$ and the Gaussian Mixture Model for which $\delta=1/2$. Assuming that the estimator knows $\delta$, we establish a nearly minimax optimal (up to logarithmic factors) estimation error rate, as a function of $\|\theta_{*}\|,\delta,d,n$. We then provide an upper bound to the case of estimating $\delta$, assuming a (possibly inaccurate) knowledge of $\theta_{*}$. The bound is proved to be tight when $\theta_{*}$ is an accurately known constant. These results are then combined to an algorithm which estimates $\theta_{*}$ with $\delta$ unknown a priori, and theoretical guarantees on its error are stated.
originalAbstract: We consider a high-dimensional mean estimation problem over a binary hidden Markov model, which illuminates the interplay between memory in data, sample size, dimension, and signal strength in statistical inference. In this model, an estimator observes $n$ samples of a $d$-dimensional parameter vector $\theta_{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, multiplied by a random sign $ S_i $ ($1\le i\le n$), and corrupted by isotropic standard Gaussian noise. The sequence of signs $\{S_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}\in\{-1,1\}^{n}$ is drawn from a stationary homogeneous Markov chain with flip probability $\delta\in[0,1/2]$. As $\delta$ varies, this model smoothly interpolates two well-studied models: the Gaussian Location Model for which $\delta=0$ and the Gaussian Mixture Model for which $\delta=1/2$. Assuming that the estimator knows $\delta$, we establish a nearly minimax optimal (up to logarithmic factors) estimation error rate, as a function of $\|\theta_{*}\|,\delta,d,n$. We then provide an upper bound to the case of estimating $\delta$, assuming a (possibly inaccurate) knowledge of $\theta_{*}$. The bound is proved to be tight when $\theta_{*}$ is an accurately known constant. These results are then combined to an algorithm which estimates $\theta_{*}$ with $\delta$ unknown a priori, and theoretical guarantees on its error are stated.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimation from noisy observations of a high-dimensional vector whose sign changes over time. Each observation contains the vector multiplied by a hidden positive or negative sign, plus standard isotropic Gaussian noise. The signs follow a stationary Markov chain, so the probability of flipping controls how much memory the data contains.

When the flip probability is zero, the model becomes a Gaussian location model; at one half, it becomes a Gaussian mixture model. Assuming the flip probability is known, the authors establish an estimation error rate that is nearly minimax optimal, up to logarithmic factors. The rate accounts jointly for signal strength, flip probability, dimension, and sample size.

The authors then study estimating the flip probability when the vector is known only approximately. Their bound is tight when that vector is an accurately known constant. Finally, they combine these results into an algorithm that estimates the vector without knowing the flip probability in advance, with theoretical error guarantees. The analysis clarifies how temporal dependence interacts with the other quantities governing statistical estimation.
summary.tldr: The paper derives near-optimal mean-estimation rates with known Markov sign-flip probability and develops guarantees when that probability is unknown.

title: Mean Estimation in High-Dimensional Binary Markov Gaussian Mixture Models

abstract: We consider the problem of partial identification, the estimation of bounds on the treatment effects from observational data. Although studied using discrete treatment variables or in specific causal graphs (e.g., instrumental variables), partial identification has been recently explored using tools from deep generative modeling. We propose a new method for partial identification of average treatment effects (ATEs) in general causal graphs using implicit generative models comprising continuous and discrete random variables. Since ATE with continuous treatment is generally non-regular, we leverage the partial derivatives of response functions to define a regular approximation of ATE, a quantity we call uniform average treatment derivative (UATD). We prove that our algorithm converges to tight bounds on ATE in linear structural causal models (SCMs). For nonlinear SCMs, we empirically show that using UATD leads to tighter and more stable bounds than methods that directly optimize the ATE.

This paper develops a method for bounding average treatment effects in general causal graphs using implicit generative models that can contain both continuous and discrete variables.

The authors address this by defining a regular approximation from partial derivatives of response functions. They call this quantity the uniform average treatment derivative, or UATD. It provides an alternative target for optimization while retaining a connection to the treatment-effect question.

For linear structural causal models, the authors prove that their algorithm converges to tight bounds on average treatment effects. For nonlinear models, the evidence is empirical: optimizing with UATD produces tighter and more stable bounds than directly optimizing the average treatment effect. The paper thus combines a guarantee for the linear setting with an experimentally supported strategy for handling the more difficult nonlinear case.
summary.tldr: Implicit generative models and a derivative-based treatment-effect approximation enable tight linear-case bounds and more stable nonlinear-case estimates.

title: Partial Identification of Treatment Effects with Implicit Generative Models

abstract: We study what dataset assumption permits solving offline two-player zero-sum Markov games. In stark contrast to the offline single-agent Markov decision process, we show that the single strategy concentration assumption is insufficient for learning the Nash equilibrium (NE) strategy in offline two-player zero-sum Markov games. On the other hand, we propose a new assumption named unilateral concentration and design a pessimism-type algorithm that is provably efficient under this assumption. In addition, we show that the unilateral concentration assumption is necessary for learning an NE strategy. Furthermore, our algorithm can achieve minimax sample complexity without any modification for two widely studied settings: dataset with uniform concentration assumption and turn-based Markov games. Our work serves as an important initial step towards understanding offline multi-agent reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from an existing dataset rather than collect new interactions. In a two-player zero-sum Markov game, the goal considered here is learning a Nash equilibrium strategy. This paper asks what assumptions about the dataset make that goal possible, focusing on how adequately the available data covers relevant strategies.

The authors show that single strategy concentration, an assumption used in offline single-agent learning, is insufficient in this game setting. They introduce unilateral concentration and design a pessimism-type algorithm that is provably efficient under that assumption. They also establish that unilateral concentration is necessary for learning a Nash equilibrium strategy in the studied framework.

The same algorithm achieves minimax sample complexity without modification in two settings: datasets satisfying uniform concentration and turn-based Markov games. These results connect a requirement on the available data to both learnability and statistical efficiency. They clarify why an assumption adequate for a single decision-maker does not automatically carry over when learning must account for an opposing player.
summary.tldr: Unilateral concentration characterizes a necessary data condition and supports efficient offline learning of Nash strategies in two-player zero-sum Markov games.

title: When are Offline Two-Player Zero-Sum Markov Games Solvable?

abstract: Zero-cost proxies (ZC proxies) are a recent architecture performance prediction technique aiming to significantly speed up algorithms for neural architecture search (NAS). Recent work has shown that these techniques show great promise, but certain aspects, such as evaluating and exploiting their complementary strengths, are under-studied. In this work, we create NAS-Bench-Suite: we evaluate 13 ZC proxies across 28 tasks, creating by far the largest dataset (and unified codebase) for ZC proxies, enabling orders-of-magnitude faster experiments on ZC proxies, while avoiding confounding factors stemming from different implementations. To demonstrate the usefulness of NAS-Bench-Suite, we run a large-scale analysis of ZC proxies, including a bias analysis, and the first information-theoretic analysis which concludes that ZC proxies capture substantial complementary information. Motivated by these findings, we present a procedure to improve the performance of ZC proxies by reducing biases such as cell size, and we also show that incorporating all 13 ZC proxies into the surrogate models used by NAS algorithms can improve their predictive performance by up to 42%. Our code and datasets are available at https://github.com/automl/naslib/tree/zerocost.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search needs efficient ways to predict which candidate networks will perform well. Zero-cost proxies provide inexpensive performance signals, but their biases and complementary strengths have received less study. This paper creates a shared dataset and codebase to make those questions easier to investigate consistently.

The resource evaluates 13 proxies across 28 tasks. Reusing these results enables experiments that are orders of magnitude faster, while a unified implementation reduces confounding differences between codebases. The authors use the resource for a large-scale bias study and an information-theoretic analysis. The latter finds that different proxies contain substantial complementary information, making their combination potentially valuable.

Based on this analysis, the paper proposes reducing proxy biases such as those associated with cell size. It also incorporates all 13 proxies into the surrogate models used by architecture-search algorithms, reporting predictive performance improvements of up to 42%. The contribution links benchmarking infrastructure to concrete methods for obtaining more useful architecture-performance predictions.
summary.tldr: A unified benchmark of 13 zero-cost proxies across 28 tasks reveals complementary signals that can improve architecture-performance prediction.

title: NAS-Bench-Suite-Zero: Accelerating Research on Zero Cost Proxies

abstract: Personalized Federated Learning faces many challenges such as expensive communication costs, training-time adversarial attacks, and performance unfairness across devices. Recent developments witness a trade-off between a reference model and local models to achieve personalization. We follow the avenue and propose a personalized FL method towards the three goals. When it is time to communicate, our method projects local models into a shared-and-fixed low-dimensional random subspace and uses infimal convolution to control the deviation between the reference model and projected local models. We theoretically show our method converges for smooth objectives with square regularizers and the convergence dependence on the projection dimension is mild. We also illustrate the benefits of robustness and fairness on a class of linear problems. Finally, we conduct a large number of experiments to show the empirical superiority of our method over several state-of-the-art methods on the three aspects.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning must balance shared learning with the needs of individual devices. It also faces communication expense, adversarial interference during training, and uneven performance across participants. This paper develops a method aimed at improving all three aspects through the relationship between a reference model and personalized local models.

When communication occurs, the method projects local models into a low-dimensional random subspace that is shared and fixed. It uses an optimization construction called infimal convolution to control the difference between the reference model and those projected local models. The projection reduces the dimension of the communicated model representation, while the deviation control governs its connection to personalization.

The authors establish convergence for smooth objectives with square regularizers and show that its dependence on projection dimension is mild. Robustness and fairness benefits are illustrated for a class of linear problems. Extensive experiments report improvements over several state-of-the-art methods across communication efficiency, robustness, and fairness. The theoretical statements therefore have specified settings, while the experiments provide broader empirical support for the three objectives.
summary.tldr: A shared low-dimensional projection and controlled model deviation improve communication, robustness, and fairness in evaluated personalized federated learning settings.

title: Personalized Federated Learning towards Communication Efficiency, Robustness and Fairness

abstract: In this paper we study two-player bilinear zero-sum games with constrained strategy spaces. An instance of natural occurrences of such constraints is when mixed strategies are used, which correspond to a probability simplex constraint. We propose and analyze the alternating mirror descent algorithm, in which each player takes turns to take action following the mirror descent algorithm for constrained optimization. We interpret alternating mirror descent as an alternating discretization of a skew-gradient flow in the dual space, and use tools from convex optimization and modified energy function to establish an $O(K^{-2/3})$ bound on its average regret after $K$ iterations. This quantitatively verifies the algorithm's better behavior than the simultaneous version of mirror descent algorithm, which is known to diverge and yields an $O(K^{-1/2})$ average regret bound. In the special case of an unconstrained setting, our results recover the behavior of alternating gradient descent algorithm for zero-sum games which was studied in (Bailey et al., COLT 2020).

paragraphs: The paper studies two-player bilinear zero-sum games in which each player's available strategies are constrained. A natural example is a mixed strategy, whose probabilities must remain nonnegative and sum to one. The question is how players should update their strategies so that their average regret decreases efficiently while respecting these restrictions.

The authors propose alternating mirror descent: players take turns updating through a method designed for constrained optimization. They analyze these updates as a discrete version of a continuous dynamical system in a transformed, dual space. Tools from convex optimization and a modified energy function make it possible to quantify the behavior of this alternating process.

After K iterations, the analysis gives an average regret bound of order K to the power of minus two-thirds. This improves on the minus-one-half rate stated for simultaneous mirror descent, whose iterates are known to diverge. The result establishes a quantitative benefit from alternating updates in the studied games. In the unconstrained special case, the analysis also recovers previously studied behavior of alternating gradient descent.
summary.tldr: Alternating mirror descent achieves a faster average-regret guarantee than simultaneous updates in constrained bilinear zero-sum games.

title: Alternating Mirror Descent for Constrained Min-Max Games

abstract: Data hiding with deep neural networks (DNNs) has experienced impressive successes in recent years. A prevailing scheme is to train an autoencoder, consisting of an encoding network to embed (or transform) secret messages in (or into) a carrier, and a decoding network to extract the hidden messages. This scheme may suffer from several limitations regarding practicability, security, and embedding capacity. In this work, we describe a different computational framework to hide images in deep probabilistic models. Specifically, we use a DNN to model the probability density of cover images, and hide a secret image in one particular location of the learned distribution. As an instantiation, we adopt a SinGAN, a pyramid of generative adversarial networks (GANs), to learn the patch distribution of one cover image. We hide the secret image by fitting a deterministic mapping from a fixed set of noise maps (generated by an embedding key) to the secret image during patch distribution learning. The stego SinGAN, behaving as the original SinGAN, is publicly communicated; only the receiver with the embedding key is able to extract the secret image. We demonstrate the feasibility of our SinGAN approach in terms of extraction accuracy and model security. Moreover, we show the flexibility of the proposed method in terms of hiding multiple images for different receivers and obfuscating the secret image.

paragraphs: This paper proposes hiding a secret image inside a learned probabilistic model. Conventional neural approaches use an encoder to place a message into a carrier and a decoder to retrieve it. Here, the hiding location is a particular point within the distribution learned by a generative model.

The authors instantiate the idea with SinGAN, a pyramid of generative adversarial networks that learns the patch distribution of one cover image. During that learning process, they also fit a deterministic mapping from a fixed collection of noise maps to the secret image. An embedding key generates those noise maps and therefore provides the means of recovering the hidden content.

The authors demonstrate feasibility in extraction accuracy and model security. They also show that the approach can accommodate multiple secret images for different receivers and can obfuscate a secret image.
summary.tldr: A SinGAN-based framework hides images at keyed locations in a learned generative distribution and demonstrates their recovery.

title: Hiding Images in Deep Probabilistic Models

abstract: Large-scale Protein Language Models (PLMs) have improved performance in protein prediction tasks, ranging from 3D structure prediction to various function predictions. In particular, AlphaFold, a ground-breaking AI system, could potentially reshape structural biology. However, the utility of the PLM module in AlphaFold, Evoformer, has not been explored beyond structure prediction. In this paper, we investigate the representation ability of three popular PLMs: ESM-1b (single sequence), MSA-Transformer (multiple sequence alignment), and Evoformer (structural), with a special focus on Evoformer. Specifically, we aim to answer the following key questions: (1) Does the Evoformer trained as part of AlphaFold produce representations amenable to predicting protein function? (2) If yes, can Evoformer replace ESM-1b and MSA-Transformer? (3) How much do these PLMs rely on evolution-related protein data? In this regard, are they complementary to each other? We compare these models by empirical study along with new insights and conclusions. All code and datasets for reproducibility are available at https://github.com/elttaes/Revisiting-PLMs .

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether representations learned by protein language models are useful for predicting protein function. Its particular focus is Evoformer, the component trained within AlphaFold for structure prediction. The motivating question is whether a representation developed for structural reasoning also contains information that can support a different kind of biological prediction.

The empirical comparison covers three models with different relationships to protein information: ESM-1b operates on single sequences, MSA-Transformer uses multiple sequence alignments, and Evoformer is associated with structural prediction. The study asks whether Evoformer’s representations support function prediction and, if so, whether they could replace the other two models. It also examines dependence on evolution-related protein data.

A further question is whether the models provide complementary information, which matters when deciding whether one representation can stand in for another. The abstract describes the comparative study and its questions but does not state which model wins or whether replacement is justified. Its supported contribution is the empirical examination of these representation choices, with code and datasets made available for reproducibility.
summary.tldr: The paper compares three protein language models to investigate Evoformer’s usefulness for function prediction and the models’ dependence on evolutionary information.

title: Exploring evolution-aware & -free protein language models as protein function predictors

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are biologically-inspired models that are capable of processing information in streams of action potentials. However, simulating and training SNNs is computationally expensive due to the need to solve large systems of coupled differential equations. In this paper, we propose a novel event-based algorithm called SparseProp for simulating and training sparse SNNs. Our algorithm reduces the computational cost of both forward pass and backward pass operations from O(N) to O(log(N)) per network spike, enabling numerically exact simulations of large spiking networks and their efficient training using backpropagation through time. By exploiting the sparsity of the network, SparseProp avoids iterating through all neurons at every spike and uses efficient state updates. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SparseProp for several classical integrate-and-fire neuron models, including simulating a sparse SNN with one million LIF neurons, which is sped up by more than four orders of magnitude compared to previous implementations. Our work provides an efficient and exact solution for training large-scale spiking neural networks and opens up new possibilities for building more sophisticated brain-inspired models.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks represent information through discrete spikes, but simulating their dynamics can require expensive calculations across many coupled neurons. SparseProp reduces this burden for sparse networks by organizing computation around spike events and exploiting the limited connections that need attention when an event occurs.

The algorithm avoids visiting every neuron after each spike and instead performs efficient state updates. It reduces the computational cost per network spike from O(N) to O(log N) for both forward and backward operations. This supports numerically exact simulation alongside training through backpropagation through time, addressing the cost of learning as well as generating network activity.

The authors demonstrate SparseProp with several classical integrate-and-fire neuron models. A simulation containing one million leaky integrate-and-fire neurons runs more than four orders of magnitude faster than previous implementations. These results show how network sparsity and event-based updates can make very large spiking systems more tractable, while preserving the numerical exactness emphasized by the method.
summary.tldr: SparseProp exploits sparse connectivity to simulate and train spiking networks with logarithmic computation per spike.

title: SparseProp: Efficient Event-Based Simulation and Training of Sparse Recurrent Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: We tackle the problem of graph out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. Existing graph OOD algorithms either rely on restricted assumptions or fail to exploit environment information in training data. In this work, we propose to simultaneously incorporate label and environment causal independence (LECI) to fully make use of label and environment information, thereby addressing the challenges faced by prior methods on identifying causal and invariant subgraphs. We further develop an adversarial training strategy to jointly optimize these two properties for casual subgraph discovery with theoretical guarantees. Extensive experiments and analysis show that LECI significantly outperforms prior methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets, establishing LECI as a practical and effective solution for graph OOD generalization.

paragraphs: Graph prediction models can struggle when the conditions encountered after training differ from those in the training data. This paper studies how to identify graph portions that capture causal, invariant information for such situations. It argues that previous methods either depend on restrictive assumptions or do not fully use available information about training environments.

LECI brings label and environment information together through two causal-independence properties. The authors develop an adversarial training strategy that optimizes these properties jointly to discover causal subgraphs. The approach gives both kinds of information an explicit role in deciding which graph structure should support predictions across changing conditions.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for its subgraph-discovery approach and evaluates it on synthetic and real-world datasets. The reported experiments and analyses show significant improvements over prior methods. These findings support the practical value of jointly using labels and environments when learning graph representations intended to generalize beyond the training distribution, alongside the theoretical motivation for the selected subgraphs.
summary.tldr: LECI jointly uses label and environment causal independence to discover subgraphs that improve graph out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Joint Learning of Label and Environment Causal Independence for Graph Out-of-Distribution Generalization

abstract: A critical yet frequently overlooked challenge in the field of deepfake detection is the lack of a standardized, unified, comprehensive benchmark. This issue leads to unfair performance comparisons and potentially misleading results. Specifically, there is a lack of uniformity in data processing pipelines, resulting in inconsistent data inputs for detection models. Additionally, there are noticeable differences in experimental settings, and evaluation strategies and metrics lack standardization. To fill this gap, we present the first comprehensive benchmark for deepfake detection, called \textit{DeepfakeBench}, which offers three key contributions: 1) a unified data management system to ensure consistent input across all detectors, 2) an integrated framework for state-of-the-art methods implementation, and 3) standardized evaluation metrics and protocols to promote transparency and reproducibility. Featuring an extensible, modular-based codebase, \textit{DeepfakeBench} contains 15 state-of-the-art detection methods, 9 deepfake datasets, a series of deepfake detection evaluation protocols and analysis tools, as well as comprehensive evaluations. Moreover, we provide new insights based on extensive analysis of these evaluations from various perspectives (\eg, data augmentations, backbones). We hope that our efforts could facilitate future research and foster innovation in this increasingly critical domain. All codes, evaluations, and analyses of our benchmark are publicly available at \url{https://github.com/SCLBD/DeepfakeBench}.

paragraphs: Comparing deepfake detectors becomes unreliable when each method receives differently processed data or is assessed under different experimental rules. A performance difference may then reflect the evaluation setup as well as the detector. DeepfakeBench addresses this problem by providing a shared framework for implementing and evaluating detection methods consistently.

The benchmark combines unified data management, integrated implementations, and standardized evaluation metrics and protocols. Its modular codebase includes 15 detection methods and nine deepfake datasets, together with evaluation procedures and analysis tools. These components make consistent inputs and comparable assessments part of the benchmark itself, supporting more transparent and reproducible comparisons.

Beyond assembling the framework, the authors conduct extensive evaluations and analyze factors including data augmentation and model backbones. The abstract reports that these analyses produce additional insights without specifying a single winning configuration. Publicly available code, evaluations, and analyses make the contribution a reusable research resource: researchers can examine detector behavior within a common experimental setting and extend that setting with further methods.
summary.tldr: DeepfakeBench standardizes data handling, detector implementations, and evaluation to make deepfake-detection comparisons more reproducible.

title: DeepfakeBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark of Deepfake Detection

abstract: Optimizer states are a major source of memory consumption for training neural networks, limiting the maximum trainable model within given memory budget. Compressing the optimizer states from 32-bit floating points to lower bitwidth is promising to reduce the training memory footprint, while the current lowest achievable bitwidth is 8-bit. In this work, we push optimizer states bitwidth down to 4-bit through a detailed empirical analysis of first and second moments. Specifically, we find that moments have complicated outlier patterns, that current block-wise quantization cannot accurately approximate. We use a smaller block size and propose to utilize both row-wise and column-wise information for better quantization. We further identify a zero point problem of quantizing the second moment, and solve this problem with a linear quantizer that excludes the zero point. Our 4-bit optimizers are evaluated on a wide variety of benchmarks including natural language understanding, machine translation, image classification, and instruction tuning. On all the tasks our optimizers can achieve comparable accuracy with their full-precision counterparts, while enjoying better memory efficiency.
originalAbstract: Optimizer states are a major source of memory consumption for training neural networks, limiting the maximum trainable model within given memory budget. Compressing the optimizer states from 32-bit floating points to lower bitwidth is promising to reduce the training memory footprint, while the current lowest achievable bitwidth is 8-bit. In this work, we push optimizer states bitwidth down to 4-bit through a detailed empirical analysis of first and second moments. Specifically, we find that moments have complicated outlier patterns, that current block-wise quantization cannot accurately approximate. We use a smaller block size and propose to utilize both row-wise and column-wise information for better quantization. We further identify a zero point problem of quantizing the second moment, and solve this problem with a linear quantizer that excludes the zero point. Our 4-bit optimizers are evaluated on a wide variety of benchmarks including natural language understanding, machine translation, image classification, and instruction tuning. On all the tasks our optimizers can achieve comparable accuracy with their full-precision counterparts, while enjoying better memory efficiency.

paragraphs: Training a neural network requires memory for optimizer states as well as model parameters. These states can consume enough space to limit the model size that fits within a memory budget. This paper reduces their representation to four bits, extending the compression beyond the eight-bit states described as the previous lowest achievable precision.

The method follows an empirical analysis of first- and second-moment statistics. The authors find complicated outlier patterns that existing block-wise quantization does not approximate accurately. They use smaller blocks and incorporate both row-wise and column-wise information to improve quantization. They also identify a problem with the zero point when quantizing second moments and address it with a linear quantizer that excludes zero.

Evaluations cover natural language understanding, machine translation, image classification, and instruction tuning. Across all evaluated tasks, the four-bit optimizers achieve accuracy comparable to full-precision counterparts while using memory more efficiently. The findings show that carefully handling the structure of optimizer statistics can enable stronger compression without the accuracy loss that a less suitable quantization scheme might introduce.
summary.tldr: Carefully designed four-bit quantization compresses optimizer states while preserving comparable accuracy across the evaluated tasks.

title: Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States

abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors oftransformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researcherschoose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find whichabstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units underinvestigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component.We automate one of the process' steps: finding the connections between the abstract neural network units that form a circuit. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. Forexample, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes theGreater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found byprevious work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery
