paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain model behavior through the internal components and connections that produce it. Prior investigations have required substantial researcher effort and intuition. This paper organizes that workflow and automates one step: finding the connections among abstract neural-network units that form a circuit for a chosen behavior.

The broader process begins with a dataset and metric that bring out the behavior of interest. Researchers then use activation patching to investigate which units participate, varying the data, metric, and units to understand their roles. The proposed algorithms operate within this investigative setup, targeting circuit connections rather than automating the entire interpretation process.

The authors validate their algorithms by reproducing earlier findings. In a GPT-2 Small circuit for a Greater-Than operation, ACDC rediscovers all five previously identified component types. It selects 68 edges from 32,000, all of which had been manually identified in prior work. This result demonstrates that automated connection discovery can recover a compact, previously studied mechanism for a specified behavior.
summary.tldr: Circuit-discovery algorithms automate finding behavior-relevant connections and recover previously identified components of a GPT-2 Small circuit.

title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability

abstract: Neuro-symbolic AI bridges the gap between purely symbolic and neural approaches to learning. This often requires maximizing the likelihood of a symbolic constraint w.r.t the neural network's output distribution. Such output distributions are typically assumed to be fully-factorized. This limits the applicability of neuro-symbolic learning to the more expressive auto-regressive distributions, e.g., transformers. Under such distributions, computing the likelihood of even simple constraints is #P-hard. Instead of attempting to enforce the constraint on the entire likelihood distribution, we propose to do so on a random, local approximation thereof. More precisely, we approximate the likelihood of the constraint with the pseudolikelihood of the constraint centered around a model sample. Our approach is factorizable, allowing us to reuse solutions to sub-problems---a main tenet for the efficient computation of neuro-symbolic losses. It also provides a local, high fidelity approximation of the likelihood: it exhibits low entropy and KL-divergence around the model sample. We tested our approach on Sudoku and shortest-path prediction cast as auto-regressive generation, and observe that we greatly improve upon the base model's ability to predict logically-consistent outputs. We also tested our approach on the task of detoxifying large language models. We observe that using a simple constraint disallowing a list of toxic words, we are able to steer the model's outputs away from toxic generations, achieving SoTA compared to previous approaches.

paragraphs: Logical rules can help neural models produce valid answers, but incorporating those rules into training becomes difficult when outputs depend on earlier outputs. Autoregressive models have exactly this dependence. The paper explains that calculating the probability of even simple constraints under such models is computationally hard, making direct constraint-based training difficult.

The proposed pseudo-semantic loss replaces that global calculation with a local approximation around an output sampled from the model. It uses the constraint's pseudolikelihood, with a factorization that allows intermediate computations to be reused. The authors also characterize the approximation as locally faithful, reporting low entropy and KL divergence around the sampled output.

On Sudoku and shortest-path generation, the approach substantially improves the base model's ability to produce logically consistent answers. For language-model detoxification, a constraint excluding specified toxic words steers generation away from toxic outputs and achieves reported state-of-the-art results against previous approaches. These findings show that local constraint approximations can provide useful training signals for expressive autoregressive models without calculating the full constraint probability.
summary.tldr: A local approximation makes logical-constraint training practical for autoregressive models and improves consistency and detoxification in the reported experiments.

title: A Pseudo-Semantic Loss for Autoregressive Models with Logical Constraints

abstract: Contextual decision-making problems have witnessed extensive applications in various fields such as online content recommendation, personalized healthcare, and autonomous vehicles, where a core practical challenge is to select a suitable surrogate model for capturing unknown complicated reward functions. It is often the case that both high approximation accuracy and explicit uncertainty quantification are desired. In this work, we propose a neural network-accompanied Gaussian process (NN-AGP) model, which leverages neural networks to approximate the unknown and potentially complicated reward function regarding the contextual variable, and maintains a Gaussian process surrogate model with respect to the decision variable. Our model is shown to outperform existing approaches by offering better approximation accuracy thanks to the use of neural networks and possessing explicit uncertainty quantification from the Gaussian process. We also analyze the maximum information gain of the NN-AGP model and prove regret bounds for the corresponding algorithms. Moreover, we conduct experiments on both synthetic and practical problems, illustrating the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Contextual decision-making requires selecting an action using information about the current situation. A model must capture how rewards depend on that context and the decision, often while expressing uncertainty about its predictions. This paper addresses the difficulty of obtaining accurate approximation and explicit uncertainty estimates within the same surrogate model.

The proposed neural network-accompanied Gaussian process, or NN-AGP, assigns complementary roles to two model types. Neural networks approximate potentially complicated dependence on contextual variables. A Gaussian process models the decision variable and supplies explicit uncertainty quantification. This division is the central design choice: the contextual component provides expressive approximation, while the decision component retains Gaussian-process uncertainty.

The authors analyze the model's maximum information gain and prove regret bounds for the associated algorithms. They also report improved approximation compared with existing approaches and evaluate effectiveness on synthetic and practical problems. The contribution therefore combines a modeling strategy with theoretical analysis and empirical evidence, supporting its use for decisions where both reward prediction and uncertainty matter.
summary.tldr: NN-AGP combines neural modeling of context with Gaussian-process modeling of decisions to support accurate reward prediction and explicit uncertainty estimates.

title: Contextual Gaussian Process Bandits with Neural Networks

abstract: The challenge of replicating research results has posed a significant impediment to the field of molecular biology. The advent of modern intelligent systems has led to notable progress in various domains. Consequently, we embarked on an investigation of intelligent monitoring systems as a means of tackling the issue of the reproducibility crisis. Specifically, we first curate a comprehensive multimodal dataset, named ProBio, as an initial step towards this objective. This dataset comprises fine-grained hierarchical annotations intended for the purpose of studying activity understanding in BioLab. Next, we devise two challenging benchmarks, transparent solution tracking and multimodal action recognition, to emphasize the unique characteristics and difficulties associated with activity understanding in BioLab settings. Finally, we provide a thorough experimental evaluation of contemporary video understanding models and highlight their limitations in this specialized domain to identify potential avenues for future research. We hope \dataset with associated benchmarks may garner increased focus on modern AI techniques in the realm of molecular biology.

paragraphs: This paper introduces ProBio as an initial step toward intelligent monitoring of molecular biology experiments. Its motivation is the difficulty of reproducing research results. To study how automated systems might understand laboratory activity, the authors create a multimodal dataset with detailed annotations organized into a hierarchy of activities.

The dataset supports two benchmarks tailored to laboratory work: tracking transparent solutions and recognizing actions using multiple modalities. These tasks emphasize that understanding a biology experiment involves challenges specific to the setting. The hierarchical annotations give researchers a structured basis for studying laboratory activity at a fine level of detail, while the benchmarks define concrete problems on which systems can be evaluated.

The authors evaluate contemporary video-understanding models and identify limitations in their performance in this specialized domain. The contribution is a research resource and an assessment of current capabilities, presented as groundwork for monitoring systems. It does not establish that automated monitoring has solved reproducibility problems. Instead, the findings identify laboratory activity understanding as an area where existing video methods need further development.
summary.tldr: ProBio supplies annotated laboratory data and two benchmarks to study activity understanding as groundwork for intelligent experiment monitoring.

title: ProBio: A Protocol-guided Multimodal Dataset for Molecular Biology Lab

abstract: Lifelong learning offers a promising paradigm of building a generalist agent that learns and adapts over its lifespan. Unlike traditional lifelong learning problems in image and text domains, which primarily involve the transfer of declarative knowledge of entities and concepts, lifelong learning in decision-making (LLDM) also necessitates the transfer of procedural knowledge, such as actions and behaviors. To advance research in LLDM, we introduce LIBERO, a novel benchmark of lifelong learning for robot manipulation. Specifically, LIBERO highlights five key research topics in LLDM: 1) how to efficiently transfer declarative knowledge, procedural knowledge, or the mixture of both; 2) how to design effective policy architectures and 3) effective algorithms for LLDM; 4) the robustness of a lifelong learner with respect to task ordering; and 5) the effect of model pretraining for LLDM. We develop an extendible procedural generation pipeline that can in principle generate infinitely many tasks. For benchmarking purpose, we create four task suites (130 tasks in total) that we use to investigate the above-mentioned research topics. To support sample-efficient learning, we provide high-quality human-teleoperated demonstration data for all tasks. Our extensive experiments present several insightful or even unexpected discoveries: sequential finetuning outperforms existing lifelong learning methods in forward transfer, no single visual encoder architecture excels at all types of knowledge transfer, and naive supervised pretraining can hinder agents' performance in the subsequent LLDM.

paragraphs: A robot learning over its lifetime must transfer knowledge about objects and concepts as well as knowledge about actions and behaviors. LIBERO provides a robot-manipulation benchmark for studying both kinds of transfer. It examines how learning earlier tasks affects the ability to acquire later ones.

The benchmark includes four task suites containing 130 tasks, with human-teleoperated demonstrations for every task. An extensible procedural generation pipeline can, in principle, produce infinitely many tasks. The suites support investigations of knowledge transfer, policy architectures, learning algorithms, sensitivity to task order, and the effects of pretraining. Demonstrations help support learning with limited task experience.

The experiments reveal that sequential fine-tuning outperforms the evaluated lifelong learning methods in forward transfer. They also find that no single visual encoder is best for every kind of knowledge transfer, and that naive supervised pretraining can hurt later lifelong decision-making performance. These findings show why choices that appear beneficial in isolation need evaluation across task sequences and different forms of robot knowledge.
summary.tldr: LIBERO benchmarks lifelong robot learning across 130 tasks and reveals that transfer depends on architecture, training strategy, and pretraining choices.

title: LIBERO: Benchmarking Knowledge Transfer for Lifelong Robot Learning

abstract: A key theme in the past decade has been that when large neural networks and large datasets combine they can produce remarkable results. In deep reinforcement learning (RL), this paradigm is commonly made possible through experience replay, whereby a dataset of past experiences is used to train a policy or value function. However, unlike in supervised or self-supervised learning, an RL agent has to collect its own data, which is often limited. Thus, it is challenging to reap the benefits of deep learning, and even small neural networks can overfit at the start of training. In this work, we leverage the tremendous recent progress in generative modeling and propose Synthetic Experience Replay (SynthER), a diffusion-based approach to flexibly upsample an agent's collected experience. We show that SynthER is an effective method for training RL agents across offline and online settings, in both proprioceptive and pixel-based environments. In offline settings, we observe drastic improvements when upsampling small offline datasets and see that additional synthetic data also allows us to effectively train larger networks. Furthermore, SynthER enables online agents to train with a much higher update-to-data ratio than before, leading to a significant increase in sample efficiency, without any algorithmic changes. We believe that synthetic training data could open the door to realizing the full potential of deep learning for replay-based RL algorithms from limited data. Finally, we open-source our code at https://github.com/conglu1997/SynthER.

paragraphs: Experience replay trains reinforcement learning agents using stored interactions, but the agent must first collect those interactions. Limited experience can make even small networks overfit, particularly early in learning. SynthER addresses this shortage by using a diffusion model to generate additional synthetic experience from the agent's collected data.

The method expands the training data available to replay-based learning. The authors evaluate it in both offline settings, where learning uses an existing dataset, and online settings, where agents continue collecting experience. Their evaluations cover environments with proprioceptive observations as well as environments represented through pixels, testing the approach across different forms of input.

For small offline datasets, synthetic expansion produces large reported improvements and allows larger networks to be trained effectively. Online agents can perform many more learning updates relative to the amount of newly collected data, improving sample efficiency without changes to the underlying learning algorithm. These findings support synthetic replay as a way to make more use of limited real experience and to support greater model capacity in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SynthER uses diffusion-generated experience to improve replay-based reinforcement learning from limited collected data.

title: Synthetic Experience Replay

abstract: As larger deep learning models are hard to interpret, there has been a recent focus on generating explanations of these black-box models. In contrast, we may have apriori explanations of how models should behave. In this paper, we formalize this notion as learning from explanation constraints and provide a learning theoretic framework to analyze how such explanations can improve the learning of our models. One may naturally ask, "When would these explanations be helpful?"Our first key contribution addresses this question via a class of models that satisfies these explanation constraints in expectation over new data. We provide a characterization of the benefits of these models (in terms of the reduction of their Rademacher complexities) for a canonical class of explanations given by gradient information in the settings of both linear models and two layer neural networks. In addition, we provide an algorithmic solution for our framework, via a variational approximation that achieves better performance and satisfies these constraints more frequently, when compared to simpler augmented Lagrangian methods to incorporate these explanations. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach over a large array of synthetic and real-world experiments.

paragraphs: Explanations are often generated after a model has learned its predictions. This paper instead considers prior knowledge about how a model should behave and turns that knowledge into constraints during learning. The goal is to understand when such explanation constraints can improve learning, as well as how to enforce them.

The theoretical framework considers model classes that satisfy the constraints in expectation over new data. For explanations expressed through gradient information, the authors characterize reductions in Rademacher complexity for linear models and two-layer neural networks. This measures how restricting acceptable behavior changes the flexibility of the model class and helps analyze the learning benefits of those restrictions.

The paper also develops an algorithm using a variational approximation. Across synthetic and real-world experiments, it achieves better performance and satisfies the explanation constraints more frequently than simpler augmented Lagrangian approaches. The expectation-based definition does not require every individual prediction to satisfy a constraint. Together, the theory and experiments connect prior explanations to both a more restricted learning problem and a practical training method.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes learning from prior explanation constraints and develops a variational method that improves performance and constraint satisfaction in experiments.

title: Learning with Explanation Constraints

abstract: In this work, we address 3D novel class discovery (NCD) that discovers novel classes from an unlabeled dataset by leveraging the knowledge of disjoint known classes. The key challenge of 3D NCD is that learned features by known class recognition are heavily biased and hinder generalization to novel classes. Since geometric parts are more generalizable across different classes, we propose to decompose novel into known parts, coined DNIK, to mitigate the above problems. DNIK learns a part concept bank encoding rich part geometric patterns from known classes so that novel 3D shapes can be represented as part concept compositions to facilitate cross-category generalization. Moreover, we formulate three constraints on part concepts to ensure diverse part concepts without collapsing. A part relation encoding module (PRE) is also developed to leverage part-wise spatial relations for better recognition. We construct three 3D NCD tasks for evaluation and extensive experiments show that our method achieves significantly superior results than SOTA baselines (+11.7%, +14.1%, and +16.3% improvements on average for three tasks, respectively). Code and data will be released.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to discover previously unseen categories of 3D objects in unlabeled data using knowledge learned from different, labeled categories. Features trained to recognize known categories can be too closely tied to those categories. The authors instead focus on geometric parts, which can recur across objects belonging to otherwise different classes.

Their method, DNIK, learns a bank of part concepts from known classes and represents unfamiliar shapes as combinations of those concepts. Three constraints encourage the bank to contain diverse concepts rather than collapse into repetitive representations. A separate part relation module incorporates spatial relationships, allowing recognition to use both the parts present and how those parts are arranged.

The authors construct three evaluation tasks and report average improvements of 11.7%, 14.1%, and 16.3% over state-of-the-art baselines on those tasks. These findings support parts as a useful basis for transferring knowledge across categories. The central contribution is a representation that makes unfamiliar whole objects describable through reusable geometric components.
summary.tldr: DNIK discovers unfamiliar 3D object categories by representing shapes through reusable part concepts and their spatial relationships.

title: Decompose Novel into Known: Part Concept Learning For 3D Novel Class Discovery

abstract: Finding an approximate second-order stationary point (SOSP) is a well-studied and fundamental problem in stochastic nonconvex optimization with many applications in machine learning.However, this problem is poorly understood in the presence of outliers, limiting the use of existing nonconvex algorithms in adversarial settings.In this paper, we study the problem of finding SOSPs in the strong contamination model, where a constant fraction of datapoints are arbitrarily corrupted.We introduce a general framework for efficiently finding an approximate SOSP with \emph{dimension-independent} accuracy guarantees, using $\widetilde{O}({D^2}/{\epsilon})$ samples where $D$ is the ambient dimension and $\epsilon$ is the fraction of corrupted datapoints.As a concrete application of our framework, we apply it to the problem of low rank matrix sensing, developing efficient and provably robust algorithms that can tolerate corruptions in both the sensing matrices and the measurements.In addition, we establish a Statistical Query lower bound providing evidence that the quadratic dependence on $D$ in the sample complexity is necessary for computationally efficient algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies nonconvex optimization when some data points have been arbitrarily corrupted. The target is an approximate second-order stationary point, a solution characterized by both its gradient and curvature. Such points are widely studied with ordinary stochastic data, but adversarial outliers make reliable optimization substantially harder.

The authors propose a general efficient framework under strong contamination, where a constant fraction of data can be corrupted. Its accuracy guarantee does not depend on ambient dimension. Its sample requirement does: it uses roughly D squared divided by epsilon samples, suppressing logarithmic factors, where D is the ambient dimension and epsilon is the corruption fraction.

Applied to low-rank matrix sensing, the framework yields provably robust algorithms that tolerate corruption in both sensing matrices and measurements. A Statistical Query lower bound supplies evidence that quadratic dependence on dimension in the sample requirement is necessary for computationally efficient methods. The distinction matters: dimension-independent accuracy does not imply dimension-independent data requirements, and the lower-bound evidence is tied to a particular computational framework.
summary.tldr: A robust optimization framework finds approximate second-order stationary points with dimension-independent accuracy despite arbitrary data corruption.

title: Robust Second-Order Nonconvex Optimization and Its Application to Low Rank Matrix Sensing

abstract: The emergence of foundation models in Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing have resulted in immense progress on downstream tasks. This progress was enabled by datasets with billions of training examples. Similar benefits are yet to be unlocked for quantum chemistry, where the potential of deep learning is constrained by comparatively small datasets with 100k to 20M training examples. These datasets are limited in size because the labels are computed using the accurate (but computationally demanding) predictions of Density Functional Theory (DFT). Notably, prior DFT datasets were created using CPU supercomputers without leveraging hardware acceleration. In this paper, we take a first step towards utilising hardware accelerators by introducing the data generator PySCF$_{\text{IPU}}$ using Intelligence Processing Units (IPUs). This allows us to create the dataset QM1B with one billion training examples containing 9-11 heavy atoms. We demonstrate that a simple baseline neural network (SchNet 9M) improves its performance by simply increasing the amount of training data without additional inductive biases. To encourage future researchers to use QM1B responsibly, we highlight several limitations of QM1B and emphasise the low resolution of our DFT options, which also serves as motivation for even larger, more accurate datasets.

paragraphs: Large training collections have helped drive progress in vision and language, but quantum chemistry datasets face an expensive labeling process. Their targets are often calculated using density functional theory, or DFT. This paper addresses that computational bottleneck by introducing PySCF_IPU, a data generator that uses Intelligence Processing Units to accelerate dataset creation.

The resulting QM1B dataset contains one billion training examples with 9–11 heavy atoms. The authors contrast this scale with existing datasets containing roughly 100,000 to 20 million examples and describe accelerator use as a first step beyond earlier CPU-supercomputer-based generation. They also test whether simply providing more data benefits a neural predictor without adding new inductive biases.

Their SchNet 9M baseline improves as the amount of training data increases. This supports the value of scale for the tested model, while the authors explicitly emphasize limitations of QM1B, especially the low resolution of its DFT choices. The dataset therefore demonstrates expanded data generation capacity while motivating future collections that combine greater scale with more accurate labels.
summary.tldr: PySCF_IPU enables the billion-example QM1B chemistry dataset, demonstrating benefits from more training data while highlighting low-resolution DFT labels.

title: Generating QM1B with PySCF$_{\text{IPU}}$

abstract: Imitation Learning (IL) is a widely used framework for learning imitative behavior from demonstrations. It is especially appealing for solving complex real-world tasks where handcrafting reward function is difficult, or when the goal is to mimic human expert behavior. However, the learned imitative policy can only follow the behavior in the demonstration. When applying the imitative policy, we may need to customize the policy behavior to meet different requirements coming from diverse downstream tasks. Meanwhile, we still want the customized policy to maintain its imitative nature. To this end, we formulate a new problem setting called policy customization. It defines the learning task as training a policy that inherits the characteristics of the prior policy while satisfying some additional requirements imposed by a target downstream task. We propose a novel and principled approach to interpret and determine the trade-off between the two task objectives. Specifically, we formulate the customization problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) with a reward function that combines 1) the inherent reward of the demonstration; and 2) the add-on reward specified by the downstream task. We propose a novel framework, Residual Q-learning, which can solve the formulated MDP by leveraging the prior policy without knowing the inherent reward or value function of the prior policy. We derive a family of residual Q-learning algorithms that can realize offline and online policy customization, and show that the proposed algorithms can effectively accomplish policy customization tasks in various environments. Demo videos and code are available on our website: https://sites.google.com/view/residualq-learning.

This paper formalizes that goal as policy customization: learning a policy that inherits properties of a prior policy and accommodates additional task objectives.

The authors express customization as a Markov decision process whose reward combines the demonstration's inherent reward with an added downstream reward. The challenge is that the prior policy's inherent reward and value function may be unknown.

Residual Q-learning solves the formulated problem by using the prior policy without requiring either of those unknown quantities. The framework yields a family of algorithms for customization using offline data or online interaction. Results across various environments show effective customization. The contribution is a way to adapt an existing imitative policy through a combined objective even when the reward underlying its original behavior is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Residual Q-learning customizes an imitative policy for new requirements without knowing its original reward or value function.

title: Residual Q-Learning: Offline and Online Policy Customization without Value

abstract: Algebraic varieties are the geometric shapes defined by systems of polynomial equations; they are ubiquitous across mathematics and science. Amongst these algebraic varieties are Q-Fano varieties: positively curved shapes which have Q-factorial terminal singularities. Q-Fano varieties are of fundamental importance in geometry as they are `atomic pieces’ of more complex shapes – the process of breaking a shape into simpler pieces in this sense is called the Minimal Model Programme.Despite their importance, the classification of Q-Fano varieties remains unknown. In this paper we demonstrate that machine learning can be used to understand this classification. We focus on eight-dimensional positively-curved algebraic varieties that have toric symmetry and Picard rank two, and develop a neural network classifier that predicts with 95% accuracy whether or not such an algebraic variety is Q-Fano. We use this to give a first sketch of the landscape of Q-Fano varieties in dimension eight.How the neural network is able to detect Q-Fano varieties with such accuracy remains mysterious, and hints at some deep mathematical theory waiting to be uncovered. Furthermore, when visualised using the quantum period, an invariant that has played an important role in recent theoretical developments, we observe that the classification as revealed by ML appears to fall within a bounded region, and is stratified by the Fano index. This suggests that it may be possible to state and prove conjectures on completeness in the future.Inspired by the ML analysis, we formulate and prove a new global combinatorial criterion for a positively curved toric variety of Picard rank two to have terminal singularities. Together with the first sketch of the landscape of Q-Fano varieties in higher dimensions, this gives strong new evidence that machine learning can be an essential tool in developing mathematical conjectures and accelerating theoretical discovery.

paragraphs: Algebraic varieties are geometric shapes specified by polynomial equations. This paper investigates how machine learning can help map part of that classification and inspire new mathematics.

title: Machine learning detects terminal singularities

abstract: Graph learning from signals is a core task in graph signal processing (GSP). A significant subclass of graph signals called the stationary graph signals that broadens the concept of stationarity of data defined on regular domains to signals on graphs is gaining increasing popularity in the GSP community. The most commonly used model to learn graphs from these stationary signals is SpecT, which forms the foundation for nearly all the subsequent, more advanced models. Despite its strengths, the practical formulation of the model, known as rSpecT, has been identified to be susceptible to the choice of hyperparameters. More critically, it may suffer from infeasibility as an optimization problem. In this paper, we introduce the first condition that ensures the infeasibility of rSpecT and design a novel model called LogSpecT, along with its practical formulation rLogSpecT to overcome this issue. Contrary to rSpecT, our novel practical model rLogSpecT is always feasible. Furthermore, we provide recovery guarantees of rLogSpecT from modern optimization tools related to epi-convergence, which could be of independent interest and significant for various learning problems. To demonstrate the practical advantages of rLogSpecT, a highly efficient algorithm based on the linearized alternating direction method of multipliers (L-ADMM) that allows closed-form solutions for each subproblem is proposed with convergence guarantees. Extensive numerical results on both synthetic and real networks not only corroborate the stability of our proposed methods, but also highlight their comparable and even superior performance than existing models.

paragraphs: Graph learning from signals tries to recover network structure from observations associated with its nodes. This paper focuses on stationary graph signals and a widely used learning formulation called SpecT. Its practical version, rSpecT, can be sensitive to hyperparameters and may become infeasible, meaning no solution satisfies its optimization constraints.

The authors establish a condition sufficient to make rSpecT infeasible and introduce LogSpecT with a practical version called rLogSpecT. The new practical formulation is always feasible. They also provide recovery guarantees using epi-convergence, connecting the behavior of optimization problems to the recovery of the graph. Feasibility and recovery are distinct contributions: having an admissible solution is the foundation for studying what that solution recovers.

To solve the new problem efficiently, the paper develops a linearized alternating-direction algorithm whose subproblems have closed-form solutions and proves convergence guarantees. Numerical studies on synthetic and real networks support the method's stability and show performance comparable to, and sometimes better than, existing models. The approach therefore addresses both a formulation-level failure and practical computation.
summary.tldr: LogSpecT replaces a potentially infeasible graph-learning formulation with an always-feasible practical model, recovery guarantees, and an efficient convergent solver.

title: LogSpecT: Feasible Graph Learning Model from Stationary Signals with Recovery Guarantees

abstract: We consider the problem of federated offline reinforcement learning (RL), a scenario under which distributed learning agents must collaboratively learn a high-quality control policy only using small pre-collected datasets generated according to different unknown behavior policies. Na\"{i}vely combining a standard offline RL approach with a standard federated learning approach to solve this problem can lead to poorly performing policies. In response, we develop the Federated Ensemble-Directed Offline Reinforcement Learning Algorithm (FEDORA), which distills the collective wisdom of the clients using an ensemble learning approach. We develop the FEDORA codebase to utilize distributed compute resources on a federated learning platform. We show that FEDORA significantly outperforms other approaches, including offline RL over the combined data pool, in various complex continuous control environments and real-world datasets. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of FEDORA in the real-world on a mobile robot. We provide our code and a video of our experiments at \url{https://github.com/DesikRengarajan/FEDORA}.

paragraphs: Federated offline reinforcement learning asks distributed agents to learn a shared control policy using only their existing datasets. Here, each dataset is small and was produced by a different, unknown behavior policy. The paper observes that simply combining a conventional offline learning method with a conventional federated learning method can produce weak policies.

FEDORA addresses this setting through ensemble learning. It draws together knowledge from the participating clients and distills that collective information into policy learning. The authors also implement the method on a federated learning platform so that it can use distributed computing resources. The central design choice is to explicitly combine client knowledge through an ensemble in this offline setting.

Experiments on complex continuous control environments and real-world datasets report substantial improvements over competing approaches, including offline learning on the pooled data. The paper also demonstrates FEDORA on a physical mobile robot. These findings suggest that how information from different behavior datasets is combined matters: pooling all recordings is not necessarily the strongest approach in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: FEDORA combines distributed offline learning through an ensemble and outperforms alternatives, including pooled-data learning, in the reported evaluations.

title: Federated Ensemble-Directed Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce a fairness-aware dataset for job recommendation in advertising, designed to foster research in algorithmic fairness within real-world scenarios. It was collected and prepared to comply with privacy standards and business confidentiality. An additional challenge is the lack of access to protected user attributes such as gender, for which we propose a pragmatic solution to obtain a proxy estimate. Despite being anonymized and including a proxy for a sensitive attribute, our dataset preserves predictive power and maintains a realistic and challenging benchmark. This dataset addresses a significant gap in the availability of fairness-focused resources for high-impact domains like advertising -- the actual impact being having access or not to precious employment opportunities, where balancing fairness and utility is a common industrial challenge. We also explore various stages in the advertising process where unfairness can occur and introduce a method to compute a fair utility metric for the job recommendations in online systems case from a biased dataset. Experimental evaluations of bias mitigation techniques on the released dataset demonstrate potential improvements in fairness and the associated trade-offs with utility.The dataset is hosted at https://huggingface.co/datasets/criteo/FairJob. Source code for the experiments is hosted at https://github.com/criteo-research/FairJob-dataset/.

paragraphs: Job advertising affects which people encounter employment opportunities, making fairness a consequential part of recommendation quality. FairJob supplies a real-world dataset for studying that problem. It was collected and prepared with privacy standards and business confidentiality in mind, addressing a shortage of fairness-focused data for this application.

A practical obstacle is the absence of protected user attributes such as gender. The authors propose a proxy estimate and incorporate it into the anonymized dataset. They report that the resulting data retain predictive power and provide a realistic, challenging benchmark. The sensitive-attribute information is therefore estimated, an important feature of how fairness can be studied using this resource.

The paper also examines stages of advertising where unfairness can arise and introduces a way to calculate a fair utility metric from biased data. Experiments apply bias mitigation techniques to the released dataset, demonstrating potential fairness improvements and accompanying utility trade-offs. The resource connects fairness evaluation to the practical constraints of online job recommendation.
summary.tldr: FairJob provides anonymized job-advertising data, a sensitive-attribute proxy, and evaluation methods for studying fairness and utility trade-offs.

title: FairJob: A Real-World Dataset for Fairness in Online Systems

abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) for specific tasks usually involves fine-tuning through reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) on preference data. While these data often come from diverse labelers' groups (e.g., different demographics, ethnicities, company teams, etc.), traditional RLHF approaches adopt a "one-size-fits-all" approach, i.e., they indiscriminately assume and optimize a single preference model, thus not being robust to unique characteristics and needs of the various groups. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Group Robust Preference Optimization (GRPO) method to align LLMs to individual groups' preferences robustly. Our approach builds upon reward-free direct preference optimization methods, but unlike previous approaches, it seeks a robust policy which maximizes the worst-case group performance. To achieve this, GRPO adaptively and sequentially weights the importance of different groups, prioritizing groups with worse cumulative loss. We theoretically study the feasibility of GRPO and analyze its convergence for the log-linear policy class. By fine-tuning LLMs with GRPO using diverse group-based global opinion data, we significantly improved performance for the worst-performing groups, reduced loss imbalances across groups, and improved probability accuracies compared to non-robust baselines.

paragraphs: Preference feedback can come from groups with different needs and judgments. Combining all those judgments into a single preference model can obscure how poorly a language model serves particular groups. This paper proposes Group Robust Preference Optimization, or GRPO, to account explicitly for group differences during preference-based fine-tuning.

GRPO builds on direct preference optimization methods that do not require a separate reward model. Its objective is to improve worst-case group performance. During training, it repeatedly adjusts the weights assigned to groups, placing more emphasis on those with worse cumulative loss. This makes underperforming groups influence subsequent learning more strongly instead of treating all feedback through one undifferentiated objective.

The authors study feasibility and convergence for the log-linear policy class. They also fine-tune language models using global opinion data organized by group. Compared with non-robust baselines, the experiments show significant improvements for the worst-performing groups, smaller loss disparities, and better probability accuracies. These results support the value of making group-level performance an explicit optimization target.
summary.tldr: GRPO adaptively emphasizes poorly served groups during direct preference training, improving worst-group performance in the reported experiments.

title: Group Robust Preference Optimization in Reward-free RLHF

abstract: Visual foundation models have achieved remarkable results in zero-shot image classification and segmentation, but zero-shot change detection remains an open problem. In this paper, we propose the segment any change models (AnyChange), a new type of change detection model that supports zero-shot prediction and generalization on unseen change types and data distributions.AnyChange is built on the segment anything model (SAM) via our training-free adaptation method, bitemporal latent matching.By revealing and exploiting intra-image and inter-image semantic similarities in SAM's latent space, bitemporal latent matching endows SAM with zero-shot change detection capabilities in a training-free way. We also propose a point query mechanism to enable AnyChange's zero-shot object-centric change detection capability.We perform extensive experiments to confirm the effectiveness of AnyChange for zero-shot change detection.AnyChange sets a new record on the SECOND benchmark for unsupervised change detection, exceeding the previous SOTA by up to 4.4\% F$_1$ score, and achieving comparable accuracy with negligible manual annotations (1 pixel per image) for supervised change detection. Code is available at https://github.com/Z-Zheng/pytorch-change-models.

paragraphs: Detecting what changed between images is a different challenge from identifying objects within a single image. This paper introduces AnyChange, which adapts the Segment Anything Model to change detection without additional training. The goal is zero-shot prediction that can extend to unseen kinds of change and unfamiliar data distributions.

The adaptation method, bitemporal latent matching, uses semantic similarities within each image and between images in SAM's internal representation space. Those relationships give the model a basis for detecting changes across the two times. A point-query mechanism also allows object-centered change detection, making it possible to direct the comparison toward an object of interest.

Experiments support the approach's effectiveness for zero-shot change detection. On SECOND, the authors report a new unsupervised result exceeding the previous state of the art by up to 4.4% in F1 score. They also report accuracy comparable to supervised change detection with one annotated pixel per image, showing the usefulness of very limited user guidance in their evaluation.
summary.tldr: AnyChange adapts SAM without training to detect changes between images, with optional point queries for object-centered comparisons.

title: Segment Any Change

abstract: This paper demonstrates that pre-trained language models (PLMs) are strong foundation models for on-device meteorological variable modeling. We present LM-Weather, a generic approach to taming PLMs, that have learned massive sequential knowledge from the universe of natural language databases, to acquire an immediate capability to obtain highly customized models for heterogeneous meteorological data on devices while keeping high efficiency. Concretely, we introduce a lightweight personalized adapter into PLMs and endows it with weather pattern awareness. During communication between clients and the server, low-rank-based transmission is performed to effectively fuse the global knowledge among devices while maintaining high communication efficiency and ensuring privacy. Experiments on real-wold dataset show that LM-Weather outperforms the state-of-the-art results by a large margin across various tasks (e.g., forecasting and imputation at different scales). We provide extensive and in-depth analyses experiments, which verify that LM-Weather can (1) indeed leverage sequential knowledge from natural language to accurately handle meteorological sequence, (2) allows each devices obtain highly customized models under significant heterogeneity, and (3) generalize under data-limited and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios.

paragraphs: LM-Weather investigates whether the sequence knowledge learned by pretrained language models can support meteorological modeling on devices. The challenge is to adapt that knowledge to weather measurements while accommodating substantial differences between devices' data. The paper presents a generic approach for building efficient, customized models from a shared language-model foundation.

A lightweight personalized adapter introduces awareness of weather patterns into the pretrained model. Devices and a server exchange information using low-rank transmission, which the authors describe as enabling communication-efficient global knowledge sharing while maintaining privacy. The design combines local customization with access to information learned across devices.

Experiments on real-world data report large improvements over state-of-the-art results for tasks including forecasting and filling in missing measurements at different scales. Further analyses support transfer of language-derived sequential knowledge, personalization under strong data heterogeneity, and generalization with limited data or out-of-distribution inputs. These findings make pretrained language models a promising foundation for the evaluated meteorological sequence tasks, with lightweight adaptation connecting shared knowledge to local conditions.
summary.tldr: LM-Weather adapts pretrained language models to device-specific weather sequences through lightweight personalization and efficient knowledge sharing.

title: Personalized Adapter for Large Meteorology Model on Devices: Towards Weather Foundation Models

abstract: The advent of large vision-language models (LVLMs) has spurred research into their applications in multi-modal contexts, particularly in video understanding. Traditional VideoQA benchmarks, despite providing quantitative metrics, often fail to encompass the full spectrum of video content and inadequately assess models' temporal comprehension. To address these limitations, we introduce MMBench-Video, a quantitative benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate LVLMs' proficiency in video understanding. MMBench-Video incorporates lengthy videos from YouTube and employs free-form questions, mirroring practical use cases. The benchmark is meticulously crafted to probe the models' temporal reasoning skills, with all questions human-annotated according to a carefully constructed ability taxonomy.We employ GPT-4 for automated assessment, demonstrating superior accuracy and robustness over earlier LLM-based evaluations. Utilizing MMBench-Video, we have conducted comprehensive evaluations that include both proprietary and open-source LVLMs for images and videos. MMBench-Video stands as a valuable resource for the research community, facilitating improved evaluation of LVLMs and catalyzing progress in the field of video understanding.

paragraphs: MMBench-Video evaluates how well large vision-language models understand lengthy videos containing multiple shots. The paper argues that existing video question-answering benchmarks do not adequately cover video content or assess temporal understanding. Its benchmark uses long YouTube videos and free-form questions to create an evaluation closer to practical video-understanding tasks.

The questions are human-annotated according to a deliberately constructed taxonomy of abilities, with particular attention to temporal reasoning. This organizes the benchmark around the skills being tested, rather than relying solely on an overall question-answering score. The free-form format allows models to produce answers without choosing from a fixed list.

The authors use GPT-4 for automated assessment and report greater accuracy and robustness than earlier language-model-based evaluation approaches. They evaluate both proprietary and open-source vision-language models, including models for images and videos. The contribution combines an evaluation dataset, an ability structure, and an assessment procedure to make broader video comprehension more systematically measurable.
summary.tldr: MMBench-Video tests long-video understanding and temporal reasoning through human-annotated free-form questions and automated assessment.

title: MMBench-Video: A Long-Form Multi-Shot Benchmark for Holistic Video Understanding

abstract: Knowledge Distillation is the mechanism by which the insights gained from a larger teacher model are transferred to a smaller student model. However, the transfer suffers when the teacher model is significantly larger than the student. To overcome this, prior works have proposed training intermediately sized models, Teacher Assistants (TAs) to help the transfer process. However, training TAs is expensive, as training these models is a knowledge transfer task in itself. Further, these TAs are larger than the student model and training them especially in large data settings can be computationally intensive. In this paper, we propose a novel framework called Controlled Information Flow for Knowledge Distillation (CIFD) consisting of two components. First, we propose a significantly smaller alternatives to TAs, the Rate-Distortion Module (RDM) which uses the teacher's penultimate layer embedding and a information rate-constrained bottleneck layer to replace the Teacher Assistant model. RDMs are smaller and easier to train than TAs, especially in large data regimes, since they operate on the teacher embeddings and do not need to relearn low level input feature extractors. Also, by varying the information rate across the bottleneck, RDMs can replace TAs of different sizes. Secondly, we propose the use of Information Bottleneck Module in the student model, which is crucial for regularization in the presence of a large number of RDMs. We show comprehensive state-of-the-art results of the proposed method over large datasets like Imagenet. Further, we show the significant improvement in distilling CLIP like models over a huge 12M image-text dataset. It outperforms CLIP specialized distillation methods across five zero-shot classification datasets and two zero-shot image-text retrieval datasets.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers information from a large teacher model to a smaller student, but a large capacity gap can make that transfer difficult. Intermediate teacher assistants can help, yet training them adds substantial computational cost. CIFD replaces these assistants with smaller modules that regulate how much information passes from teacher to student.

Its Rate-Distortion Modules operate on embeddings from the teacher's penultimate layer. Each uses an information-constrained bottleneck, and adjusting that constraint lets the module take the role of differently sized assistants. Reusing teacher embeddings avoids relearning low-level feature extraction. A second component places an Information Bottleneck Module inside the student to regularize learning when many Rate-Distortion Modules provide guidance.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on large datasets including ImageNet. They also evaluate distillation of CLIP-like models using a dataset of 12 million image-text pairs. CIFD outperforms specialized CLIP distillation methods on five zero-shot classification datasets and two zero-shot retrieval datasets. The results support controlling the information transfer itself as a useful alternative to training larger intermediary networks.
summary.tldr: CIFD replaces costly teacher assistants with small information bottlenecks that improve knowledge transfer to student models.

title: CIFD: Controlled Information Flow to Enhance Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Text-to-image generative models have recently attracted considerable interest, enabling the synthesis of high-quality images from textual prompts. However, these models often lack the capability to generate specific subjects from given reference images or to synthesize novel renditions under varying conditions. Methods like DreamBooth and Subject-driven Text-to-Image (SuTI) have made significant progress in this area. Yet, both approaches primarily focus on enhancing similarity to reference images and require expensive setups, often overlooking the need for efficient training and avoiding overfitting to the reference images. In this work, we present the $\lambda$-Harmonic reward function, which provides a reliable reward signal and enables early stopping for faster training and effective regularization. By combining the Bradley-Terry preference model, the $\lambda$-Harmonic reward function also provides preference labels for subject-driven generation tasks. We propose Reward Preference Optimization (RPO), which offers a simpler setup (requiring only 3\% of the negative samples used by DreamBooth) and fewer gradient steps for fine-tuning. Unlike most existing methods, our approach does not require training a text encoder or optimizing text embeddings and achieves text-image alignment by fine-tuning only the U-Net component. Empirically, $\lambda$-Harmonic proves to be a reliable approach for model selection in subject-driven generation tasks. Based on preference labels and early stopping validation from the $\lambda$-Harmonic reward function, our algorithm achieves a state-of-the-art CLIP-I score of 0.833 and a CLIP-T score of 0.314 on DreamBench.

The findings support using the same reward framework for preference supervision and training control in the evaluated subject-generation task.
summary.tldr: RPO uses a reward-derived preference signal and early stopping to efficiently fine-tune subject-specific image generation.

title: Subject-driven Text-to-Image Generation via Preference-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Neural wave functions accomplished unprecedented accuracies in approximating the ground state of many-electron systems, though at a high computational cost. Recent works proposed amortizing the cost by learning generalized wave functions across different structures and compounds instead of solving each problem independently. Enforcing the permutation antisymmetry of electrons in such generalized neural wave functions remained challenging as existing methods require discrete orbital selection via non-learnable hand-crafted algorithms. This work tackles the problem by defining overparametrized, fully learnable neural wave functions suitable for generalization across molecules. We achieve this by relying on Pfaffians rather than Slater determinants. The Pfaffian allows us to enforce the antisymmetry on arbitrary electronic systems without any constraint on electronic spin configurations or molecular structure. Our empirical evaluation finds that a single neural Pfaffian calculates the ground state and ionization energies with chemical accuracy across various systems. On the TinyMol dataset, we outperform the `gold-standard' CCSD(T) CBS reference energies by 1.9m$E_h$ and reduce energy errors compared to previous generalized neural wave functions by up to an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: Neural wave functions can approximate the lowest-energy states of many-electron systems very accurately, but solving each system independently is costly. Learning one wave function across multiple molecular structures offers a way to share that effort. A difficulty is preserving electron permutation antisymmetry while allowing the model to generalize across different systems.

Previous generalized approaches rely on handcrafted, non-learnable procedures for discrete orbital selection. This paper replaces the Slater-determinant construction with Pfaffians to create overparameterized, fully learnable wave functions. The construction enforces antisymmetry without imposing restrictions on electronic spin configurations or molecular structure. That flexibility makes the representation suitable for learning across molecules.

Empirically, a single neural Pfaffian computes ground-state and ionization energies with chemical accuracy across various systems. On TinyMol, the authors report outperforming the CCSD(T) CBS reference energies by 1.9 milli-Hartree and reducing errors relative to earlier generalized neural wave functions by up to an order of magnitude. These results support the representation’s usefulness for accurate calculations shared across multiple electronic systems.
summary.tldr: Neural Pfaffians provide fully learnable wave functions that enforce electron antisymmetry and achieve accurate energy calculations across multiple systems.

title: Neural Pfaffians: Solving Many Many-Electron Schrödinger Equations

abstract: Detecting dependencies among variables is a fundamental task across scientific disciplines. We propose a novel neural network model for graph structure inference, which aims to learn a mapping from observational data to the corresponding underlying dependence structures. The model is trained with variably shaped and coupled simulated input data and requires only a single forward pass through the trained network for inference. Central to our approach is a novel bilinear attention mechanism (BAM) operating on covariance matrices of transformed data while respecting the geometry of the manifold of symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices. Inspired by graphical lasso methods, our model optimizes over continuous graph representations in the SPD space, where inverse covariance matrices encode conditional independence relations. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the robustness of our method in detecting diverse dependencies, excelling in undirected graph estimation and showing competitive performance in completed partially directed acyclic graph estimation via a novel two-step approach. The trained model effectively detects causal relationships and generalizes well across different functional forms of nonlinear dependencies.

paragraphs: Inferring relationships among observed variables is central to many scientific analyses. This paper trains a neural model to map observational datasets directly to dependence structures, using simulated training data with varying shapes and couplings. Inference then requires only a single forward pass.

The central bilinear attention mechanism operates on covariance matrices of transformed data while respecting symmetric-positive-definite geometry. Inspired by graphical lasso, the model uses continuous graph representations in a space where inverse covariance encodes conditional independence.

Experiments show strong undirected-graph estimation, robustness across dependencies, and competitive completed-partially-directed-acyclic-graph estimation through a two-step approach. The abstract also reports generalization across nonlinear functional forms. It does not spell out causal-identification assumptions; observational dependence estimates should not be read as unrestricted proof of causal direction without the conditions underlying the evaluated graph-inference setting.
summary.tldr: Bilinear attention over covariance geometry supports rapid inference of variable-dependence graphs.

title: Graph Structure Inference with BAM: Neural Dependency Processing via Bilinear Attention

abstract: One key challenge in Out-of-Distribution (OOD) detection is the absence of ground-truth OOD samples during training. One principled approach to address this issue is to use samples from external datasets as outliers ($\textit{i.e.}$, pseudo OOD samples) to train OOD detectors. However, we find empirically that the outlier samples often present a distribution shift compared to the true OOD samples, especially in Long-Tailed Recognition (LTR) scenarios, where ID classes are heavily imbalanced, $\textit{i.e.}$, the true OOD samples exhibit very different probability distribution to the head and tailed ID classes from the outliers. In this work, we propose a novel approach, namely $\textit{normalized outlier distribution adaptation}$ (AdaptOD), to tackle this distribution shift problem. One of its key components is $\textit{dynamic outlier distribution adaptation}$ that effectively adapts a vanilla outlier distribution based on the outlier samples to the true OOD distribution by utilizing the OOD knowledge in the predicted OOD samples during inference. Further, to obtain a more reliable set of predicted OOD samples on long-tailed ID data, a novel $\textit{dual-normalized energy loss}$ is introduced in AdaptOD, which leverages class- and sample-wise normalized energy to enforce a more balanced prediction energy on imbalanced ID samples. This helps avoid bias toward the head samples and learn a substantially better vanilla outlier distribution than existing energy losses during training. It also eliminates the need of manually tuning the sensitive margin hyperparameters in energy losses. Empirical results on three popular benchmarks for OOD detection in LTR show the superior performance of AdaptOD over state-of-the-art methods.Code is available at https://github.com/mala-lab/AdaptOD.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detectors often train with external examples standing in for the unfamiliar inputs they will eventually encounter. Those substitutes can differ from actual out-of-distribution data. The authors find this mismatch especially problematic when familiar classes are heavily imbalanced, because common and rare classes interact differently with the substitute and true outlier distributions.

AdaptOD addresses both the initial training distribution and its later adaptation. During training, a dual-normalized energy loss normalizes across classes and samples to reduce bias toward frequent classes. This produces a more balanced prediction energy and a better initial outlier distribution, while removing the need to manually tune sensitive energy-loss margins.

During inference, dynamic outlier distribution adaptation uses information from samples predicted to be out of distribution to adjust the initial distribution. The training normalization helps make that predicted set more reliable. Experiments on three benchmarks for long-tailed out-of-distribution detection show superior performance over state-of-the-art methods. The contribution combines imbalance-aware training with adaptation informed by the inputs encountered during inference.
summary.tldr: AdaptOD combines balanced energy-based training with inference-time adaptation to improve out-of-distribution detection under class imbalance.

title: Long-Tailed Out-of-Distribution Detection via Normalized Outlier Distribution Adaptation

abstract: Graph Anomaly Detection (GAD) aims to identify uncommon, deviated, or suspicious objects within graph-structured data. Existing methods generally focus on a single graph object type (node, edge, graph, etc.) and often overlook the inherent connections among different object types of graph anomalies. For instance, a money laundering transaction might involve an abnormal account and the broader community it interacts with. To address this, we present UniGAD, the first unified framework for detecting anomalies at node, edge, and graph levels jointly. Specifically, we develop the Maximum Rayleigh Quotient Subgraph Sampler (MRQSampler) that unifies multi-level formats by transferring objects at each level into graph-level tasks on subgraphs. We theoretically prove that MRQSampler maximizes the accumulated spectral energy of subgraphs (i.e., the Rayleigh quotient) to preserve the most significant anomaly information. To further unify multi-level training, we introduce a novel GraphStitch Network to integrate information across different levels, adjust the amount of sharing required at each level, and harmonize conflicting training goals. Comprehensive experiments show that UniGAD outperforms both existing GAD methods specialized for a single task and graph prompt-based approaches for multiple tasks, while also providing robust zero-shot task transferability.

paragraphs: Graph anomalies can involve individual nodes, connections, or entire graphs, and those levels can be related. An unusual transaction, for instance, may connect an abnormal account with a suspicious wider community. UniGAD addresses these relationships by detecting anomalies jointly at node, edge, and graph levels.

Its MRQSampler converts objects from each level into subgraphs, making the different detection problems share a graph-level format. The authors prove that the sampler maximizes accumulated spectral energy, expressed through the Rayleigh quotient, to preserve significant anomaly information. A GraphStitch Network then exchanges information across levels, adjusts how much they share, and reconciles conflicting training objectives.

Experiments show that UniGAD outperforms both methods specialized for individual anomaly-detection tasks and graph-prompt approaches designed for multiple tasks. The authors also report robust zero-shot transfer between tasks. The results support combining a common input format with adaptive information sharing, so that relationships among anomaly levels can contribute to detection while their training requirements are handled jointly.
summary.tldr: UniGAD detects node, edge, and graph anomalies jointly by converting them into subgraph tasks and adaptively sharing information across levels.

title: UniGAD: Unifying Multi-level Graph Anomaly Detection

abstract: Forecasting is an important task in many domains. However, existing forecasting benchmarks lack comprehensive confidence assessment, focusing on limited question types, and often consist of artificial questions that do not reflect real-world needs. To address these gaps, we introduce FOReCAst (Future Outcome Reasoning and Confidence Assessment), a benchmark that evaluates models' ability to make predictions and their confidence in them. FOReCAst spans diverse forecasting scenarios involving Boolean questions, timeframe prediction, and quantity estimation, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of both prediction accuracy and confidence calibration for real-world applications.

However, existing forecasting benchmarks lack comprehensive confidence assessment, focusing on limited question types, and often consist of artificial questions that do not reflect real-world needs. To address these gaps, we introduce FOReCAst (Future Outcome Reasoning and Confidence Assessment), a benchmark that evaluates models' ability to make predictions and their confidence in them. FOReCAst spans diverse forecasting scenarios involving Boolean questions, timeframe prediction, and quantity estimation, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of both prediction accuracy and confidence calibration for real-world applications.

paragraphs: A forecasting model must do more than produce a plausible prediction: its confidence should also be meaningful. FOReCAst makes both parts of forecasting explicit evaluation targets. The paper identifies shortcomings in existing benchmarks, including narrow question formats, incomplete confidence assessment, and artificial questions that do not adequately reflect practical forecasting needs.

The benchmark covers three kinds of questions: whether an outcome will occur, when it will occur, and what numerical quantity to expect. These formats place different demands on a forecaster. A yes-or-no answer concerns an outcome's occurrence, while a timeframe or quantity prediction requires a more specific estimate. Including all three broadens the forecasting abilities the benchmark can assess.

FOReCAst evaluates prediction accuracy alongside confidence calibration, meaning how well expressed confidence corresponds to prediction reliability. Its stated contribution is this broader evaluation framework across diverse forecasting scenarios. By assessing answers and confidence together, it supports examining whether a model provides useful estimates of its uncertainty as well as accurate predictions for real-world applications.
summary.tldr: FOReCAst evaluates forecasting accuracy and confidence calibration across yes-or-no outcomes, timeframe predictions, and quantity estimates.

title: Introducing FOReCAst: The Future Outcome Reasoning and Confidence Assessment Benchmark

abstract: Foundation models have recently shown strong potential as web agents, capable of interpreting high-level instructions and interacting with complex web interfaces. However, existing training paradigms for these agents often rely on predefined task datasets and curated demonstrations, limiting their scalability, adaptability, and capacity for self-improvement. In this work, we introduce *Self-guided hierArchical exploration for Generalist wEb agents* (SAGE), a new training framework designed to support autonomous skill acquisition through self-guided hierarchical exploration. Our method introduces a three-tier exploration strategy: a pre-exploration phase to build structural understanding of web environments, a top-level exploration strategy to generate a self-evolving curriculum of tasks from easy to hard, and a low-level exploration mechanism that combines planning-based rollouts with step-wise learning to improve policy efficiency. Together, these components form a scalable, supervision-free framework for web agent training. Experimental results on WebVoyager and WebArena demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms prior approaches, enabling foundation model agents to learn complex web tasks with greater generalization and robustness.

paragraphs: Web agents can interpret instructions and operate complex interfaces, but their training often depends on predefined tasks and curated demonstrations. SAGE introduces a framework for agents to acquire skills through self-guided exploration. Its aim is to make training more scalable and adaptable by letting the agent develop its own progression of tasks.

The framework organizes exploration into three levels. Pre-exploration builds an understanding of the web environment's structure. Top-level exploration generates a curriculum that evolves from easier tasks toward harder ones. Low-level exploration combines planning-based rollouts with learning at individual steps to improve policy efficiency. Together, these components connect understanding an environment, deciding what to practice, and learning how to execute.

Experiments on WebVoyager and WebArena show significant improvements over prior approaches, including greater generalization and robustness on complex web tasks. The authors describe the combined framework as supervision-free. The results support hierarchical exploration as a training strategy in which task discovery and skill improvement reinforce one another, reducing reliance on externally prepared demonstrations and task collections.
summary.tldr: SAGE trains web agents through self-guided exploration and evolving task curricula, improving performance and generalization on two web benchmarks.

title: Self-Guided Hierarchical Exploration for Generalist Foundation Model Web Agents

abstract: Analysis of noninvasive microvascular blood flow can improve the diagnosis, prognosis, and management of many medical conditions, including cardiovascular, peripheral vascular, and sickle cell disease. This paper introduces SAM2Flow, an interactive optical flow estimation model to analyze long Oblique Back-illumination Microscopy (OBM) videos of *in vivo* microvascular flow. Inspired by the Segment Anything Model (SAM2), SAM2Flow enables users to specify regions of interest through user prompts for focused flow estimation. SAM2Flow also incorporates a dual memory attention mechanism, comprising both motion and context memory, to achieve efficient and stable flow estimations over extended video sequences. According to our experiments, SAM2Flow achieves SOTA accuracy in foreground optical flow estimation on both microvascular flow and public datasets, with a fast inference speed of over $20$ fps on $512\times512$ inputs. Based on the temporally robust flow estimation, SAM2Flow demonstrated superior performance in downstream physiological applications compared to existing models. The code and dataset will be published with this paper.

paragraphs: SAM2Flow estimates motion in long microscopy videos of blood moving through small vessels in living tissue. Such measurements can support analysis of microcirculation. The model focuses on Oblique Back-illumination Microscopy and provides an interactive interface: users specify regions of interest through prompts, allowing the system to concentrate flow estimation on the areas they want to examine.

Inspired by SAM2, the method combines this prompting capability with a dual memory attention mechanism. One memory retains motion information, while the other retains context. Their combined purpose is to make flow estimates stable and efficient over extended sequences, connecting information across time rather than treating every portion of a long video independently.

The authors report state-of-the-art foreground optical-flow accuracy on microvascular-flow data and public datasets. Inference exceeds 20 frames per second for 512-by-512 inputs. They also find improved performance in downstream physiological applications compared with existing models. Those findings connect temporally robust motion estimation with useful physiological analysis, while the reported evidence concerns the evaluated imaging and downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: SAM2Flow combines user-directed regions with motion and context memory to estimate microvascular flow accurately across long videos.

title: SAM2Flow: Interactive Optical Flow Estimation with Dual Memory for in vivo Microcirculation Analysis

abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely adopted parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method validated across NLP and CV domains. However, LoRA faces an inherent low-rank bottleneck: narrowing its performance gap with full fine-tuning requires increasing the rank of its parameter matrix, resulting in significant parameter overhead. Recent linear LoRA variants have attempted to enhance expressiveness by introducing additional linear mappings; however, their composition remains inherently linear and fails to fundamentally improve LoRA’s representational capacity. To address this limitation, we propose \ourmethod, which incorporates an Adaptive Nonlinear Layer (ANL) between two linear projectors to capture \emph{fixed} and \emph{learnable} nonlinearities. This combination forms an {\fontfamily{lmtt}\selectfont \textbf{MLP-like structure}} with a compressed rank, enabling flexible and precise approximation of diverse target functions while theoretically guaranteeing lower approximation errors and bounded gradients. Extensive experiments on 22 datasets and 6 pretrained models demonstrate that \ourmethod: (\textbf{I}) not only matches or surpasses full fine-tuning performance with only $6.18\%\sim25\%$ of LoRA’s parameters but also (\textbf{II}) outperforms state-of-the-art PEFT methods by up to $10.88\%$ in both NLP and CV tasks, and \textbf{(III)} exhibits robust performance across various rank configurations.
