paragraphs: LoRA adapts pretrained models using compact, low-rank parameter updates. Increasing its expressive capacity often requires a larger rank and more trainable parameters. The paper argues that adding further linear mappings does not fundamentally resolve this restriction, because their composition remains linear.

AuroRA places an Adaptive Nonlinear Layer between two linear projectors. The layer combines fixed and learnable nonlinearities, creating a compact structure resembling a multilayer perceptron. This changes the kinds of transformations the adaptation can represent while retaining a compressed rank. The authors provide theoretical guarantees of lower approximation errors and bounded gradients for their construction.

Experiments span 22 datasets and six pretrained models in language and computer vision. The authors report matching or exceeding full fine-tuning performance while using only 6.18% to 25% of LoRA’s parameters, along with gains of up to 10.88% over state-of-the-art parameter-efficient methods. They also report robustness across rank settings. These findings support nonlinear adaptation as a way to improve the tradeoff between parameter count and performance in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: AuroRA adds nonlinear transformations to compact adapters, reporting strong fine-tuning performance with a fraction of LoRA’s parameters.

title: AuroRA: Breaking Low-Rank Bottleneck of LoRA with Nonlinear Mapping

abstract: The evolution of the human brain has led to the development of complex synaptic plasticity, enabling dynamic adaptation to a constantly evolving world. This progress inspires our exploration into a new paradigm for Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs): a Plasticity-Driven Learning Framework (PDLF). This paradigm diverges from traditional neural network models that primarily focus on direct training of synaptic weights, leading to static connections that limit adaptability in dynamic environments. Instead, our approach delves into the heart of synaptic behavior, prioritizing the learning of plasticity rules themselves. This shift in focus from weight adjustment to mastering the intricacies of synaptic change offers a more flexible and dynamic pathway for neural networks to evolve and adapt. Our PDLF does not merely adapt existing concepts of functional and Presynaptic-Dependent Plasticity but redefines them, aligning closely with the dynamic and adaptive nature of biological learning. This reorientation enhances key cognitive abilities in artificial intelligence systems, such as working memory and multitasking capabilities, and demonstrates superior adaptability in complex, real-world scenarios. Moreover, our framework sheds light on the intricate relationships between various forms of plasticity and cognitive functions, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of the brain's learning mechanisms. Integrating this groundbreaking plasticity-centric approach in SNNs marks a significant advancement in the fusion of neuroscience and artificial intelligence. It paves the way for developing AI systems that not only learn but also adapt in an ever-changing world, much like the human brain.

paragraphs: Neural network learning commonly focuses on adjusting connection weights. This paper shifts the learning target to plasticity: the rules that determine how those connections change. Its Plasticity-Driven Learning Framework applies that idea to spiking neural networks, taking inspiration from the brain's capacity to adapt through changing synaptic behavior.

The framework reworks functional and presynaptic-dependent forms of plasticity around this objective. Learning a rule for synaptic change gives the network a mechanism for dynamic adaptation, rather than making the learned connection values the sole outcome of training. The central design question becomes how connections should evolve as the network encounters changing demands.

The authors report improvements in working memory, multitasking, and adaptability in complex real-world scenarios. They also describe relationships between different forms of plasticity and cognitive functions. These findings position learned plasticity as a route toward more adaptable spiking networks and as a way to investigate how mechanisms of synaptic change relate to particular abilities associated with biological learning.
summary.tldr: The framework learns rules for changing synapses in spiking networks, with reported improvements in memory, multitasking, and adaptation.

title: Learning the Plasticity: Plasticity-Driven Learning Framework in Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: Designing effective agentic systems requires the seamless composition and integration of agents, tools, and models within dynamic and uncertain environments. Most existing methods rely on static, semantic retrieval approaches for tool or agent discovery. However, effective reuse and composition of existing components remain challenging due to incomplete capability descriptions and the limitations of retrieval methods. Component selection suffers because the decisions are not based on capability, cost, and real-time utility. To address these challenges, we introduce a structured, automated framework for agentic system composition that is inspired by the knapsack problem. Our framework enables a composer agent to systematically identify, select, and assemble an optimal set of agentic components by jointly considering performance, budget constraints, and compatibility. By dynamically testing candidate components and modeling their utility in real-time, our approach streamlines the assembly of agentic systems and facilitates scalable reuse of resources. Empirical evaluation with Claude 3.5 Sonnet across five benchmarking datasets shows that our online-knapsack-based composer consistently lies on the Pareto frontier, achieving higher success rates at significantly lower component costs compared to our baselines. In the single-agent setup, the online knapsack composer shows a success rate improvement of up to 31.6\% in comparison to the retrieval baselines. In multi-agent systems, the online knapsack composer increases success rate from 37\% to 87\% when agents are selected from an agent inventory of 100+ agents. The substantial performance gap confirms the robust adaptability of our method across diverse domains and budget constraints.

paragraphs: Building an agent system involves choosing tools, models, and other agents that work well together within a budget. Searching their written descriptions can be unreliable because descriptions may omit capabilities and do not directly establish present usefulness. This paper treats component selection as an optimization problem involving performance, cost, and compatibility.

Its composer agent uses an approach inspired by the knapsack problem: assemble a valuable collection while respecting resource constraints. The composer actively tests candidates and updates estimates of their utility during selection. This makes observed capabilities part of the decision, providing a structured way to reuse existing components as task requirements and budgets vary.

Evaluations using Claude 3.5 Sonnet on five datasets place the composer consistently on the reported performance–cost Pareto frontier. Single-agent success improves by up to 31.6% relative to retrieval baselines. In a multi-agent setting with more than 100 available agents, success rises from 37% to 87%. These findings support testing and budget-aware selection as useful ingredients in automated agent assembly.
summary.tldr: A knapsack-inspired composer tests and selects agent components to improve task success while controlling component costs.

title: Automated Composition of Agents: A Knapsack Approach for Agentic Component Selection

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel in graph mining tasks thanks to their message-passing mechanism, which aligns with the homophily assumption. However, connected nodes can also exhibit inconsistent behaviors, termed heterophilic patterns, sparking interest in heterophilic GNNs (HTGNNs). Although the message-passing mechanism seems unsuitable for heterophilic graphs owing to the propagation of dissimilar messages, it is still popular in HTGNNs and consistently achieves notable success. Some efforts have investigated such an interesting phenomenon, but are limited in the data perspective. The model-perspective understanding remains largely unexplored, which is conducive to guiding the designs of HTGNNs. To fill this gap, we build the connection between node discriminability and the compatibility matrix (CM). We reveal that the effectiveness of the message passing in HTGNNs may be credited to increasing the proposed Compatibility Matrix Discriminability (CMD). However, the issues of sparsity and noise pose great challenges to leveraging CM. Thus, we propose CMGNN, a novel approach to alleviate these issues while enhancing the CM and node embeddings explicitly. A thorough evaluation involving 13 datasets and comparison against 20 well-established baselines highlights the superiority of CMGNN.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why message passing can work on graphs where connected nodes differ. Standard graph neural networks fit naturally with homophily, the assumption that neighbors are similar. Yet methods for heterophilic graphs often still succeed by exchanging information between neighbors, motivating a closer explanation from the model’s perspective.

The authors connect how well nodes can be distinguished with a compatibility matrix and introduce Compatibility Matrix Discriminability. Their analysis suggests that successful message passing in heterophilic networks may be explained by increases in this quantity. This provides a proposed model-level account of the phenomenon, extending beyond explanations centered only on properties of the input data.

Using that connection, they develop CMGNN to improve the compatibility matrix and node embeddings explicitly while mitigating sparsity and noise. Those two issues make the matrix difficult to use effectively. Evaluation across 13 datasets and against 20 established baselines favors CMGNN. The contribution therefore links an explanatory measure with an architecture designed around it, while retaining the qualified claim about why message passing succeeds.
summary.tldr: CMGNN uses compatibility-matrix discriminability to explain and improve message passing on graphs with dissimilar neighbors.

title: Understanding and Enhancing Message Passing on Heterophilic Graphs via Compatibility Matrix

abstract: Foundation models have shown remarkable success across scientific domains, yet their impact in chemistry remains limited due to the absence of diverse, large-scale, high-quality datasets that reflect the field's multifaceted nature. We present the ChemPile, an open dataset containing over 75 billion tokens of curated chemical data, specifically built for training and evaluating general-purpose models in the chemical sciences. The dataset mirrors the human learning journey through chemistry---from educational foundations to specialized expertise---spanning multiple modalities and content types including structured data in diverse chemical representations (SMILES, SELFIES, IUPAC names, InChI, molecular renderings), scientific and educational text, executable code, and chemical images. ChemPile integrates foundational knowledge (textbooks, lecture notes), specialized expertise (scientific articles and language-interfaced data), visual understanding (molecular structures, diagrams), and advanced reasoning (problem-solving traces and code)---mirroring how human chemists develop expertise through diverse learning materials and experiences. Constructed through hundreds of hours of expert curation, the ChemPile captures both foundational concepts and domain-specific complexity. We provide standardized training, validation, and test splits, enabling robust benchmarking. ChemPile is openly released via HuggingFace with a consistent API, permissive license, and detailed documentation. We hope the ChemPile will serve as a catalyst for chemical AI, enabling the development of the next generation of chemical foundation models.

paragraphs: Chemistry draws on many forms of knowledge, from molecular notation and diagrams to textbooks, research articles, and executable code. ChemPile is a 250 GB dataset designed to bring these materials together for general-purpose chemical foundation models. It contains more than 75 billion tokens of curated chemical data for training and evaluation.

The collection follows a progression from introductory learning to specialized expertise. It includes educational material, scientific text, problem-solving traces, code, chemical images, and structured representations such as SMILES, SELFIES, IUPAC names, and InChI. This breadth matters because the resource represents chemistry through multiple content types rather than concentrating all training material in one form. Hundreds of hours of expert curation went into its construction.

The authors provide standardized training, validation, and test splits to support comparable evaluation. They also release the dataset through HuggingFace with a consistent API, documentation, and a permissive license. The paper's contribution is this shared data resource and its organization; enabling stronger chemical foundation models is the intended future benefit.
summary.tldr: ChemPile provides over 75 billion tokens of curated, multimodal chemistry data with standardized splits for training and evaluating foundation models.

title: ChemPile: A 250 GB Diverse and Curated Dataset for Chemical Foundation Models

abstract: Autoformalization, the automatic translation of mathematical content from natural language into machine-verifiable formal languages, has seen significant progress driven by advances in large language models (LLMs). Nonetheless, a primary barrier to further improvements is the limited availability of parallel corpora that map informal mathematical text to its formal counterpart. To address this limitation, we propose ATLAS (Autoformalizing Theorems through Lifting, Augmentation, and Synthesis of Data), a novel data generation framework designed to produce large-scale, high-quality parallel corpora of theorem statements. Distinct from prior approaches, ATLAS begins with a concept repository, accelerates the improvement of the student model through expert iteration combined with knowledge distillation, and introduces two novel augmentation strategies that exploit the structural characteristics of formal languages. Running the proposed ATLAS framework for 10 iterations, we construct an undergraduate-level dataset of 117k theorem statements and develop the ATLAS Translator by fine-tuning Llama3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA. This model establishes a new state of the art, demonstrating statistically significant improvements over both the Herald Translator and the Kimina-Autoformalizer across all benchmarks (p<0.05, two-sided t-test). Furthermore, we demonstrate that the full-parameter fine-tuning of a stronger base model on the ATLAS dataset leads to superior performance. The datasets, model, and code are available at https://github.com/XiaoyangLiu-sjtu/ATLAS.

paragraphs: Autoformalization translates ordinary mathematical writing into a formal language that machines can check. Training models for this task requires paired informal and formal statements, but such examples are scarce. ATLAS addresses that data bottleneck by generating a large parallel collection of theorem statements, making data construction central to improving the translator.

The framework starts from a repository of concepts and improves a student model through expert iteration and knowledge distillation. It also introduces two augmentation strategies that use the structure of formal languages. After 10 iterations, the authors produce 117,000 undergraduate-level theorem statements and train the ATLAS Translator by applying LoRA fine-tuning to Llama3.1-8B-Instruct.

The translator outperforms Herald Translator and Kimina-Autoformalizer across all evaluated benchmarks, with statistically significant differences under the reported two-sided t-tests. Full-parameter fine-tuning of a stronger base model on the same dataset delivers further improvement. Together, these results support the value of ATLAS’s generated training data for translating theorem statements, including when paired with a more capable underlying model.
summary.tldr: ATLAS generates paired informal and formal theorem statements that improve mathematical autoformalization across the evaluated benchmarks.

title: ATLAS: Autoformalizing Theorems through Lifting, Augmentation, and Synthesis of Data

abstract: We present a theoretical analysis of the Jacobian of a attention block within a transformer, showing that it is governed by the query, key, and value projections that define the attention mechanism. Leveraging this insight, we introduce a method that systematically alters the spectral properties of each attention layer to reduce the Jacobian’s condition number, thereby improving the overall conditioning of the attention layers within a transformer network. We empirically show that this improved Jacobian conditioning translates to enhanced performance in practice. Our approach is simple, broadly applicable, and can be easily integrated as a drop-in replacement for a wide range of existing attention mechanisms. We validate its effectiveness across diverse transformer architectures and tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements in performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies transformer attention through its Jacobian, which describes how changes to a block's input affect its output. The authors show that this behavior is governed by the query, key, and value projections that define attention. Their analysis connects these familiar components to the mathematical conditioning of the attention block.

Based on that connection, the proposed method systematically changes the spectral properties of each attention layer to reduce the Jacobian's condition number. Conditioning concerns how unevenly a transformation responds to changes in different directions. The intervention therefore targets the sensitivity structure of attention, using the theoretical analysis to guide a modification of the mechanism.

Experiments across multiple transformer architectures and tasks show consistent performance improvements associated with better Jacobian conditioning. The authors describe the method as simple and suitable as a drop-in replacement for a broad range of attention mechanisms. The contribution is both an explanation of what controls attention's conditioning and an empirically validated way to alter it, connecting a mathematical property of individual layers with practical model performance.
summary.tldr: The paper improves transformer performance by modifying attention's spectral properties to reduce the condition number of its Jacobian.

title: Spectral Conditioning of Attention Improves Transformer Performance

abstract: In the single-positive multi-label (SPML) setting, each image in a dataset is labeled with the presence of a single class, while the true presence of other classes remains unknown. The challenge is to narrow the performance gap between this partially-labeled setting and fully-supervised learning, which often requires a significant annotation budget. Prior SPML methods were developed and benchmarked on synthetic datasets created by randomly sampling single positive labels from fully-annotated datasets like Pascal VOC, COCO, NUS-WIDE, and CUB200. However, this synthetic approach does not reflect real-world scenarios and fails to capture the fine-grained complexities that can lead to difficult misclassifications. In this work, we introduce the L48 dataset, a fine-grained, real-world multi-label dataset derived from recordings of bird sounds. L48 provides a natural SPML setting with single-positive annotations on a challenging, fine-grained domain, as well as two extended settings in which domain priors give access to additional negative labels. We benchmark existing SPML methods on L48 and observe significant performance differences compared to synthetic datasets and analyze method weaknesses, underscoring the need for more realistic and difficult benchmarks.

paragraphs: In single-positive multi-label learning, an example has one confirmed label even though several classes may be present. The remaining classes are unknown, so an absent annotation cannot simply be treated as evidence of absence. This setting matters when fully labeling every example would require substantial annotation effort.

The L48 dataset brings this problem into a real-world, fine-grained domain using bird-sound recordings. Earlier benchmarks commonly simulated partial labeling by randomly retaining one positive label from fully annotated datasets. L48 instead supplies a natural single-positive setting, together with two extensions where domain knowledge provides additional negative labels. These settings let researchers study different amounts of available label information.

When existing methods are evaluated on L48, their performance differs significantly from results on synthetic benchmarks. The authors also analyze weaknesses exposed by the dataset. The contribution is therefore both a new evaluation resource and evidence that synthetic label removal can miss important difficulties encountered in real partially labeled data, particularly when distinctions between classes are fine-grained.
summary.tldr: L48 uses bird-sound data to benchmark naturally incomplete labels, revealing method behavior that differs from synthetic partial-label benchmarks.

title: Merlin L48 Spectrogram Dataset

abstract: The new paradigm of test-time scaling has yielded remarkable breakthroughs in Large Language Models (LLMs) (e.g. reasoning models) and in generative vision models, allowing models to allocate additional computation during inference to effectively tackle increasingly complex problems. Despite the improvements of this approach, an important limitation emerges: the substantial increase in computation time makes the process slow and impractical for many applications. Given the success of this paradigm and its growing usage, we seek to preserve its benefits while eschewing the inference overhead. In this work we propose one solution to the critical problem of integrating test-time scaling knowledge into a model during post-training. Specifically, we replace reward guided test-time noise optimization in diffusion models with a Noise Hypernetwork that modulates initial input noise. We propose a theoretically grounded framework for learning this reward-tilted distribution for distilled generators, through a tractable noise-space objective that maintains fidelity to the base model while optimizing for desired characteristics. We show that our approach recovers a substantial portion of the quality gains from explicit test-time optimization at a fraction of the computational cost.

paragraphs: Extra computation during generation can improve diffusion-model outputs, but repeatedly optimizing each sample's starting noise makes inference slower. This paper asks whether the benefits of that optimization can be learned during post-training. Its goal is to retain much of the quality improvement while reducing the computation required for each new generation.

The proposed Noise Hypernetwork modulates the initial noise supplied to a distilled generator. Instead of performing reward-guided noise optimization at test time, the network learns a noise distribution that favors desired outcomes. A theoretically grounded, tractable objective operates in noise space and balances the desired characteristics with fidelity to the base model.

The reported results recover a substantial portion of explicit test-time optimization's quality gains at a fraction of its computational cost. The claim is therefore about retaining much of the benefit, rather than reproducing every gain. The approach illustrates how a repeated inference-time search can be partly absorbed into a learned component, shifting work into post-training while keeping generation comparatively efficient.
summary.tldr: Noise Hypernetworks learn to shape diffusion inputs, recovering much of reward-guided noise optimization's quality improvement with lower inference cost.

title: Noise Hypernetworks: Amortizing Test-Time Compute in Diffusion Models

abstract: Generation of images containing multiple humans, performing complex actions, while preserving their facial identities, is a significant challenge. A major factor contributing to this is the lack of a a dedicated benchmark. To address this, we introduce MultiHuman-Testbench, a novel benchmark for rigorously evaluating generative models for multi-human generation. The benchmark comprises 1800 samples, including carefully curated text prompts, describing a range of simple to complex human actions. These prompts are matched with a total of 5,550 unique human face images, sampled uniformly to ensure diversity across age, ethnic background, and gender. Alongside captions, we provide human-selected pose conditioning images which accurately match the prompt. We propose a multi-faceted evaluation suite employing four key metrics to quantify face count, ID similarity, prompt alignment, and action detection. We conduct a thorough evaluation of a diverse set of models, including zero-shot approaches and training-based methods, with and without regional priors. We also propose novel techniques to incorporate image and region isolation using human segmentation and Hungarian matching, significantly improving ID similarity. Our proposed benchmark and key findings provide valuable insights and a standardized tool for advancing research in multi-human image generation.

paragraphs: Generating several people in one image requires coordinating their identities, number, and actions. MultiHuman-Testbench provides a dedicated evaluation setting for this combination. It contains 1,800 samples with prompts spanning simple to complex human actions, paired with 5,550 unique face images sampled uniformly to support diversity across age, ethnic background, and gender.

The benchmark also supplies human-selected pose-conditioning images that match the prompts. Its evaluation suite separately measures face count, identity similarity, prompt alignment, and action detection. These dimensions make it possible to assess whether a generator satisfies different parts of a multi-person request, rather than treating an image’s overall plausibility as sufficient evidence of success.

The authors evaluate zero-shot and training-based methods, including approaches with and without regional priors. They also introduce image and region isolation techniques using human segmentation and Hungarian matching, reporting significant gains in identity similarity. The benchmark and accompanying methods provide a standardized way to investigate where multi-human generation succeeds and where preserving individual identities remains difficult.
summary.tldr: MultiHuman-Testbench evaluates identity, count, prompts, and actions in multi-person image generation and introduces techniques that improve identity similarity.

title: MultiHuman-Testbench: Benchmarking Image Generation for Multiple Humans

abstract: Despite their remarkable performance on various tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) still struggle with logical reasoning, particularly in complex and multi-step reasoning processes. Among various efforts to enhance LLMs' reasoning capabilities, synthesizing large-scale, high-quality logical reasoning datasets has emerged as a promising direction. However, existing methods often rely on predefined templates for logical reasoning data generation, limiting their adaptability to real-world scenarios. To address the limitation, we propose **LogicTree**, a novel framework for efficiently synthesizing multi-step logical reasoning dataset that excels in both complexity and instantiation. By iteratively searching for applicable logic rules based on structural pattern matching to perform backward deduction, **LogicTree** constructs multi-step logic trees that capture complex reasoning patterns. Furthermore, we employ a two-stage LLM-based approach to instantiate various real-world scenarios for each logic tree, generating consistent real-world reasoning processes that carry contextual significance. This helps LLMs develop generalizable logical reasoning abilities across diverse scenarios rather than merely memorizing templates. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves an average improvement of 9.4\% in accuracy on complex logical reasoning tasks.
originalAbstract: Despite their remarkable performance on various tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) still struggle with logical reasoning, particularly in complex and multi-step reasoning processes. Among various efforts to enhance LLMs' reasoning capabilities, synthesizing large-scale, high-quality logical reasoning datasets has emerged as a promising direction. However, existing methods often rely on predefined templates for logical reasoning data generation, limiting their adaptability to real-world scenarios. To address the limitation, we propose **LogicTree**, a novel framework for efficiently synthesizing multi-step logical reasoning dataset that excels in both complexity and instantiation. By iteratively searching for applicable logic rules based on structural pattern matching to perform backward deduction, **LogicTree** constructs multi-step logic trees that capture complex reasoning patterns. Furthermore, we employ a two-stage LLM-based approach to instantiate various real-world scenarios for each logic tree, generating consistent real-world reasoning processes that carry contextual significance. This helps LLMs develop generalizable logical reasoning abilities across diverse scenarios rather than merely memorizing templates. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves an average improvement of 9.4\% in accuracy on complex logical reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Language models still struggle with complex reasoning that requires several connected logical steps. Synthetic training data offers one route to improvement, but predefined templates can restrict how well examples reflect varied real-world situations. LogicTree aims to generate both richer reasoning structures and meaningful contextual versions of those structures.

The framework builds logic trees through backward deduction. At each stage, structural pattern matching identifies applicable logical rules, allowing the process to expand into a multistep reasoning pattern. A two-stage language-model procedure then turns each tree into different real-world scenarios while maintaining consistent reasoning. This separates the construction of a logical structure from the task of expressing it in a concrete context.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks report an average 9.4% accuracy improvement on complex logical reasoning tasks. The stated purpose of contextualizing the trees is to help models learn reasoning that transfers across scenarios, rather than merely memorize templates. The findings support this structured synthetic-data approach as a way to strengthen multistep reasoning.
summary.tldr: LogicTree builds multistep logical structures and instantiates them in varied scenarios to create training data for stronger reasoning.

title: LogicTree: Improving Complex Reasoning of LLMs via Instantiated Multi-step Synthetic Logical Data

abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies provide gene expression measurements with spatial resolution, enabling the dissection of tissue structure and function. A fundamental challenge in ST analysis is clustering spatial spots into coherent functional regions. While existing models effectively integrate expression and spatial signals, they largely overlook sequence-level biological priors encoded in the DNA sequences of expressed genes. To bridge this gap, we propose SAINT (Sequence-Aware Integration for Nucleotide-informed Transcriptomics), a unified framework that augments spatial representation learning with nucleotide-derived features. We construct sequence-augmented datasets across 14 tissue sections from three widely used ST benchmarks (DLPFC, HBC, and MBA), retrieving reference DNA sequences for each expressed gene and encoding them using a pretrained Nucleotide Transformer. For each spot, gene-level embeddings are aggregated via expression-weighted and attention-based pooling, then fused with spatial-expression representations through a late fusion module. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAINT consistently improves clustering performance across multiple datasets. Experiments validate the superiority, effectiveness, sensitivity, and transferability of our framework, confirming the complementary value of incorporating sequence-level priors into spatial transcriptomics clustering.

Existing approaches combine expression measurements with spatial information, but often leave out biological information encoded in the DNA sequences of the expressed genes. SAINT adds this sequence information to the clustering representation.

summary.tldr: SAINT improves spatial transcriptomics clustering by combining DNA-sequence embeddings with gene-expression and spatial representations.

title: SAINT: Sequence-Aware Integration for Spatial Transcriptomics Multi-View Clustering

abstract: We propose a randomized block-coordinate variant of the classic Frank-Wolfe algorithm for convex optimization with block-separable constraints. Despite its lower iteration cost, we show that it achieves a similar convergence rate in duality gap as the full Frank-Wolfe algorithm. We also show that, when applied to the dual structural support vector machine (SVM) objective, this yields an online algorithm that has the same low iteration complexity as primal stochastic subgradient methods. However, unlike stochastic subgradient methods, the block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe algorithm allows us to compute the optimal step-size and yields a computable duality gap guarantee. Our experiments indicate that this simple algorithm outperforms competing structural SVM solvers.

However, unlike stochastic subgradient methods, the block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe algorithm allows us to compute the optimal step-size and yields a computable duality gap guarantee. Our experiments indicate that this simple algorithm outperforms competing structural SVM solvers.

paragraphs: This paper develops a cheaper way to run the Frank-Wolfe algorithm on convex problems whose constraints separate into blocks. Instead of performing the full update at every iteration, the proposed method randomly selects a block to update. The central question is whether this reduction in work per iteration preserves useful progress toward the optimum.

The authors show that the randomized method achieves a similar convergence rate to full Frank-Wolfe when measured by the duality gap. That gap provides a certificate of how far the current solution may be from optimality. Applied to the dual formulation of a structural support vector machine, the method becomes an online algorithm with iteration costs comparable to primal stochastic subgradient methods.

The resulting solver also supports an optimal step-size calculation and a computable duality-gap guarantee. These features provide both a principled update size and a way to assess remaining optimization error. Experiments indicate that the algorithm outperforms competing structural SVM solvers, supporting the practical value of combining inexpensive updates with an explicit measure of solution quality.
summary.tldr: Randomized block updates make Frank-Wolfe inexpensive for structural SVMs while retaining convergence guarantees and a computable optimality certificate.

title: Block-Coordinate Frank-Wolfe Optimization for Structural SVMs

abstract: Sum of Squares Error and Normalized Cut are two widely used clustering functional. It is known their minimum values are monotone with respect to the input number of clusters and this monotonicity does not allow for a simple automatic selection of a correct number of clusters. Here we study monotonicity not just on the minimizers but on the entire clustering lattice. We show the value of Sum of Squares Error is strictly monotone under the strict refinement relation of clusterings and we obtain data-dependent bounds on the difference between the value of a clustering and one of its refinements. Using analogous techniques we show the value of Normalized Cut is strictly anti-monotone. These results imply that even if we restrict our solutions to form a chain of clustering, like the one we get from hierarchical algorithms, we cannot rely on the functional values in order to choose the number of clusters. By using these results we get some data-dependent bounds on the difference of the values of any two clusterings.

paragraphs: Clustering scores are often used to compare possible groupings, but their behavior can complicate choosing how many clusters to use. The minimum values of Sum of Squares Error and Normalized Cut are known to vary monotonically with cluster count. The paper expands the analysis beyond optimal clusterings to the full collection of clusterings ordered by refinement.

A refinement splits existing groups into smaller ones. The authors establish strict monotonicity for Sum of Squares Error under strict refinement and a corresponding strict anti-monotonicity result for Normalized Cut. They also derive bounds, dependent on the data, on the change in score between a clustering and its refinement.

These results show that restricting attention to a nested sequence, such as the output of hierarchical clustering, does not resolve the cluster-count selection problem using these functional values alone. The paper further obtains data-dependent bounds on score differences between any two clusterings. Its contribution is a clearer mathematical account of how these objectives respond to changes in grouping structure.
summary.tldr: Strict monotonicity results show why Sum of Squares Error and Normalized Cut alone cannot select cluster count even along a hierarchical clustering sequence.

title: Strict Monotonicity of Sum of Squares Error and Normalized Cut in the Lattice of Clusterings

abstract: We propose an interpretable rule-based classification system based on ideas from Boolean compressed sensing. We represent the problem of learning individual conjunctive clauses or individual disjunctive clauses as a Boolean group testing problem, and apply a novel linear programming relaxation to find solutions. We derive results for exact rule recovery which parallel the conditions for exact recovery of sparse signals in the compressed sensing literature: although the general rule recovery problem is NP-hard, under some conditions on the Boolean ‘sensing’ matrix, the rule can be recovered exactly. This is an exciting development in rule learning where most prior work focused on heuristic solutions. Furthermore we construct rule sets from these learned clauses using set covering and boosting. We show competitive classification accuracy using the proposed approach.

We derive results for exact rule recovery which parallel the conditions for exact recovery of sparse signals in the compressed sensing literature: although the general rule recovery problem is NP-hard, under some conditions on the Boolean ‘sensing’ matrix, the rule can be recovered exactly. This is an exciting development in rule learning where most prior work focused on heuristic solutions. Furthermore we construct rule sets from these learned clauses using set covering and boosting. We show competitive classification accuracy using the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Interpretable classifiers can express decisions through logical rules, but finding the correct rules is computationally difficult. This paper connects rule learning to Boolean compressed sensing. It treats learning a single conjunctive clause, which combines conditions with AND, or a single disjunctive clause, which combines them with OR, as a Boolean group testing problem.

The authors introduce a linear programming relaxation for solving these problems. They also derive conditions for exact recovery that parallel sparse-signal recovery results in compressed sensing. The general rule recovery problem remains NP-hard. Exact recovery is guaranteed under certain conditions on the Boolean sensing matrix, making the contribution a conditional theoretical result rather than a general solution to the hard problem.

To build complete classifiers, the method combines learned clauses into rule sets using set covering and boosting. The resulting approach achieves competitive classification accuracy. Its significance is the combination of interpretable rule construction with exact recovery theory, extending a field where much previous work relied on heuristic solutions.
summary.tldr: Boolean compressed sensing yields interpretable rule learners with conditional exact-recovery guarantees and competitive classification accuracy.

title: Exact Rule Learning via Boolean Compressed Sensing

abstract: The method of random projections has become popular for large-scale applications in statistical learning, information retrieval, bio-informatics and other applications. Using a well-designed \textbfcoding scheme for the projected data, which determines the number of bits needed for each projected value and how to allocate these bits, can significantly improve the effectiveness of the algorithm, in storage cost as well as computational speed. In this paper, we study a number of simple coding schemes, focusing on the task of similarity estimation and on an application to training linear classifiers. We demonstrate that \textbfuniform quantization outperforms the standard and influential method \citeProc:Datar_SCG04, which used a \em window-and-random offset scheme. Indeed, we argue that in many cases coding with just a small number of bits suffices. Furthermore, we also develop a \textbfnon-uniform 2-bit coding scheme that generally performs well in practice, as confirmed by our experiments on training linear support vector machines (SVM). Proofs and additional experiments are available at \em arXiv:1308.2218. In the context of using coded random projections for \textbfapproximate near neighbor search by building hash tables (\em arXiv:1403.8144) \citeReport:RPCodeLSH2014, we show that the step of random offset in \citeProc:Datar_SCG04 is again not needed and may hurt the performance. Furthermore, we show that, unless the target similarity level is high, it usually suffices to use only 1 or 2 bits to code each hashed value for this task. Section \refsec_LSH presents some experimental results for LSH.

paragraphs: Random projections produce transformed data values, but storing those values still requires choosing how many bits to use and what those bits represent. This paper studies how simple coding choices affect similarity estimation and linear classification. The motivation is that a suitable representation can improve both storage requirements and computational speed.

The authors show that uniform quantization outperforms a widely used scheme based on windows and random offsets. They also introduce a non-uniform two-bit code that performs well in their linear support vector machine experiments. These findings support the argument that retaining many bits for every projected value is unnecessary in many cases.

The paper also considers hash tables for approximate near-neighbor search. In that setting, it finds that adding a random offset is unnecessary and can reduce performance. One or two bits per hashed value usually suffice unless the desired similarity level is high. The conclusion is qualified: compact codes can be effective, but the appropriate precision depends on the task and target similarity.
summary.tldr: Simple low-bit codes can make random projections more efficient, with one or two bits often sufficient depending on the task and target similarity.

title: Coding for Random Projections

abstract: We develop an automated technique for detecting damped Lyman-αabsorbers (DLAs) along spectroscopic sightlines to quasi-stellar objects (QSOs or quasars). The detection of DLAs in large-scale spectroscopic surveys such as SDSS–III is critical to address outstanding cosmological questions, such as the nature of galaxy formation. We use nearly 50000 QSO spectra to learn a tailored Gaussian process model for quasar emission spectra, which we apply to the DLA detection problem via Bayesian model selection. We demonstrate our method’s effectiveness with a large-scale validation experiment on over 100000 spectra, with excellent performance.
originalAbstract: We develop an automated technique for detecting damped Lyman-αabsorbers (DLAs) along spectroscopic sightlines to quasi-stellar objects (QSOs or quasars). We use nearly 50000 QSO spectra to learn a tailored Gaussian process model for quasar emission spectra, which we apply to the DLA detection problem via Bayesian model selection. We demonstrate our method’s effectiveness with a large-scale validation experiment on over 100000 spectra, with excellent performance.

paragraphs: The paper develops an automated method for detecting damped Lyman-alpha absorbers along spectroscopic sightlines to quasars. Finding these absorbers in large spectroscopic surveys is important for investigating cosmological questions, including galaxy formation. The research addresses the detection problem at survey scale, where a method must work across large collections of spectra.

The authors learn a Gaussian process model tailored to quasar emission spectra using nearly 50,000 spectra. They then use Bayesian model selection to apply that learned model to absorber detection. This connects a statistical description of quasar emission to a probabilistic decision about the presence of an absorber in an observed spectrum.

A validation experiment on more than 100,000 spectra demonstrates the method's effectiveness, with performance described as excellent. The stated finding is evidence for automated detection on a large spectral collection. The contribution combines a learned emission model, Bayesian model selection, and large-scale validation to support the observational work needed for the broader cosmological questions.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process model learned from quasar spectra enables automated absorber detection through Bayesian model selection.

title: Finding Galaxies in the Shadows of Quasars with Gaussian Processes

abstract: We present a systematic study on how to morph a well-trained neural network to a new one so that its network function can be completely preserved. We define this as network morphism in this research. After morphing a parent network, the child network is expected to inherit the knowledge from its parent network and also has the potential to continue growing into a more powerful one with much shortened training time. The first requirement for this network morphism is its ability to handle diverse morphing types of networks, including changes of depth, width, kernel size, and even subnet. To meet this requirement, we first introduce the network morphism equations, and then develop novel morphing algorithms for all these morphing types for both classic and convolutional neural networks. The second requirement is its ability to deal with non-linearity in a network. We propose a family of parametric-activation functions to facilitate the morphing of any continuous non-linear activation neurons. Experimental results on benchmark datasets and typical neural networks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed network morphism scheme.

paragraphs: Network morphism changes a trained neural network's architecture while completely preserving the function it computes. This paper develops a systematic framework for doing so. Preserving the parent network's behavior allows the child network to inherit learned knowledge, with the potential for further growth and substantially shorter subsequent training.

The authors formulate network morphism equations and develop algorithms for changing depth, width, kernel size, and subnet structure. The methods cover both classic neural networks and convolutional networks. This breadth matters because architectural growth can take several forms, and a useful preservation scheme must accommodate more than a single type of modification.

Nonlinear activations create another requirement for function-preserving transformations. The paper introduces a family of parameterized activation functions to facilitate morphing neurons with any continuous nonlinear activation. Benchmark experiments on typical networks demonstrate the scheme's effectiveness. The exact preservation objective concerns the transformation itself; becoming a more powerful model through continued training is presented as the resulting network's potential.
summary.tldr: Network morphism changes trained network architectures while preserving their functions, enabling knowledge reuse during further growth.

title: Network Morphism

abstract: Most models in machine learning contain at least one hyperparameter to control for model complexity. Choosing an appropriate set of hyperparameters is both crucial in terms of model accuracy and computationally challenging. In this work we propose an algorithm for the optimization of continuous hyperparameters using inexact gradient information. An advantage of this method is that hyperparameters can be updated before model parameters have fully converged. We also give sufficient conditions for the global convergence of this method, based on regularity conditions of the involved functions and summability of errors. Finally, we validate the empirical performance of this method on the estimation of regularization constants of L2-regularized logistic regression and kernel Ridge regression. Empirical benchmarks indicate that our approach is highly competitive with respect to state of the art methods.
originalAbstract: Most models in machine learning contain at least one hyperparameter to control for model complexity. In this work we propose an algorithm for the optimization of continuous hyperparameters using inexact gradient information. An advantage of this method is that hyperparameters can be updated before model parameters have fully converged. We also give sufficient conditions for the global convergence of this method, based on regularity conditions of the involved functions and summability of errors. Finally, we validate the empirical performance of this method on the estimation of regularization constants of L2-regularized logistic regression and kernel Ridge regression. Empirical benchmarks indicate that our approach is highly competitive with respect to state of the art methods.

paragraphs: Hyperparameters influence model complexity, so choosing them affects both predictive accuracy and the computational effort spent on training. This paper proposes an algorithm for optimizing continuous hyperparameters using approximate gradient information. Its key practical feature is that hyperparameter updates can occur before the model's own parameters have fully converged.

Allowing inexact gradients changes how model fitting and hyperparameter selection can be coordinated. Instead of requiring a fully converged fit before every update, the method can work with intermediate information. The authors provide sufficient conditions for global convergence of the procedure, involving regularity of the relevant functions and summability of the approximation errors.

The experiments tune regularization constants for L2-regularized logistic regression and kernel ridge regression. The reported benchmarks find the approach highly competitive with state-of-the-art methods. The contribution thus combines a way to update hyperparameters during incomplete training with theory describing when controlled approximation errors are compatible with convergence. The stated guarantees depend on those conditions, rather than allowing arbitrary gradient inaccuracies.
summary.tldr: Approximate gradients allow continuous hyperparameters to be updated before model fitting converges, with convergence guaranteed under sufficient conditions.

title: Hyperparameter optimization with approximate gradient

abstract: Spectral clustering has become a popular technique due to its high performance in many contexts. It comprises three main steps: create a similarity graph between N objects to cluster, compute the first k eigenvectors of its Laplacian matrix to define a feature vector for each object, and run k-means on these features to separate objects into k classes. Each of these three steps becomes computationally intensive for large N and/or k. We propose to speed up the last two steps based on recent results in the emerging field of graph signal processing: graph filtering of random signals, and random sampling of bandlimited graph signals. We prove that our method, with a gain in computation time that can reach several orders of magnitude, is in fact an approximation of spectral clustering, for which we are able to control the error. We test the performance of our method on artificial and real-world network data.

Each of these three steps becomes computationally intensive for large N and/or k. We propose to speed up the last two steps based on recent results in the emerging field of graph signal processing: graph filtering of random signals, and random sampling of bandlimited graph signals. We prove that our method, with a gain in computation time that can reach several orders of magnitude, is in fact an approximation of spectral clustering, for which we are able to control the error. We test the performance of our method on artificial and real-world network data.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering first builds a graph expressing similarities between objects. It then uses eigenvectors of the graph’s Laplacian to represent the objects as feature vectors and applies k-means to form clusters. Computing these representations and clustering them can become expensive as the number of objects or desired clusters grows.

This paper accelerates those last two stages using graph signal processing. Its ingredients are filtering random signals on the graph and randomly sampling bandlimited graph signals. These operations provide a route to approximating the spectral clustering computation without carrying out the original feature-construction and clustering stages in their full form.

The authors prove that the resulting procedure approximates spectral clustering and provide control over its approximation error. They report that computational savings can reach several orders of magnitude and evaluate the approach on artificial and real network data. The contribution therefore connects potentially substantial speed improvements with an explicit mathematical account of approximation, while leaving graph construction outside the two stages it targets.
summary.tldr: Graph filtering and sampling yield a controlled approximation to spectral clustering with potentially substantial computational savings.

title: Compressive Spectral Clustering

abstract: We present the first differentially private algorithms for reinforcement learning, which apply to the task of evaluating a fixed policy. We establish two approaches for achieving differential privacy, provide a theoretical analysis of the privacy and utility of the two algorithms, and show promising results on simple empirical examples.
originalAbstract: We present the first differentially private algorithms for reinforcement learning, which apply to the task of evaluating a fixed policy. We establish two approaches for achieving differential privacy, provide a theoretical analysis of the privacy and utility of the two algorithms, and show promising results on simple empirical examples.

paragraphs: This paper brings differential privacy to reinforcement learning through the task of evaluating a fixed policy. The policy is the decision rule under assessment; the learning task here is to estimate how it performs. Keeping that rule fixed gives the work a specific scope within the broader range of reinforcement learning problems.

The authors present two approaches for achieving differential privacy and identify them as the first differentially private algorithms for reinforcement learning. They analyze both privacy and utility theoretically. These are complementary questions: an evaluation method needs a privacy guarantee, but its output must also remain useful for assessing the policy.

The work also includes simple empirical examples with promising results. Those examples complement the formal analysis by showing how the proposed algorithms behave in concrete evaluations. The central contribution is therefore a combination of private policy-evaluation methods, theoretical treatment of their usefulness, and initial experimental evidence. The empirical claim remains limited to the simple examples described, while the algorithmic contribution specifically concerns fixed-policy evaluation.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces two differentially private approaches to fixed-policy evaluation, with theoretical privacy and utility analysis and promising simple experiments.

title: Differentially Private Policy Evaluation

abstract: Combining abstract, symbolic reasoning with continuous neural reasoning is a grand challenge of representation learning. As a step in this direction, we propose a new architecture, called neural equivalence network, for the problem of learning continuous semantic representations of algebraic and logical expressions. These networks are trained to represent semantic equivalence, even of expressions that are syntactically very different. The challenge is that semantic representations must be computed in a syntax-directed manner, because semantics is compositional, but at the same time, small changes in syntax can lead to very large changes in semantics, which can be difficult for continuous neural architectures. We perform an exhaustive evaluation on the task of checking equivalence on a highly diverse class of symbolic algebraic and boolean expression types, showing that our model significantly outperforms existing architectures.

As a step in this direction, we propose a new architecture, called neural equivalence network, for the problem of learning continuous semantic representations of algebraic and logical expressions. These networks are trained to represent semantic equivalence, even of expressions that are syntactically very different. The challenge is that semantic representations must be computed in a syntax-directed manner, because semantics is compositional, but at the same time, small changes in syntax can lead to very large changes in semantics, which can be difficult for continuous neural architectures. We perform an exhaustive evaluation on the task of checking equivalence on a highly diverse class of symbolic algebraic and boolean expression types, showing that our model significantly outperforms existing architectures.

paragraphs: Algebraic and logical expressions can have the same meaning despite looking very different. This paper introduces neural equivalence networks to learn continuous representations that capture such semantic equivalence. The goal is to connect symbolic expressions with neural representations while preserving information about what those expressions mean.

The central difficulty is that representations must follow an expression's syntax because meaning is built compositionally from its parts. Yet a small syntactic change can produce a large change in meaning. Continuous neural architectures must therefore account for both equivalent expressions with very different structures and expressions whose similar structures conceal substantial semantic differences.

The authors evaluate the architecture on equivalence checking across a highly diverse collection of algebraic and Boolean expression types. They report that it significantly outperforms existing architectures in this evaluation. The finding supports the proposed network as a step toward combining symbolic and continuous reasoning, with the demonstrated task specifically being recognition of equivalence across the tested expression families.
summary.tldr: Neural equivalence networks learn continuous representations of symbolic meaning and improve equivalence checking across diverse algebraic and Boolean expressions.

title: Learning Continuous Semantic Representations of Symbolic Expressions

abstract: A new computationally efficient dependence measure, and an adaptive statistical test of independence, are proposed. The dependence measure is the difference between analytic embeddings of the joint distribution and the product of the marginals, evaluated at a finite set of locations (features). These features are chosen so as to maximize a lower bound on the test power, resulting in a test that is data-efficient, and that runs in linear time (with respect to the sample size n). The optimized features can be interpreted as evidence to reject the null hypothesis, indicating regions in the joint domain where the joint distribution and the product of the marginals differ most. Consistency of the independence test is established, for an appropriate choice of features. In real-world benchmarks, independence tests using the optimized features perform comparably to the state-of-the-art quadratic-time HSIC test, and outperform competing O(n) and O(n log n) tests.

paragraphs: The paper develops a statistical test for deciding whether two variables are independent. It compares their joint distribution with the distribution obtained by combining their separate marginal distributions. Independence means these descriptions agree. The proposed dependence measure represents both distributions through analytic kernel embeddings and checks their differences at a finite collection of feature locations.

The method chooses these locations to maximize a lower bound on test power: the ability to detect dependence when it is present. This makes feature selection part of the testing procedure. The selected locations also offer an interpretation of the result, highlighting regions where the observed joint behavior differs most from what independence would imply.

The test runs in time linear in sample size, and the authors establish consistency for an appropriate choice of features. On real-world benchmarks, optimized features give performance comparable to the quadratic-time HSIC test and better than competing linear-time and O(n log n) tests. These findings support efficient, interpretable dependence testing without claiming that every feature choice works equally well.
summary.tldr: An adaptive independence test selects informative kernel features to detect dependence in linear time and reveal where it occurs.

title: An Adaptive Test of Independence with Analytic Kernel Embeddings

abstract: Noisy data, non-convex objectives, model misspecification, and numerical instability can all cause undesired behaviors in machine learning systems. As a result, detecting actual implementation errors can be extremely difficult. We demonstrate a methodology in which developers use an interactive proof assistant to both implement their system and to state a formal theorem defining what it means for their system to be correct. The process of proving this theorem interactively in the proof assistant exposes all implementation errors since any error in the program would cause the proof to fail. As a case study, we implement a new system, Certigrad, for optimizing over stochastic computation graphs, and we generate a formal (i.e. machine-checkable) proof that the gradients sampled by the system are unbiased estimates of the true mathematical gradients. We train a variational autoencoder using Certigrad and find the performance comparable to training the same model in TensorFlow.

This paper demonstrates a development method that pairs the implementation with a formal mathematical statement of what correctness means.

Developers implement the system inside an interactive proof assistant and prove the corresponding correctness theorem there. An implementation error that violates the formal statement prevents the proof from succeeding. The resulting assurance is tied to the stated mathematical property, giving developers a precise target against which to check the program.

Its machine-checkable proof establishes that sampled gradients are unbiased estimates of the true mathematical gradients. This demonstrates both a concrete verified property and the use of the verified system for a substantive learning task.
summary.tldr: Certigrad demonstrates how proof-assisted development can establish that a learning system's sampled gradients are unbiased.

title: Developing Bug-Free Machine Learning Systems With Formal Mathematics

abstract: Domain adaptation is critical for success in new, unseen environments. Adversarial adaptation models have shown tremendous progress towards adapting to new environments by focusing either on discovering domain invariant representations or by mapping between unpaired image domains. While feature space methods are difficult to interpret and sometimes fail to capture pixel-level and low-level domain shifts, image space methods sometimes fail to incorporate high level semantic knowledge relevant for the end task. We propose a model which adapts between domains using both generative image space alignment and latent representation space alignment. Our approach, Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Domain Adaptation (CyCADA), guides transfer between domains according to a specific discriminatively trained task and avoids divergence by enforcing consistency of the relevant semantics before and after adaptation. We evaluate our method on a variety of visual recognition and prediction settings, including digit classification and semantic segmentation of road scenes, advancing state-of-the-art performance for unsupervised adaptation from synthetic to real world driving domains.

Aligning internal features can overlook changes in pixels and low-level appearance, while translating images can neglect the higher-level meaning needed for the prediction task.

CyCADA combines alignment in image space with alignment in the model’s internal representation space. A discriminatively trained task guides the transfer, and consistency requirements preserve relevant semantics before and after adaptation. The purpose is to connect changes in visual appearance to the meaning that the downstream recognition system needs to retain.

The authors evaluate the approach on digit classification and road-scene semantic segmentation, among other visual settings. They report an advance over the state of the art for unsupervised adaptation from synthetic driving imagery to real driving environments. The finding supports the value of coordinating appearance and representation changes while keeping task-relevant semantics consistent throughout the transfer.
summary.tldr: CyCADA aligns images and internal features while preserving task semantics, improving unsupervised synthetic-to-real driving adaptation.

title: CyCADA: Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Domain Adaptation

abstract: Verifying the robustness property of a general Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) network is an NP-complete problem. Although finding the exact minimum adversarial distortion is hard, giving a certified lower bound of the minimum distortion is possible. Current available methods of computing such a bound are either time-consuming or deliver low quality bounds that are too loose to be useful. In this paper, we exploit the special structure of ReLU networks and provide two computationally efficient algorithms (Fast-Lin, Fast-Lip) that are able to certify non-trivial lower bounds of minimum adversarial distortions. Experiments show that (1) our methods deliver bounds close to (the gap is 2-3X) exact minimum distortions found by Reluplex in small networks while our algorithms are more than 10,000 times faster; (2) our methods deliver similar quality of bounds (the gap is within 35% and usually around 10%; sometimes our bounds are even better) for larger networks compared to the methods based on solving linear programming problems but our algorithms are 33-14,000 times faster; (3) our method is capable of solving large MNIST and CIFAR networks up to 7 layers with more than 10,000 neurons within tens of seconds on a single CPU core. In addition, we show that there is no polynomial time algorithm that can approximately find the minimum $\ell_1$ adversarial distortion of a ReLU network with a $0.99\ln n$ approximation ratio unless NP=P, where $n$ is the number of neurons in the network.

paragraphs: Certifying robustness asks how much an input must change before an adversarial example becomes possible. Exact verification for general ReLU networks is computationally hard. This paper instead computes certified lower bounds on the smallest adversarial distortion, providing a guaranteed threshold even when the exact minimum is impractical to obtain.

The authors introduce Fast-Lin and Fast-Lip, which exploit ReLU network structure. On small networks, their bounds are within a factor of two to three of exact minimum distortions computed by Reluplex, with more than a 10,000-fold speed advantage. On larger networks, they report bounds of similar quality to linear-programming methods and substantial speed improvements.

The experiments also cover MNIST and CIFAR networks with up to seven layers and more than 10,000 neurons, processed within tens of seconds on one CPU core. Separately, the paper proves a conditional hardness result: unless P equals NP, no polynomial-time algorithm achieves the stated 0.99 ln n approximation ratio for minimum l1 adversarial distortion. This distinguishes fast certification of lower bounds from solving the underlying minimum-distortion problem.
summary.tldr: Fast-Lin and Fast-Lip efficiently certify lower bounds on adversarial distortion by exploiting ReLU network structure.

title: Towards Fast Computation of Certified Robustness for ReLU Networks

abstract: Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods are limited typically to a small number of agents. When the agent number increases largely, the learning becomes intractable due to the curse of the dimensionality and the exponential growth of agent interactions. In this paper, we present Mean Field Reinforcement Learning where the interactions within the population of agents are approximated by those between a single agent and the average effect from the overall population or neighboring agents; the interplay between the two entities is mutually reinforced: the learning of the individual agent’s optimal policy depends on the dynamics of the population, while the dynamics of the population change according to the collective patterns of the individual policies. We develop practical mean field Q-learning and mean field Actor-Critic algorithms and analyze the convergence of the solution to Nash equilibrium. Experiments on Gaussian squeeze, Ising model, and battle games justify the learning effectiveness of our mean field approaches. In addition, we report the first result to solve the Ising model via model-free reinforcement learning methods.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning becomes difficult as the number of agents grows because the space of interactions expands rapidly. The paper proposes a mean field approximation: represent interactions through an individual agent and the average effect of the population or its neighbors. This reduces the interaction structure that the learner must explicitly handle.

The approximation still captures feedback between individual and collective behavior. An agent learns its policy in response to population dynamics, while those dynamics change as individual policies collectively change. The authors develop mean field Q-learning and mean field Actor-Critic algorithms around this relationship and analyze convergence of the solution to a Nash equilibrium.

Experiments on Gaussian squeeze, the Ising model, and battle games support the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The authors also report the first solution of the Ising model using model-free reinforcement learning. The central contribution is a practical route to learning with large agent populations by replacing detailed interactions with an average-effect approximation while retaining the mutual influence of agents and population.
summary.tldr: Mean field reinforcement learning approximates many-agent interactions through average population effects to make learning more tractable.

title: Mean Field Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: There are great interests as well as many challenges in applying reinforcement learning (RL) to recommendation systems. In this setting, an online user is the environment; neither the reward function nor the environment dynamics are clearly defined, making the application of RL challenging. In this paper, we propose a novel model-based reinforcement learning framework for recommendation systems, where we develop a generative adversarial network to imitate user behavior dynamics and learn her reward function. Using this user model as the simulation environment, we develop a novel Cascading DQN algorithm to obtain a combinatorial recommendation policy which can handle a large number of candidate items efficiently. In our experiments with real data, we show this generative adversarial user model can better explain user behavior than alternatives, and the RL policy based on this model can lead to a better long-term reward for the user and higher click rate for the system.

paragraphs: Applying reinforcement learning to recommendations requires a model of how users respond and what outcomes they value. Both are difficult to specify directly: the user acts as the environment, but neither the response dynamics nor the reward function is clearly defined. This paper addresses those uncertainties through a learned user model.

The framework uses a generative adversarial network to imitate user behavior dynamics and learn a reward function. It then treats that user model as a simulation environment for learning recommendations. A proposed Cascading DQN algorithm constructs a combinatorial recommendation policy while handling a large pool of candidate items efficiently. User modeling and policy learning therefore form connected parts of the same model-based approach.

In experiments using real data, the adversarial user model explains behavior better than the alternatives considered. Policies learned with this model can also produce higher long-term user reward and a higher system click rate. These results support the usefulness of learning a user environment for recommendation, while retaining the paper's empirical and qualified claim about improved outcomes.
summary.tldr: An adversarially learned user simulator supports efficient reinforcement learning for recommendations and improves reported behavioral and reward outcomes.

title: Generative Adversarial User Model for Reinforcement Learning Based Recommendation System

abstract: Good data stewardship requires removal of data at the request of the data’s owner. This raises the question if and how a trained machine-learning model, which implicitly stores information about its training data, should be affected by such a removal request. Is it possible to “remove” data from a machine-learning model? We study this problem by defining certified removal: a very strong theoretical guarantee that a model from which data is removed cannot be distinguished from a model that never observed the data to begin with. We develop a certified-removal mechanism for linear classifiers and empirically study learning settings in which this mechanism is practical.

We study this problem by defining certified removal: a very strong theoretical guarantee that a model from which data is removed cannot be distinguished from a model that never observed the data to begin with. paragraphs: A request to delete training data raises a question about the model that already learned from it. Removing the original record does not by itself describe what should happen to information stored implicitly in the trained model. This paper studies how to give removal from a model a precise meaning that can support a theoretical guarantee.

The authors define certified removal through indistinguishability: after removal, the resulting model cannot be distinguished from one that never encountered the deleted data. This establishes a reference point for evaluating a removal procedure. The objective concerns the trained model's relationship to the removed information, extending the deletion question beyond whether the underlying data record still exists.

The paper develops a mechanism meeting this certified-removal objective for linear classifiers and empirically examines learning settings where it is practical. Its contribution combines a formal standard with a concrete mechanism in that model class. The empirical study addresses whether the guarantee can be made useful in practice within the settings considered.
summary.tldr: The paper defines certified data removal and develops a mechanism for linear classifiers whose resulting models are indistinguishable from models that never saw the removed data.

title: Certified Data Removal from Machine Learning Models

abstract: Many cooperative multiagent reinforcement learning environments provide agents with a sparse team-based reward, as well as a dense agent-specific reward that incentivizes learning basic skills. Training policies solely on the team-based reward is often difficult due to its sparsity. Also, relying solely on the agent-specific reward is sub-optimal because it usually does not capture the team coordination objective. A common approach is to use reward shaping to construct a proxy reward by combining the individual rewards. However, this requires manual tuning for each environment. We introduce Multiagent Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (MERL), a split-level training platform that handles the two objectives separately through two optimization processes. An evolutionary algorithm maximizes the sparse team-based objective through neuroevolution on a population of teams. Concurrently, a gradient-based optimizer trains policies to only maximize the dense agent-specific rewards. The gradient-based policies are periodically added to the evolutionary population as a way of information transfer between the two optimization processes. This enables the evolutionary algorithm to use skills learned via the agent-specific rewards toward optimizing the global objective. Results demonstrate that MERL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, such as MADDPG, on a number of difficult coordination benchmarks.
