paragraphs: Cooperative reinforcement learning can provide two kinds of feedback: rare rewards for team success and frequent rewards for individual skills. Team rewards can be difficult to learn from because they are sparse, while individual rewards usually fail to capture coordination fully. Combining them into a proxy reward also requires manual tuning for each environment.

Multiagent Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning, or MERL, handles the objectives through separate optimization processes. An evolutionary algorithm optimizes the sparse team objective across a population of teams. At the same time, a gradient-based optimizer trains policies using only the dense rewards assigned to individual agents.

Periodically, the gradient-trained policies enter the evolutionary population. This transfers learned skills into the process that evaluates team performance, allowing evolution to use those skills toward the shared objective. The authors report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods, including MADDPG, on difficult coordination benchmarks. The results support separating skill acquisition from team-level optimization while maintaining an explicit route for exchanging useful policies.
summary.tldr: MERL combines evolution for team rewards with gradient learning for individual skills, improving performance on difficult coordination benchmarks.

title: Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning for Sample-Efficient Multiagent Coordination

abstract: Supervised learning requires the specification of a loss function to minimise. While the theory of admissible losses from both a computational and statistical perspective is well-developed, these offer a panoply of different choices. In practice, this choice is typically made in an \emph{ad hoc} manner. In hopes of making this procedure more principled, the problem of \emph{learning the loss function} for a downstream task (e.g., classification) has garnered recent interest. However, works in this area have been generally empirical in nature. In this paper, we revisit the {\sc SLIsotron} algorithm of Kakade et al. (2011) through a novel lens, derive a generalisation based on Bregman divergences, and show how it provides a principled procedure for learning the loss. In detail, we cast {\sc SLIsotron} as learning a loss from a family of composite square losses. By interpreting this through the lens of \emph{proper losses}, we derive a generalisation of {\sc SLIsotron} based on Bregman divergences. The resulting {\sc BregmanTron} algorithm jointly learns the loss along with the classifier. It comes equipped with a simple guarantee of convergence for the loss it learns, and its set of possible outputs comes with a guarantee of agnostic approximability of Bayes rule. Experiments indicate that the {\sc BregmanTron} significantly outperforms the {\sc SLIsotron}, and that the loss it learns can be minimized by other algorithms for different tasks, thereby opening the interesting problem of \emph{loss transfer} between domains.

summary.tldr: BregmanTron jointly learns a classifier and its loss, combining theoretical guarantees with empirical gains and evidence for possible loss transfer.

title: Supervised learning: no loss no cry

abstract: Thompson sampling is an efficient algorithm for sequential decision making, which exploits the posterior uncertainty to address the exploration-exploitation dilemma. There has been significant recent interest in integrating Bayesian neural networks into Thompson sampling. Most of these methods rely on global variable uncertainty for exploration. In this paper, we propose a new probabilistic modeling framework for Thompson sampling, where local latent variable uncertainty is used to sample the mean reward. Variational inference is used to approximate the posterior of the local variable, and semi-implicit structure is further introduced to enhance its expressiveness. Our experimental results on eight contextual bandit benchmark datasets show that Thompson sampling guided by local uncertainty achieves state-of-the-art performance while having low computational complexity.
originalAbstract: Thompson sampling is an efficient algorithm for sequential decision making, which exploits the posterior uncertainty to address the exploration-exploitation dilemma. There has been significant recent interest in integrating Bayesian neural networks into Thompson sampling. Most of these methods rely on global variable uncertainty for exploration. In this paper, we propose a new probabilistic modeling framework for Thompson sampling, where local latent variable uncertainty is used to sample the mean reward. Variational inference is used to approximate the posterior of the local variable, and semi-implicit structure is further introduced to enhance its expressiveness. Our experimental results on eight contextual bandit benchmark datasets show that Thompson sampling guided by local uncertainty achieves state-of-the-art performance while having low computational complexity.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling uses posterior uncertainty to balance exploring uncertain options with choosing options that appear rewarding. Neural approaches often represent that uncertainty through global variables. This paper proposes a probabilistic framework in which uncertainty in local latent variables instead supplies the sampled mean rewards used for decision making.

The authors approximate the local-variable posterior with variational inference. They then introduce a semi-implicit structure to make that approximation more expressive. The modeling choice places the source of exploration in the local uncertainty representation, providing an alternative to the global-variable uncertainty used by many Bayesian neural approaches.

Experiments on eight contextual bandit benchmark datasets show state-of-the-art performance together with low computational complexity. These findings support local uncertainty as an effective guide for Thompson sampling on the evaluated tasks. The significance is that the representation of uncertainty is itself a design decision: the paper changes where uncertainty enters reward sampling and reports strong results without requiring the same global uncertainty formulation as the methods motivating the work.
summary.tldr: Thompson sampling driven by local latent uncertainty achieves strong contextual bandit benchmark performance with low computational complexity.

title: Thompson Sampling via Local Uncertainty

abstract: Counterfactual estimation using synthetic controls is one of the most successful recent methodological developments in causal inference. Despite its popularity, the current description only considers time series aligned across units and synthetic controls expressed as linear combinations of observed control units. We propose a continuous-time alternative that models the latent counterfactual path explicitly using the formalism of controlled differential equations. This model is directly applicable to the general setting of irregularly-aligned multivariate time series and may be optimized in rich function spaces – thereby improving on some limitations of existing approaches.
originalAbstract: Counterfactual estimation using synthetic controls is one of the most successful recent methodological developments in causal inference. Despite its popularity, the current description only considers time series aligned across units and synthetic controls expressed as linear combinations of observed control units. We propose a continuous-time alternative that models the latent counterfactual path explicitly using the formalism of controlled differential equations. This model is directly applicable to the general setting of irregularly-aligned multivariate time series and may be optimized in rich function spaces – thereby improving on some limitations of existing approaches.

paragraphs: Synthetic controls estimate a counterfactual trajectory: how a unit’s outcomes might have evolved under the alternative being studied. The paper focuses on two restrictions in the existing formulation. Time series are assumed to align across units, and the synthetic control is represented as a linear combination of observed control units.

The proposed alternative works in continuous time and explicitly models the latent counterfactual path using controlled differential equations. Treating the counterfactual as a path gives the method a formulation that can directly accommodate multivariate observations recorded at irregularly aligned times. The target of estimation remains the unobserved trajectory needed for policy analysis.

The model can also be optimized within rich function spaces, expanding the available representations beyond the stated linear-combination formulation. The contribution is therefore a methodological extension of synthetic controls to more flexible temporal and functional settings. Its stated benefit is direct applicability to irregular multivariate time series, addressing the alignment and representation restrictions identified by the authors.
summary.tldr: A continuous-time synthetic-control formulation models counterfactual paths for irregularly aligned multivariate time series.

title: Policy Analysis using Synthetic Controls in Continuous-Time

abstract: Generalized linear models (GLMs) such as logistic regression are among the most widely used arms in data analyst’s repertoire and often used on sensitive datasets. A large body of prior works that investigate GLMs under differential privacy (DP) constraints provide only private point estimates of the regression coefficients, and are not able to quantify parameter uncertainty. In this work, with logistic and Poisson regression as running examples, we introduce a generic noise-aware DP Bayesian inference method for a GLM at hand, given a noisy sum of summary statistics. Quantifying uncertainty allows us to determine which of the regression coefficients are statistically significantly different from zero. We provide a previously unknown tight privacy analysis and experimentally demonstrate that the posteriors obtained from our model, while adhering to strong privacy guarantees, are close to the non-private posteriors.

In this work, with logistic and Poisson regression as running examples, we introduce a generic noise-aware DP Bayesian inference method for a GLM at hand, given a noisy sum of summary statistics. Quantifying uncertainty allows us to determine which of the regression coefficients are statistically significantly different from zero. We provide a previously unknown tight privacy analysis and experimentally demonstrate that the posteriors obtained from our model, while adhering to strong privacy guarantees, are close to the non-private posteriors.

paragraphs: Generalized linear models are widely used on sensitive datasets, but many differentially private methods return only a single estimate of each regression coefficient. Such estimates do not describe uncertainty about the parameters. This paper develops a Bayesian approach that provides parameter distributions while accounting for the noise introduced to protect privacy.

The method starts from a noisy sum of summary statistics and performs noise-aware inference for the chosen generalized linear model. Logistic and Poisson regression serve as running examples. Because the output captures uncertainty, it can support judgments about which coefficients are statistically distinguishable from zero, extending the analysis beyond private point estimates.

The authors provide a tight privacy analysis and experimentally compare the resulting posterior distributions with their non-private counterparts. In those experiments, the private posteriors remain close to the non-private ones while satisfying strong privacy guarantees. The findings suggest that explicitly modeling privacy noise can preserve useful uncertainty information, allowing privacy protection and Bayesian parameter assessment to be handled within one framework.
summary.tldr: This noise-aware Bayesian method produces private parameter uncertainty estimates for generalized linear models from noisy summary statistics.

title: Differentially Private Bayesian Inference for Generalized Linear Models

abstract: Meta-learning, or learning-to-learn, seeks to design algorithms that can utilize previous experience to rapidly learn new skills or adapt to new environments. Representation learning—a key tool for performing meta-learning—learns a data representation that can transfer knowledge across multiple tasks, which is essential in regimes where data is scarce. Despite a recent surge of interest in the practice of meta-learning, the theoretical underpinnings of meta-learning algorithms are lacking, especially in the context of learning transferable representations. In this paper, we focus on the problem of multi-task linear regression—in which multiple linear regression models share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Here, we provide provably fast, sample-efficient algorithms to address the dual challenges of (1) learning a common set of features from multiple, related tasks, and (2) transferring this knowledge to new, unseen tasks. Both are central to the general problem of meta-learning. Finally, we complement these results by providing information-theoretic lower bounds on the sample complexity of learning these linear features.

Representation learning—a key tool for performing meta-learning—learns a data representation that can transfer knowledge across multiple tasks, which is essential in regimes where data is scarce. Despite a recent surge of interest in the practice of meta-learning, the theoretical underpinnings of meta-learning algorithms are lacking, especially in the context of learning transferable representations. In this paper, we focus on the problem of multi-task linear regression—in which multiple linear regression models share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Here, we provide provably fast, sample-efficient algorithms to address the dual challenges of (1) learning a common set of features from multiple, related tasks, and (2) transferring this knowledge to new, unseen tasks. Both are central to the general problem of meta-learning. Finally, we complement these results by providing information-theoretic lower bounds on the sample complexity of learning these linear features.

This paper develops theoretical foundations for such transfer in a specific setting: multiple linear regression tasks share a common low-dimensional linear representation.

The authors provide provably fast and sample-efficient algorithms for two linked problems. The first is discovering shared features from several related tasks. The second is using those features to learn previously unseen tasks. Studying both steps makes explicit how a representation is acquired and how it subsequently supports adaptation when data is scarce.

The paper also establishes information-theoretic lower bounds on the number of samples needed to learn the linear features. These complement the algorithmic guarantees by describing fundamental data requirements for the problem. The results supply a rigorous treatment of representation-based meta-learning within the shared linear model setting, where the structure connecting tasks is precisely specified.
summary.tldr: The paper gives efficient algorithms and sample-complexity lower bounds for learning and transferring shared linear representations across regression tasks.

title: Provable Meta-Learning of Linear Representations

abstract: The Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test is a classical procedure for graph isomorphism testing. The WL test has also been widely used both for designing graph kernels and for analyzing graph neural networks. In this paper, we propose the Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) distance, a notion of distance between labeled measure Markov chains (LMMCs), of which labeled graphs are special cases. The WL distance is polynomial time computable and is also compatible with the WL test in the sense that the former is positive if and only if the WL test can distinguish the two involved graphs. The WL distance captures and compares subtle structures of the underlying LMMCs and, as a consequence of this, it is more discriminating than the distance between graphs used for defining the state-of-the-art Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman graph kernel. Inspired by the structure of the WL distance we identify a neural network architecture on LMMCs which turns out to be universal w.r.t. continuous functions defined on the space of all LMMCs (which includes all graphs) endowed with the WL distance. Finally, the WL distance turns out to be stable w.r.t. a natural variant of the Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance for comparing metric Markov chains that we identify. Hence, the WL distance can also be construed as a polynomial time lower bound for the GW distance which is in general NP-hard to compute.

title: Weisfeiler-Lehman Meets Gromov-Wasserstein

abstract: Certified defenses such as randomized smoothing have shown promise towards building reliable machine learning systems against $\ell_p$ norm bounded attacks. However, existing methods are insufficient or unable to provably defend against semantic transformations, especially those without closed-form expressions (such as defocus blur and pixelate), which are more common in practice and often unrestricted. To fill up this gap, we propose generalized randomized smoothing (GSmooth), a unified theoretical framework for certifying robustness against general semantic transformations via a novel dimension augmentation strategy. Under the GSmooth framework, we present a scalable algorithm that uses a surrogate image-to-image network to approximate the complex transformation. The surrogate model provides a powerful tool for studying the properties of semantic transformations and certifying robustness. Experimental results on several datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach for robustness certification against multiple kinds of semantic transformations and corruptions, which is not achievable by the alternative baselines.

The surrogate provides a way to study transformation properties and support robustness certification when the transformation itself is difficult to handle analytically.

The contribution expands the kinds of input changes that a certification approach can address. summary.tldr: GSmooth extends robustness certification to complex semantic transformations using dimension augmentation and learned transformation surrogates.

title: GSmooth: Certified Robustness against Semantic Transformations via Generalized Randomized Smoothing

abstract: In the pursuit of explaining implicit regularization in deep learning, prominent focus was given to matrix and tensor factorizations, which correspond to simplified neural networks. It was shown that these models exhibit an implicit tendency towards low matrix and tensor ranks, respectively. Drawing closer to practical deep learning, the current paper theoretically analyzes the implicit regularization in hierarchical tensor factorization, a model equivalent to certain deep convolutional neural networks. Through a dynamical systems lens, we overcome challenges associated with hierarchy, and establish implicit regularization towards low hierarchical tensor rank. This translates to an implicit regularization towards locality for the associated convolutional networks. Inspired by our theory, we design explicit regularization discouraging locality, and demonstrate its ability to improve the performance of modern convolutional networks on non-local tasks, in defiance of conventional wisdom by which architectural changes are needed. Our work highlights the potential of enhancing neural networks via theoretical analysis of their implicit regularization.

paragraphs: Implicit regularization describes preferences that arise from learning even without an explicit penalty enforcing them. Earlier analyses of matrix and tensor factorizations found tendencies toward low-rank solutions. This paper extends that line of work to hierarchical tensor factorization, a model equivalent to certain deep convolutional networks and therefore closer to practical deep learning.

Using a dynamical systems analysis, the authors establish a tendency toward low hierarchical tensor rank. For the associated convolutional networks, that result translates into a preference for locality. The theoretical connection identifies a structural bias in the learning process: the kinds of solutions favored by training depend on the hierarchy of the model.

The authors then use this insight to design explicit regularization that discourages locality. They demonstrate improved performance of modern convolutional networks on non-local tasks, showing that a training objective can help address a bias often approached through architectural changes. The result links theoretical diagnosis to a practical intervention, while the formal equivalence applies to the particular convolutional networks associated with the analyzed factorization.
summary.tldr: The paper connects implicit low-rank learning in hierarchical tensor models to locality in certain convolutional networks, then uses that insight to improve non-local tasks.

title: Implicit Regularization in Hierarchical Tensor Factorization and Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Federated learning is a powerful distributed learning scheme that allows numerous edge devices to collaboratively train a model without sharing their data. However, training is resource-intensive for edge devices, and limited network bandwidth is often the main bottleneck. Prior work often overcomes the constraints by condensing the models or messages into compact formats, e.g., by gradient compression or distillation. In contrast, we propose ProgFed, the first progressive training framework for efficient and effective federated learning. It inherently reduces computation and two-way communication costs while maintaining the strong performance of the final models. We theoretically prove that ProgFed converges at the same asymptotic rate as standard training on full models. Extensive results on a broad range of architectures, including CNNs (VGG, ResNet, ConvNets) and U-nets, and diverse tasks from simple classification to medical image segmentation show that our highly effective training approach saves up to $20%$ computation and up to $63%$ communication costs for converged models. As our approach is also complimentary to prior work on compression, we can achieve a wide range of trade-offs by combining these techniques, showing reduced communication of up to $50\times$ at only $0.1%$ loss in utility. Code is available at https://github.com/a514514772/ProgFed.

However, local training consumes device resources, and communication can be constrained by network bandwidth. ProgFed addresses these costs through progressive training, changing the training framework itself to reduce computation and communication in both directions.

The authors prove that ProgFed has the same asymptotic convergence rate as standard training of full models. Their experiments span several convolutional architectures and U-nets, with tasks ranging from classification to medical image segmentation. These results position ProgFed as a complementary training strategy whose resource savings can extend beyond those obtained from compact messages alone.
summary.tldr: ProgFed uses progressive federated training to reduce computation and communication while maintaining strong performance and the standard asymptotic convergence rate.

title: ProgFed: Effective, Communication, and Computation Efficient Federated Learning by Progressive Training

abstract: We introduce a new training paradigm that enforces interval constraints on neural network parameter space to control forgetting. Contemporary Continual Learning (CL) methods focus on training neural networks efficiently from a stream of data, while reducing the negative impact of catastrophic forgetting, yet they do not provide any firm guarantees that network performance will not deteriorate uncontrollably over time. In this work, we show how to put bounds on forgetting by reformulating continual learning of a model as a continual contraction of its parameter space. To that end, we propose Hyperrectangle Training, a new training methodology where each task is represented by a hyperrectangle in the parameter space, fully contained in the hyperrectangles of the previous tasks. This formulation reduces the NP-hard CL problem back to polynomial time while providing full resilience against forgetting. We validate our claim by developing InterContiNet (Interval Continual Learning) algorithm which leverages interval arithmetic to effectively model parameter regions as hyperrectangles. Through experimental results, we show that our approach performs well in a continual learning setup without storing data from previous tasks.

paragraphs: Continual learning trains a network on a stream of tasks while trying to retain earlier capabilities. The paper targets catastrophic forgetting, where learning new information damages previous performance. Its central proposal is to control which parameter values remain available as training proceeds, turning retention into a constraint on the model’s parameter space.

Hyperrectangle Training represents each task with a region defined by intervals for the network’s parameters. Each new region must fit entirely inside the regions associated with previous tasks. Continual learning therefore becomes a sequence of contractions of the allowed parameter space. The authors use this formulation to establish bounds on forgetting and claim full resilience against forgetting within it.

The paper presents this reformulation as reducing the NP-hard continual-learning problem to polynomial time. Its InterContiNet algorithm uses interval arithmetic to represent and work with the parameter regions. Experiments show good continual-learning performance without retaining data from previous tasks, linking the proposed geometric constraints to an implemented approach that does not require replaying stored examples.
summary.tldr: Hyperrectangle Training constrains successive tasks to nested parameter regions to bound forgetting, with an interval-based implementation that does not store past-task data.

title: Continual Learning with Guarantees via Weight Interval Constraints

abstract: A large body of the "Inverse Reinforcement Learning" (IRL) literature focuses on recovering the reward function from a set of demonstrations of an expert agent who acts optimally or noisily optimally. Nevertheless, some recent works move away from the optimality assumption to study the "Learning from a Learner (LfL)" problem, where the challenge is inferring the reward function of a learning agent from a sequence of demonstrations produced by progressively improving policies. In this work, we take one of the initial steps in addressing the multi-agent version of this problem and propose a new algorithm, MA-LfL (Multiagent Learning from a Learner). Unlike the state-of-the-art literature, which recovers the reward functions from trajectories produced by agents in some equilibrium, we study the problem of inferring the reward functions of interacting agents in a general sum stochastic game without assuming any equilibrium state. The MA-LfL algorithm is rigorously built on a theoretical result that ensures its validity in the case of agents learning according to a multi-agent soft policy iteration scheme. We empirically test MA-LfL and we observe high positive correlation between the recovered reward functions and the ground truth.

paragraphs: Inferring an agent's reward function from its behavior is often studied using demonstrations from an expert or an agent already near optimal performance. Learning from a Learner instead uses demonstrations produced as a policy improves. This paper extends that perspective to interacting agents whose behavior changes during learning in a general-sum stochastic game.

The proposed MA-LfL algorithm aims to recover the agents' reward functions without assuming that their demonstrations come from an equilibrium. This distinction matters because ongoing adaptation is part of the observed process. The method treats a sequence of improving policies as evidence about what the agents are trying to achieve.

A theoretical result establishes the algorithm's validity when the agents learn through a multi-agent soft policy iteration scheme. The guarantee is therefore tied to a particular learning process, even though equilibrium is not required. Empirical tests show high positive correlation between recovered rewards and ground truth, supporting the approach's ability to infer reward structure in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: MA-LfL infers rewards from interacting agents still learning, with theoretical validity under multi-agent soft policy iteration.

title: Multi-Agent Learning from Learners

abstract: Optimal transport (OT) theory focuses, among all maps $T:\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d$ that can morph a probability measure $\mu$ onto another $\nu$, on those that are the “thriftiest”, i.e. such that the average cost $c(x, T(x))$ between $x$ and its image $T(x)$ is as small as possible. Many computational approaches have been proposed to estimate such Monge maps when $c$ is the squared-Euclidean distance, e.g., using entropic maps [Pooladian+2021], or input convex neural networks [Makkuva+2020, Korotin+2020]. We propose a new research direction, that leverages a specific translation invariant cost $c(x, y):=h(x-y)$ inspired by the elastic net. Here, $h:=\tfrac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|_2^2+\tau(\cdot)$, where $\tau$ is a convex function. We highlight a surprising link tying together a generalized entropic map for $h$, Bregman centroids induced by $h$, and the proximal operator of $\tau$. We show how setting $\tau$ to be a sparsity-inducing norm results in the first application of Occam ’s razor to transport. These maps yield, mechanically, displacement vectors $\Delta(x):= T(x)-x$ that are sparse, with sparsity patterns that vary depending on $x$. We showcase the ability of our method to estimate meaningful OT maps for high-dimensional single-cell transcription data. We use our methods in the $34000$-d space of gene counts for cells, without using a prior dimensionality reduction, thus retaining the ability to interpret all displacements at the gene level.

This paper changes that cost to favor transformations that alter only a small number of features. The aim is to make transport maps interpretable in high-dimensional spaces, where the individual coordinates can carry meaningful information.

It works directly in that space without prior dimensionality reduction, retaining gene-level interpretation of the estimated changes. The contribution therefore joins a mathematical construction for sparse transport with an application where keeping the original coordinates makes the resulting maps easier to interpret.
summary.tldr: A sparsity-promoting transport cost yields interpretable maps that change selected features, demonstrated directly in 34,000-dimensional gene-count data.

title: Monge, Bregman and Occam: Interpretable Optimal Transport in High-Dimensions with Feature-Sparse Maps

abstract: Contrastively trained encoders have recently been proven to invert the data-generating process: they encode each input, e.g., an image, into the true latent vector that generated the image (Zimmermann et al., 2021). However, real-world observations often have inherent ambiguities. For instance, images may be blurred or only show a 2D view of a 3D object, so multiple latents could have generated them. This makes the true posterior for the latent vector probabilistic with heteroscedastic uncertainty. In this setup, we extend the common InfoNCE objective and encoders to predict latent distributions instead of points. We prove that these distributions recover the correct posteriors of the data-generating process, including its level of aleatoric uncertainty, up to a rotation of the latent space. In addition to providing calibrated uncertainty estimates, these posteriors allow the computation of credible intervals in image retrieval. They comprise images with the same latent as a given query, subject to its uncertainty. Code is at https://github.com/mkirchhof/Probabilistic_Contrastive_Learning .

paragraphs: An observation may not uniquely reveal the latent factors that generated it. A blurred image or a two-dimensional view of a three-dimensional object can be compatible with multiple latent explanations. This paper studies contrastive learning in that ambiguous setting, where uncertainty is inherent in the observation and its amount can differ between inputs.

The authors extend the InfoNCE objective and the encoder so that each input is represented by a probability distribution over latents rather than a single point. In the setup they study, they prove that these predicted distributions recover the correct posterior distributions, including their aleatoric uncertainty. Recovery is defined up to a rotation of the latent space, preserving that qualification on the theoretical result.

These distributions support calibrated uncertainty estimates and credible intervals for image retrieval. A retrieval result can therefore express which images share the query’s latent explanation while accounting for ambiguity in the query itself. The contribution links a probabilistic contrastive objective to recovery of meaningful uncertainty, extending the representation from one latent estimate to a distribution of plausible explanations.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic contrastive learning recovers latent posteriors and inherent input uncertainty up to rotation in the studied setup.

title: Probabilistic Contrastive Learning Recovers the Correct Aleatoric Uncertainty of Ambiguous Inputs

abstract: Understanding geometric properties of the latent spaces of natural language processing models allows the manipulation of these properties for improved performance on downstream tasks. One such property is the amount of data spread in a model’s latent space, or how fully the available latent space is being used. We demonstrate that the commonly used measures of data spread, average cosine similarity and a partition function min/max ratio I(V), do not provide reliable metrics to compare the use of latent space across data distributions. We propose and examine six alternative measures of data spread, all of which improve over these current metrics when applied to seven synthetic data distributions. Of our proposed measures, we recommend one principal component-based measure and one entropy-based measure that provide reliable, relative measures of spread and can be used to compare models of different sizes and dimensionalities.

paragraphs: The geometry of a language model’s latent representations can help explain how it uses its available representational space. This paper focuses on data spread: how fully representations occupy that space. Reliable measurement matters if researchers want to compare models or manipulate geometric properties in pursuit of better downstream performance.

The authors demonstrate that two commonly used measures, average cosine similarity and a partition-function minimum-to-maximum ratio, do not reliably compare space usage across different data distributions. They propose six alternative measures and examine them on seven synthetic distributions. All six improve on the existing measures in that evaluation, showing that familiar summaries can miss aspects of spread that alternative measurements capture.

From these alternatives, the paper recommends one measure based on principal components and another based on entropy. Both provide reliable relative comparisons and support comparisons across models of different sizes and representation dimensions. The contribution is a better basis for measuring latent geometry; the stated experiments establish comparative measurement behavior rather than a downstream performance gain from changing a model’s representations.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies unreliable latent-space spread metrics and recommends principal-component and entropy-based alternatives for comparing different models.

title: Reliable Measures of Spread in High Dimensional Latent Spaces

abstract: Fine-tuning a pre-trained language model (PLM) emerges as the predominant strategy in many natural language processing applications. However, even fine-tuning the PLMs and doing inference are expensive, especially on edge devices with low computing power. Some general approaches (e.g. quantization and distillation) have been widely studied to reduce the compute/memory of PLM fine-tuning, while very few one-shot compression techniques are explored. In this paper, we investigate the neural tangent kernel (NTK)–which reveals the gradient descent dynamics of neural networks–of the multilayer perceptrons (MLP) modules in a PLM and propose to coin a lightweight PLM through NTK-approximating MLP fusion. To achieve this, we reconsider the MLP as a bundle of sub-MLPs, and cluster them into a given number of centroids, which can then be restored as a compressed MLP and surprisingly shown to well approximate the NTK of the original PLM. Extensive experiments of PLM fine-tuning on both natural language understanding (NLU) and generation (NLG) tasks are provided to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method MLP fusion. Our code is available at https://github.com/weitianxin/MLP_Fusion.

This paper explores a one-shot compression approach focused on the multilayer perceptron modules within a language model. Its guiding question is whether those modules can shrink while preserving important aspects of their learning behavior.

The authors view an MLP as a collection of smaller sub-MLPs and cluster them into a chosen number of centroids. Those centroids form a compressed MLP. The construction aims to approximate the original module’s neural tangent kernel, which describes gradient-descent dynamics in the associated theoretical framework.

Experiments cover fine-tuning for natural-language understanding and generation and support the effectiveness of MLP fusion. The contribution links a concrete compression operation to preservation of a learning-dynamics representation. The abstract does not give compression ratios or numerical quality losses, so it establishes the method and evaluation scope without specifying a universal efficiency–accuracy tradeoff.
summary.tldr: MLP fusion compresses language-model feedforward modules by clustering submodules while approximating their neural tangent kernel.

title: NTK-approximating MLP Fusion for Efficient Language Model Fine-tuning

abstract: We prove that the combination of a target network and over-parameterized linear function approximation establishes a weaker convergence condition for bootstrapped value estimation in certain cases, even with off-policy data. Our condition is naturally satisfied for expected updates over the entire state-action space or learning with a batch of complete trajectories from episodic Markov decision processes. Notably, using only a target network or an over-parameterized model does not provide such a convergence guarantee. Additionally, we extend our results to learning with truncated trajectories, showing that convergence is achievable for all tasks with minor modifications, akin to value truncation for the final states in trajectories. Our primary result focuses on temporal difference estimation for prediction, providing high-probability value estimation error bounds and empirical analysis on Baird’s counterexample and a Four-room task. Furthermore, we explore the control setting, demonstrating that similar convergence conditions apply to Q-learning.

summary.tldr: Target networks and over-parameterized linear models jointly provide convergence guarantees for bootstrapped value learning under the paper’s stated conditions.

title: Target Networks and Over-parameterization Stabilize Off-policy Bootstrapping with Function Approximation

abstract: The inadequate mixing of conventional Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods for multi-modal distributions presents a significant challenge in practical applications such as Bayesian inference and molecular dynamics. Addressing this, we propose Diffusive Gibbs Sampling (DiGS), an innovative family of sampling methods designed for effective sampling from distributions characterized by distant and disconnected modes. DiGS integrates recent developments in diffusion models, leveraging Gaussian convolution to create an auxiliary noisy distribution that bridges isolated modes in the original space and applying Gibbs sampling to alternately draw samples from both spaces. A novel Metropolis-within-Gibbs scheme is proposed to enhance mixing in the denoising sampling step. DiGS exhibits a better mixing property for sampling multi-modal distributions than state-of-the-art methods such as parallel tempering, attaining substantially improved performance across various tasks, including mixtures of Gaussians, Bayesian neural networks and molecular dynamics.

paragraphs: Sampling becomes difficult when a probability distribution has several important regions separated by large gaps. Conventional Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods can explore one region without moving effectively to the others. This poor mixing is a practical problem in applications such as Bayesian inference and molecular dynamics, where samples need to represent multiple possible configurations.

Diffusive Gibbs Sampling introduces an auxiliary noisy distribution using Gaussian convolution. This smoothing creates connections between modes that are isolated in the original space. The sampler alternates between the original and noisy spaces using Gibbs sampling, making the auxiliary space part of the exploration process. A new Metropolis-within-Gibbs scheme further improves mixing during the denoising sampling step.

The authors report better mixing than leading alternatives, including parallel tempering, and substantially improved performance on Gaussian mixtures, Bayesian neural networks, and molecular dynamics tasks. The central idea is to use a noisy companion distribution to support movement between separated regions. Its reported benefits concern more effective exploration of multimodal distributions across these evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: Diffusive Gibbs Sampling alternates between original and noise-smoothed distributions to improve exploration of distant probability modes.

title: Diffusive Gibbs Sampling

abstract: In drug development, early phase dose-finding clinical trials are carried out to identify an optimal dose to administer to patients in larger confirmatory clinical trials. Standard trial procedures do not optimize for participant benefit and do not consider participant heterogeneity, despite consequences to participants’ health and downstream impacts to under-represented population subgroups. Many novel drugs also do not obey parametric modelling assumptions made in common dose-finding procedures. We present Safe Allocation for Exploration of Treatments SAFE-T, a procedure for adaptive dose-finding that adheres to safety constraints, improves utility for heterogeneous participants, and works well with small sample sizes. SAFE-T flexibly learns non-parametric multi-output Gaussian process models for dose toxicity and efficacy, using Bayesian optimization, and provides accurate final dose recommendations. We provide theoretical guarantees for the satisfaction of safety constraints. Using a comprehensive set of realistic synthetic scenarios, we demonstrate empirically that SAFE-T generally outperforms comparable methods and maintains performance across variations in sample size and subgroup distribution. Finally, we extend SAFE-T to a new adaptive setting, demonstrating its potential to improve traditional clinical trial procedures.

paragraphs: SAFE-T addresses early-phase clinical trials that seek a suitable drug dose for later confirmatory studies. The paper highlights two concerns with standard procedures: participant benefit may not be optimized, and differences between participant subgroups may be overlooked. The contribution brings participant utility, subgroup differences, and constrained exploration into one adaptive framework.
summary.tldr: SAFE-T adaptively selects doses for heterogeneous participants with safety guarantees and promising results in realistic synthetic trials.

title: Safe Exploration in Dose Finding Clinical Trials with Heterogeneous Participants

abstract: A key property of neural networks driving their success is their ability to learn features from data. Understanding feature learning from a theoretical viewpoint is an emerging field with many open questions. In this work we capture finite-width effects with a systematic theory of network kernels in deep non-linear neural networks. We show that the Bayesian prior of the network can be written in closed form as a superposition of Gaussian processes, whose kernels are distributed with a variance that depends inversely on the network width $N$. A large deviation approach, which is exact in the proportional limit for the number of data points $P=\alpha N\to\infty$, yields a pair of forward-backward equations for the maximum a posteriori kernels in all layers at once. We study their solutions perturbatively, to demonstrate how the backward propagation across layers aligns kernels with the target. An alternative field-theoretic formulation shows that kernel adaptation of the Bayesian posterior at finite-width results from fluctuations in the prior: larger fluctuations correspond to a more flexible network prior and thus enable stronger adaptation to data. We thus find a bridge between the classical edge-of-chaos NNGP theory and feature learning, exposing an intricate interplay between criticality, response functions, and feature scale.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theory of how finite network width affects feature learning in deep nonlinear networks. It describes the network’s Bayesian prior as a mixture of Gaussian processes, with variation among their kernels decreasing inversely with network width. These kernels describe the relationships between inputs that the network represents.

The authors use a large-deviation analysis to obtain coupled forward and backward equations for the most probable kernels across all layers. The analysis is exact in a proportional limit where dataset size and network width grow together at a fixed ratio. A perturbative study of the equations shows how backward propagation aligns kernels with the prediction target.

Larger fluctuations make the prior more flexible and permit stronger adaptation. This connects finite-width feature learning with edge-of-chaos Gaussian-process theory, showing how criticality, response behavior, and feature scale interact within the analyzed framework.
summary.tldr: A finite-width kernel theory links feature learning to fluctuations in a network’s Bayesian prior and their alignment with training targets.

title: Critical feature learning in deep neural networks

abstract: Autonomous agents trained using deep reinforcement learning (RL) often lack the ability to successfully generalise to new environments, even when these environments share characteristics with the ones they have encountered during training. In this work, we investigate how the sampling of individual environment instances, or levels, affects the zero-shot generalisation (ZSG) ability of RL agents. We discover that, for deep actor-critic architectures sharing their base layers, prioritising levels according to their value loss minimises the mutual information between the agent’s internal representation and the set of training levels in the generated training data. This provides a novel theoretical justification for the regularisation achieved by certain adaptive sampling strategies. We then turn our attention to unsupervised environment design (UED) methods, which assume control over level generation. We find that existing UED methods can significantly shift the training distribution, which translates to low ZSG performance. To prevent both overfitting and distributional shift, we introduce data-regularised environment design (DRED). DRED generates levels using a generative model trained to approximate the ground truth distribution of an initial set of level parameters. Through its grounding, DRED achieves significant improvements in ZSG over adaptive level sampling strategies and UED methods.

paragraphs: An agent's ability to generalize depends partly on which environments it experiences during training. This paper studies how selecting or generating individual levels affects zero-shot transfer. It considers both adaptive sampling of available levels and unsupervised environment design, where the training procedure can create levels itself.

For deep actor-critic models with shared base layers, the authors show that prioritizing levels by value loss minimizes mutual information between the agent's internal representation and the training-level set in the generated data. A generative model learns to approximate their underlying distribution and produces new levels from that grounding. The authors report significant zero-shot generalization improvements over adaptive sampling strategies and existing environment-design methods, supporting distribution-aware generation as a useful training approach.
summary.tldr: DRED improves zero-shot reinforcement learning transfer by generating training levels from a model grounded in an initial level distribution.

title: DRED: Zero-Shot Transfer in Reinforcement Learning via Data-Regularised Environment Design

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) is a classical machine learning paradigm dealing with labeled and unlabeled data. However, it often suffers performance degradation in real-world open-set scenarios, where unlabeled data contains outliers from novel categories that do not appear in labeled data. Existing studies commonly tackle this challenging open-set SSL problem with detect-and-filter strategy, which attempts to purify unlabeled data by detecting and filtering outliers. In this paper, we propose a novel binary decomposition strategy, which refrains from error-prone procedure of outlier detection by directly transforming the original open-set SSL problem into a number of standard binary SSL problems. Accordingly, a concise yet effective approach named BDMatch is presented. BDMatch confronts two attendant issues brought by binary decomposition, i.e. class-imbalance and representation-compromise, with adaptive logit adjustment and label-specific feature learning respectively. Comprehensive experiments on diversified benchmarks clearly validate the superiority of BDMatch as well as the effectiveness of our binary decomposition strategy.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines labeled examples with unlabeled ones. In an open-set setting, some unlabeled examples belong to categories absent from the labeled collection. These unfamiliar categories can damage learning. A common response is to identify and remove them, but errors in that screening step can undermine the resulting training data.

This paper changes the learning problem itself. Its binary decomposition strategy converts the original task into several standard binary semi-supervised problems, avoiding the explicit outlier detection procedure. The resulting method, BDMatch, addresses two difficulties introduced by this transformation: uneven class proportions and compromises in the learned representations. It uses adaptive logit adjustment for the first and label-specific feature learning for the second.

Experiments across varied benchmarks report that BDMatch outperforms the compared approaches and support the effectiveness of binary decomposition. The contribution is a different way to handle unfamiliar unlabeled categories: reorganize the classification task while explicitly addressing the training difficulties that this reorganization creates.
summary.tldr: BDMatch tackles open-set semi-supervised learning by decomposing it into binary tasks instead of detecting and filtering unfamiliar examples.

title: Binary Decomposition: A Problem Transformation Perspective for Open-Set Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: Leveraging massive knowledge from large language models (LLMs), recent machine learning models show notable successes in general-purpose task solving in diverse domains such as computer vision and robotics. However, several significant challenges remain: (i) most of these models rely on 2D images yet exhibit a limited capacity for 3D input; (ii) these models rarely explore the tasks inherently defined in 3D world, e.g., 3D grounding, embodied reasoning and acting. We argue these limitations significantly hinder current models from performing real-world tasks and approaching general intelligence. To this end, we introduce LEO, an embodied multi-modal generalist agent that excels in perceiving, grounding, reasoning, planning, and acting in the 3D world. LEO is trained with a unified task interface, model architecture, and objective in two stages: (i) 3D vision-language (VL) alignment and (ii) 3D vision-language-action (VLA) instruction tuning. We collect large-scale datasets comprising diverse object-level and scene-level tasks, which require considerable understanding of and interaction with the 3D world. Moreover, we meticulously design an LLM-assisted pipeline to produce high-quality 3D VL data. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate LEO’s remarkable proficiency across a wide spectrum of tasks, including 3D captioning, question answering, embodied reasoning, navigation and manipulation. Our ablative studies and scaling analyses further provide valuable insights for developing future embodied generalist agents. Code and data are available on project page.

paragraphs: LEO is an agent designed to understand and act in three-dimensional environments. The paper addresses a gap in general-purpose models: many can interpret images but have limited support for 3D inputs and tasks that require spatial understanding. These tasks include connecting language to objects in a scene, reasoning about an environment, and deciding how to move or manipulate objects.

The researchers train LEO using a shared task interface, architecture, and learning objective. Training first aligns 3D visual information with language, then uses instructions to connect vision and language with actions. They also assemble large datasets covering individual objects and whole scenes, and build a language-model-assisted pipeline for producing 3D vision-language training data.

Experiments demonstrate capabilities across captioning, question answering, embodied reasoning, navigation, and manipulation. The breadth of these evaluations supports the idea that one agent can learn several complementary 3D skills through a unified setup. Ablation studies and scaling analyses additionally examine the system’s development, providing evidence intended to inform future embodied generalist agents.
summary.tldr: LEO combines 3D vision, language, and action training in one agent that handles diverse spatial understanding and interaction tasks.

title: An Embodied Generalist Agent in 3D World

abstract: Publications proposing novel machine learning methods are often primarily rated by exhibited predictive performance on selected problems. In this position paper we argue that predictive performance alone is not a good indicator for the worth of a publication. Using it as such even fosters problems like inefficiencies of the machine learning research community as a whole and setting wrong incentives for researchers. We therefore put out a call for the publication of ``negative'' results, which can help alleviate some of these problems and improve the scientific output of the machine learning research community. To substantiate our position, we present the advantages of publishing negative results and provide concrete measures for the community to move towards a paradigm where their publication is normalized.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges the practice of judging a machine learning publication mainly by the predictive performance of its proposed method on selected problems. The authors argue that performance alone is an inadequate measure of scientific worth. Their concern is about how research is valued and communicated, as well as how individual methods are assessed.

The paper links this evaluation practice to inefficiencies across the research community and to incentives that can steer researchers in unhelpful directions. It calls for publishing negative results as part of the response. The argument is that findings without a demonstrated predictive improvement can still contribute to scientific progress and deserve a place in the published record.

To support this position, the authors discuss advantages of publishing negative results and propose concrete community measures to make their publication routine. The contribution is an argument for changing research norms, rather than a claim that a new model improves prediction. Its proposed outcome is a scientific record whose value is assessed more broadly than whether each paper reports a performance gain.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that normalizing negative results would improve research incentives and broaden how machine learning publications are valued.

title: Position: Embracing Negative Results in Machine Learning

abstract: With the breakthrough of large models, Segment Anything Model (SAM) and its extensions have been attempted to apply in diverse tasks of computer vision. Underwater salient instance segmentation is a foundational and vital step for various underwater vision tasks, which often suffer from low segmentation accuracy due to the complex underwater circumstances and the adaptive ability of models. Moreover, the lack of large-scale datasets with pixel-level salient instance annotations has impeded the development of machine learning techniques in this field. To address these issues, we construct the first large-scale underwater salient instance segmentation dataset (USIS10K), which contains 10,632 underwater images with pixel-level annotations in 7 categories from various underwater scenes. Then, we propose an Underwater Salient Instance Segmentation architecture based on Segment Anything Model (USIS-SAM) specifically for the underwater domain. We devise an Underwater Adaptive Visual Transformer (UA-ViT) encoder to incorporate underwater domain visual prompts into the segmentation network. We further design an out-of-the-box underwater Salient Feature Prompter Generator (SFPG) to automatically generate salient prompters instead of explicitly providing foreground points or boxes as prompts in SAM. Comprehensive experimental results show that our USIS-SAM method can achieve superior performance on USIS10K datasets compared to the state-of-the-art methods. Datasets and codes are released on https://github.com/LiamLian0727/USIS10K.

paragraphs: Underwater salient instance segmentation identifies prominent individual objects and their pixel boundaries in underwater images. Complex underwater conditions and difficulty adapting models to this domain can reduce accuracy. The paper addresses both this modeling problem and a shortage of large datasets with the detailed instance annotations needed to train and evaluate such systems.

The authors introduce USIS10K, containing 10,632 underwater images with pixel-level annotations across seven categories and varied underwater scenes. They also develop USIS-SAM, an underwater-specific architecture based on the Segment Anything Model. This replaces the explicit foreground points or boxes otherwise supplied as SAM prompts in the described setup. Experiments on USIS10K report superior performance over state-of-the-art comparison methods. The contribution combines a dedicated evaluation resource with domain adaptation and automatic prompting, addressing complementary obstacles to underwater segmentation.
summary.tldr: USIS-SAM adapts Segment Anything to underwater imagery with automatic prompts, alongside a new dataset of 10,632 annotated images.

title: Diving into Underwater: Segment Anything Model Guided Underwater Salient Instance Segmentation and A Large-scale Dataset

abstract: Decentralized Gradient Descent (D-GD) allows a set of users to perform collaborative learning without sharing their data by iteratively averaging local model updates with their neighbors in a network graph. The absence of direct communication between non-neighbor nodes might lead to the belief that users cannot infer precise information about the data of others. In this work, we demonstrate the opposite, by proposing the first attack against D-GD that enables a user (or set of users) to reconstruct the private data of other users outside their immediate neighborhood. Our approach is based on a reconstruction attack against the gossip averaging protocol, which we then extend to handle the additional challenges raised by D-GD. We validate the effectiveness of our attack on real graphs and datasets, showing that the number of users compromised by a single or a handful of attackers is often surprisingly large. We empirically investigate some of the factors that affect the performance of the attack, namely the graph topology, the number of attackers, and their position in the graph.

paragraphs: Decentralized gradient descent lets users train collaboratively by exchanging and averaging model updates with neighbors in a network. Their raw datasets remain local. This paper examines whether the lack of direct communication between distant users prevents one participant from recovering another participant’s private data.

The authors develop an attack that can reconstruct data belonging to users outside the attackers’ immediate neighborhood. They first attack the gossip averaging protocol underlying the communication process, then extend that reconstruction approach to address the additional challenges of decentralized gradient descent. The result shows that indirect interactions through shared updates can expose information beyond direct communication links.

Experiments on real graphs and datasets demonstrate the attack’s effectiveness. A single attacker or a small group often compromises a surprisingly large number of users in the reported evaluations. The authors also investigate how graph topology, attacker count, and attacker placement affect performance. These findings challenge the assumption that network separation alone provides protection for private training data.
summary.tldr: A reconstruction attack shows that decentralized learning participants can recover private data from users beyond their immediate neighbors.

title: Privacy Attacks in Decentralized Learning

abstract: In practice, training using federated learning can be orders of magnitude slower than standard centralized training. This severely limits the amount of experimentation and tuning that can be done, making it challenging to obtain good performance on a given task. Server-side proxy data can be used to run training simulations, for instance for hyperparameter tuning. This can greatly speed up the training pipeline by reducing the number of tuning runs to be performed overall on the true clients. However, it is challenging to ensure that these simulations accurately reflect the dynamics of the real federated training. In particular, the proxy data used for simulations often comes as a single centralized dataset without a partition into distinct clients, and partitioning this data in a naive way can lead to simulations that poorly reflect real federated training. In this paper we address the challenge of how to partition centralized data in a way that reflects the statistical heterogeneity of the true federated clients. We propose a fully federated, theoretically justified, algorithm that efficiently learns the distribution of the true clients and observe improved server-side simulations when using the inferred distribution to create simulated clients from the centralized data.

Server-side proxy data can be used to run training simulations, for instance for hyperparameter tuning. This can greatly speed up the training pipeline by reducing the number of tuning runs to be performed overall on the true clients. However, it is challenging to ensure that these simulations accurately reflect the dynamics of the real federated training. In particular, the proxy data used for simulations often comes as a single centralized dataset without a partition into distinct clients, and partitioning this data in a naive way can lead to simulations that poorly reflect real federated training. In this paper we address the challenge of how to partition centralized data in a way that reflects the statistical heterogeneity of the true federated clients. We propose a fully federated, theoretically justified, algorithm that efficiently learns the distribution of the true clients and observe improved server-side simulations when using the inferred distribution to create simulated clients from the centralized data.

paragraphs: Federated training can be much slower than centralized training, making repeated tuning expensive. One way to reduce that burden is to simulate training on proxy data held by the server. Those simulations are useful only if they reflect the statistical differences among the real clients participating in federated learning.

A centralized proxy dataset usually has no natural division into clients. Splitting it naively can produce simulated clients whose data distributions differ from the real population, leading to misleading training dynamics. The paper addresses this partitioning problem with a fully federated algorithm that efficiently learns a distribution describing the true clients and has theoretical justification.

The inferred distribution is then used to divide centralized data into simulated clients. The authors observe improved server-side simulations when using these partitions. This matters because realistic simulations can support experimentation before costly runs on actual clients: the contribution improves how the proxy environment represents client heterogeneity, which is a key ingredient in making those experiments informative.
summary.tldr: A federated algorithm learns client heterogeneity to create more realistic simulated clients from centralized proxy data.

title: Improved Modelling of Federated Datasets using Mixtures-of-Dirichlet-Multinomials

abstract: This paper describes MAIA, a Multimodal Automated Interpretability Agent. MAIA is a system that uses neural models to automate neural model understanding tasks like feature interpretation and failure mode discovery. It equips a pre-trained vision-language model with a set of tools that support iterative experimentation on subcomponents of other models to explain their behavior. These include tools commonly used by human interpretability researchers: for synthesizing and editing inputs, computing maximally activating exemplars from real-world datasets, and summarizing and describing experimental results. Interpretability experiments proposed by MAIA compose these tools to describe and explain system behavior. We evaluate applications of MAIA to computer vision models. We first characterize MAIA’s ability to describe (neuron-level) features in learned representations of images. Across several trained models and a novel dataset of synthetic vision neurons with paired ground-truth descriptions, MAIA produces descriptions comparable to those generated by expert human experimenters. We then show that MAIA can aid in two additional interpretability tasks: reducing sensitivity to spurious features, and automatically identifying inputs likely to be mis-classified.

MAIA combines these operations to investigate features rather than relying on a single observation. They also show that MAIA can help reduce sensitivity to spurious features and identify inputs likely to receive incorrect predictions, connecting interpretation with practical diagnosis of model behavior.
summary.tldr: MAIA uses a vision-language model and experimental tools to interpret visual features and help discover model failures.

title: A Multimodal Automated Interpretability Agent

abstract: Undeniably, Large Language Models (LLMs) have stirred an extraordinary wave of innovation in the machine learning research domain, resulting in substantial impact across diverse fields such as reinforcement learning, robotics, and computer vision. Their incorporation has been rapid and transformative, marking a significant paradigm shift in the field of machine learning research. However, the field of experimental design, grounded on black-box optimization, has been much less affected by such a paradigm shift, even though integrating LLMs with optimization presents a unique landscape ripe for exploration. In this position paper, we frame the field of black-box optimization around sequence-based foundation models and organize their relationship with previous literature. We discuss the most promising ways foundational language models can revolutionize optimization, which include harnessing the vast wealth of information encapsulated in free-form text to enrich task comprehension, utilizing highly flexible sequence models such as Transformers to engineer superior optimization strategies, and enhancing performance prediction over previously unseen search spaces.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that black-box optimization and experimental design offer substantial opportunities for foundation models. It frames the field around sequence-based models and connects that perspective to existing research. The contribution is a research agenda for integrating language and sequence modeling into optimization, rather than a reported benchmark victory for one new algorithm.

One proposed direction uses information contained in free-form text to improve understanding of an optimization task. A second uses flexible sequence architectures, such as Transformers, to develop better optimization strategies. These directions concern different parts of the process: interpreting what a task involves and deciding how to search for good solutions.

A third direction concerns predicting performance in search spaces that have not previously been encountered. Together, the proposals suggest using foundation models both to incorporate broader task knowledge and to support optimization across unfamiliar settings. The authors present these as promising ways to reshape the field, organizing future work around capabilities that language and sequence models may bring to experimental design.
summary.tldr: This position paper proposes using foundation models for task understanding, optimization strategy design, and performance prediction in unfamiliar search spaces.

title: Position: Leverage Foundational Models for Black-Box Optimization

abstract: In contrast with Mercer kernel-based approaches as used e.g. in Kernel Principal Component Analysis (KPCA), it was previously shown that Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) inherently relates to asymmetric kernels and Asymmetric Kernel Singular Value Decomposition (KSVD) has been proposed. However, the existing formulation to KSVD cannot work with infinite-dimensional feature mappings, the variational objective can be unbounded, and needs further numerical evaluation and exploration towards machine learning. In this work, i) we introduce a new asymmetric learning paradigm based on coupled covariance eigenproblem (CCE) through covariance operators, allowing infinite-dimensional feature maps. The solution to CCE is ultimately obtained from the SVD of the induced asymmetric kernel matrix, providing links to KSVD. ii) Starting from the integral equations corresponding to a pair of coupled adjoint eigenfunctions, we formalize the asymmetric Nyström method through a finite sample approximation to speed up training. iii) We provide the first empirical evaluations verifying the practical utility and benefits of KSVD and compare with methods resorting to symmetrization or linear SVD across multiple tasks.

paragraphs: Asymmetric kernel singular value decomposition extends kernel learning beyond the symmetric kernels used in methods such as kernel principal component analysis. However, the existing formulation has significant mathematical obstacles: it cannot accommodate infinite-dimensional feature mappings, and its variational objective can be unbounded. This paper develops a new formulation and investigates its practical usefulness.

The authors construct a coupled covariance eigenproblem using covariance operators. This permits infinite-dimensional feature maps, while the solution can ultimately be obtained through the singular value decomposition of an induced asymmetric kernel matrix. They also derive an asymmetric Nyström method from paired adjoint eigenfunction equations, using a finite-sample approximation to accelerate training.

The paper provides empirical evaluations across multiple tasks, comparing asymmetric kernel SVD with approaches that symmetrize the problem or use linear SVD. These experiments support the practical utility of the asymmetric approach. The overall contribution connects a more accommodating mathematical formulation, a training approximation, and empirical evidence for learning directly with asymmetric kernel structure.
summary.tldr: A coupled-covariance formulation enables asymmetric kernel learning with infinite-dimensional feature maps and introduces a Nyström approximation to speed training.

title: Learning in Feature Spaces via Coupled Covariances: Asymmetric Kernel SVD and Nyström method

abstract: In goal-conditioned hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL), a high-level policy specifies a subgoal for the low-level policy to reach. Effective HRL hinges on a suitable subgoal representation function, abstracting state space into latent subgoal space and inducing varied low-level behaviors. Existing methods adopt a subgoal representation that provides a deterministic mapping from state space to latent subgoal space. Instead, this paper utilizes Gaussian Processes (GPs) for the first probabilistic subgoal representation. Our method employs a GP prior on the latent subgoal space to learn a posterior distribution over the subgoal representation functions while exploiting the long-range correlation in the state space through learnable kernels. This enables an adaptive memory that integrates long-range subgoal information from prior planning steps allowing to cope with stochastic uncertainties. Furthermore, we propose a novel learning objective to facilitate the simultaneous learning of probabilistic subgoal representations and policies within a unified framework. In experiments, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in standard benchmarks but also in environments with stochastic elements and under diverse reward conditions. Additionally, our model shows promising capabilities in transferring low-level policies across different tasks.

paragraphs: In hierarchical reinforcement learning, a high-level policy chooses subgoals that a low-level policy tries to reach. The representation of those subgoals shapes the behaviors the lower level can learn. Existing approaches map states deterministically into a latent subgoal space; this paper instead learns a probability distribution over possible representation functions.

The method uses a Gaussian process prior and learns a posterior over subgoal representations. Learnable kernels capture long-range correlations in the state space, creating an adaptive memory that incorporates subgoal information from earlier planning steps. This provides a mechanism for handling stochastic uncertainty while retaining information that extends beyond the immediate planning decision.

A joint learning objective trains the probabilistic representations and policies within one framework. Experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on standard benchmarks, environments with stochastic elements, and differing reward conditions. The model also shows promising transfer of low-level policies between tasks. These findings support representing uncertainty in subgoals as a useful part of hierarchical policy learning.
summary.tldr: Gaussian-process subgoal representations give hierarchical reinforcement learning an adaptive memory for uncertainty and improve performance across the reported settings.

title: Probabilistic Subgoal Representations for Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) provide a robust paradigm in Bayesian deep learning. In DGPs, a set of sparse integration locations called inducing points are selected to approximate the posterior distribution of the model. This is done to reduce computational complexity and improve model efficiency. However, inferring the posterior distribution of inducing points is not straightforward. Traditional variational inference techniques methods to approximate the posterior often leads to significant bias. To address this issue, we propose an alternative named Denoising Diffusion Variational Inference (DDVI) that utilizes a denoising diffusion stochastic differential equation (SDE) for generating posterior samples of inducing variables. We refer to the score matching method in the denoising diffusion model to approximate challenging score functions using a neural network. Furthermore, by combining classical mathematical theory of SDE with the minimization of KL divergence between the approximate and true processes, we propose a novel explicit variational lower bound for the marginal likelihood function of DGP. Through extensive experiments on various datasets and comparisons with baseline methods, we empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of the DDVI method in posterior inference of inducing points for DGP models.
