paragraphs: Deep Gaussian processes use sparse inducing variables to make Bayesian inference computationally manageable. Approximating their posterior remains difficult, and restrictive variational methods can introduce substantial bias. This paper proposes a diffusion-based alternative for representing that posterior more flexibly.

Denoising Diffusion Variational Inference generates posterior samples through a denoising diffusion stochastic differential equation. A neural network approximates the required score functions using score-matching ideas. The authors combine SDE theory with minimization of a divergence between approximate and true processes to derive an explicit variational lower bound for the model’s marginal likelihood.

Experiments across several datasets compare DDVI with baseline inference methods and support its effectiveness for deep Gaussian processes. The contribution is an inference procedure and training bound, rather than a change to the basic meaning of the model’s observations. The abstract does not quantify how much posterior bias remains or establish exact posterior sampling in finite training.
summary.tldr: Diffusion-based variational inference provides a flexible posterior sampler and explicit training bound for sparse deep Gaussian processes.

title: Sparse Inducing Points in Deep Gaussian Processes: Enhancing Modeling with Denoising Diffusion Variational Inference

abstract: Large-scale recommendation systems are characterized by their reliance on high cardinality, heterogeneous features and the need to handle tens of billions of user actions on a daily basis. Despite being trained on huge volume of data with thousands of features, most Deep Learning Recommendation Models (DLRMs) in industry fail to scale with compute. Inspired by success achieved by Transformers in language and vision domains, we revisit fundamental design choices in recommendation systems. We reformulate recommendation problems as sequential transduction tasks within a generative modeling framework (“Generative Recommenders”), and propose a new architecture, HSTU, designed for high cardinality, non-stationary streaming recommendation data. HSTU outperforms baselines over synthetic and public datasets by up to 65.8% in NDCG, and is 5.3x to 15.2x faster than FlashAttention2-based Transformers on 8192 length sequences. HSTU-based Generative Recommenders, with 1.5 trillion parameters, improve metrics in online A/B tests by 12.4% and have been deployed on multiple surfaces of a large internet platform with billions of users. More importantly, the model quality of Generative Recommenders empirically scales as a power-law of training compute across three orders of magnitude, up to GPT-3/LLaMa-2 scale, which reduces carbon footprint needed for future model developments, and further paves the way for the first foundation models in recommendations.

paragraphs: Large recommendation systems process enormous streams of user actions and many different kinds of features, yet increasing their computing budget often fails to improve conventional models proportionally. This paper revisits that design problem by treating recommendation as sequential transduction within a generative framework: learning from action sequences to produce recommendations.

The proposed HSTU architecture is designed for streaming recommendation data with many distinct feature values and patterns that change over time. summary.tldr: HSTU recasts recommendation as generative sequence modeling, delivering reported gains in quality, speed, and scaling with training compute.

title: Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations

abstract: Reconstructing dynamic articulated objects from a singular monocular video is challenging, requiring joint estimation of shape, motion, and camera parameters from limited views. Current methods typically demand extensive computational resources and training time, and require additional human annotations such as predefined parametric models, camera poses, and key points, limiting their generalizability. We propose Synergistic Shape and Skeleton Optimization (S3O), a novel two-phase method that forgoes these prerequisites and efficiently learns parametric models including visible shapes and underlying skeletons. Conventional strategies typically learn all parameters simultaneously, leading to interdependencies where a single incorrect prediction can result in significant errors. In contrast, S3O adopts a phased approach: it first focuses on learning coarse parametric models, then progresses to motion learning and detail addition. This method substantially lowers computational complexity and enhances robustness in reconstruction from limited viewpoints, all without requiring additional annotations. To address the current inadequacies in 3D reconstruction from monocular video benchmarks, we collected the PlanetZoo dataset. Our experimental evaluations on standard benchmarks and the PlanetZoo dataset affirm that S3O provides more accurate 3D reconstruction, and plausible skeletons, and reduces the training time by approximately 60% compared to the state-of-the-art, thus advancing the state of the art in dynamic object reconstruction.

These estimates depend on one another, so an error in one can disrupt the others. S3O addresses this problem with a two-phase process that learns both visible geometry and an underlying skeleton.

They report more accurate 3D reconstructions, plausible skeletons, and approximately 60% less training time than the state-of-the-art comparison. These findings support staged optimization as a way to improve both efficiency and robustness when viewpoints are limited. The skeleton result concerns plausibility, while the geometric reconstruction result concerns improved accuracy in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: S3O reconstructs articulated shape and skeleton in two phases, improving reported accuracy and cutting training time by approximately 60%.

title: S3O: A Dual-Phase Approach for Reconstructing Dynamic Shape and Skeleton of Articulated Objects from Single Monocular Video

abstract: Although Recommender Systems (RS) have been well-developed for various fields of applications, they often suffer from a crisis of platform credibility with respect to RS confidence and fairness, which may drive users away, threatening the platform’s long-term success. In recent years, some works have tried to solve these issues; however, they lack strong statistical guarantees. Therefore, there is an urgent need to solve both issues with a unifying framework with robust statistical guarantees. In this paper, we propose a novel and reliable framework called Equitable and Statistically Unbiased Recommendation (ENSUR)) to dynamically generate prediction sets for users across various groups, which are guaranteed 1) to include ground-truth items with user-predefined high confidence/probability (e.g., 90%); 2) to ensure user fairness across different groups; 3) to have minimum efficient average prediction set sizes. We further design an efficient algorithm named Guaranteed User Fairness Algorithm (GUFA) to optimize the proposed method and derive upper bounds of risk and fairness metrics to speed up the optimization process. Moreover, we provide rigorous theoretical analysis concerning risk and fairness control and minimum set size. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, which aligns with our theoretical analysis.

paragraphs: ENSUR addresses confidence and fairness in recommender systems by producing prediction sets for users. Instead of treating recommendation quality solely as the accuracy of an individual prediction, it considers whether a set contains the ground-truth item, whether users across groups receive fair treatment, and how large the sets need to be.

The framework lets users specify a desired coverage probability, such as 90%. It provides guarantees for including ground-truth items, fairness across groups, and minimizing average prediction-set size. These objectives work together: a recommendation set should offer the requested confidence while remaining compact enough to be useful and satisfying the framework's fairness requirements.

The authors introduce GUFA to optimize this formulation efficiently. They derive upper bounds on risk and fairness quantities to accelerate optimization, alongside theoretical analysis of risk control, fairness control, and minimum set size. Experiments support the framework's effectiveness and agree with that analysis. The contribution is a unified statistical treatment of several recommendation goals that are often handled separately.
summary.tldr: ENSUR generates compact recommendation sets with statistical guarantees for user-selected confidence and fairness across groups.

title: ENSUR: Equitable and Statistically Unbiased Recommendation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are powerful tools but are often expensive to deploy at scale. LLM query routing mitigates this by dynamically assigning queries to models of varying cost and quality to obtain a desired tradeoff. Prior query routing approaches generate only one response from the selected model and a single response from a small (inexpensive) model was often not good enough to beat a response from a large (expensive) model due to which they end up overusing the large model and missing out on potential cost savings. However, it is well known that for small models, generating multiple responses and selecting the best can enhance quality while remaining cheaper than a single large-model response. We leverage this idea to propose BEST-Route, a novel routing framework that chooses a model and the number of responses to sample from it based on query difficulty and the quality thresholds. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method reduces costs by up to 60% with less than 1% performance drop.

paragraphs: Routing systems try to reduce language-model costs by assigning each query to a model with a suitable balance of price and quality. When the router considers only one response per model, a small model may appear inadequate. This can push too many queries toward an expensive model, even when another use of the smaller model could work.

BEST-Route expands the routing decision to include how many responses to generate. Sampling several answers from a small model and selecting the best can improve quality while still costing less than one answer from a large model. The framework chooses both the model and its sample count using query difficulty and quality thresholds.

Experiments on real-world datasets report cost reductions of up to 60% with less than a 1% performance drop. These are reported experimental outcomes, rather than a guarantee for every query. The result shows why routing and response sampling are useful to consider together: additional computation on a cheaper model can sometimes provide a better cost-quality tradeoff than switching models.
summary.tldr: BEST-Route jointly chooses a language model and response sample count, reporting up to 60% lower costs with less than 1% performance loss.

title: BEST-Route: Adaptive LLM Routing with Test-Time Optimal Compute

abstract: Algorithms for machine learning-guided design, or design algorithms, use machine learning-based predictions to propose novel objects with desired property values. Given a new design task—for example, to design novel proteins with high binding affinity to a therapeutic target—one must choose a design algorithm and specify any hyperparameters and predictive and/or generative models involved. How can these decisions be made such that the resulting designs are successful? This paper proposes a method for design algorithm selection, which aims to select design algorithms that will produce a distribution of design labels satisfying a user-specified success criterion—for example, that at least ten percent of designs’ labels exceed a threshold. It does so by combining designs’ predicted property values with held-out labeled data to reliably forecast characteristics of the label distributions produced by different design algorithms, building upon techniques from prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al., 2023). The method is guaranteed with high probability to return design algorithms that yield successful label distributions (or the null set if none exist), if the density ratios between the design and labeled data distributions are known. We demonstrate the method’s effectiveness in simulated protein and RNA design tasks, in settings with either known or estimated density ratios.

paragraphs: Machine-learning-guided design uses predicted properties to propose new objects, but choosing a design algorithm also requires choosing models and hyperparameters. This paper frames that choice around a user-defined success criterion for the distribution of actual outcomes. A criterion might require at least ten percent of proposed designs to exceed a specified property threshold.

The method combines predictions for proposed designs with held-out examples whose true labels are known. Building on prediction-powered inference, it forecasts characteristics of the outcome distribution produced by each candidate algorithm. This makes algorithm selection depend on evidence about whether a collection of designs will meet the desired criterion, rather than relying only on their predicted property values.

The authors provide a high-probability guarantee of selecting successful algorithms, or returning an empty set if none exist, when density ratios between the design and labeled-data distributions are known. That condition is part of the guarantee. Simulated protein and RNA design experiments show effectiveness with both known and estimated density ratios, extending the empirical evaluation beyond the exact-information setting used for the stated guarantee.
summary.tldr: The method selects design algorithms against user-defined success criteria, with a high-probability guarantee when the relevant distribution density ratios are known.

title: Reliable Algorithm Selection for Machine Learning-Guided Design

abstract: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) have emerged as powerful tools for generative modeling. However, their sequential computation requirements lead to significant inference-time bottlenecks. In this work, we utilize the connection between DDPMs and Stochastic Localization to prove that, under an appropriate reparametrization, the increments of DDPM satisfy an exchangeability property. This general insight enables near-black-box adaptation of various performance optimization techniques from autoregressive models to the diffusion setting. To demonstrate this, we introduce Autospeculative Decoding (ASD), an extension of the widely used speculative decoding algorithm to DDPMs that does not require any auxiliary draft models. Our theoretical analysis shows that ASD achieves a $\tilde{O}(K^{\frac{1}{3}})$ parallel runtime speedup over the $K$ step sequential DDPM. We also demonstrate that a practical implementation of autospeculative decoding accelerates DDPM inference significantly in various domains.

This paper investigates a mathematical property that can help parallelize that process. title: Diffusion Models are Secretly Exchangeable: Parallelizing DDPMs via Auto Speculation

abstract: As Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models are increasingly adopted for diverse downstream tasks and integrated into large vision-language models (VLMs), their susceptibility to adversarial perturbations has emerged as a critical concern. In this work, we introduce X-Transfer, a novel attack method that exposes a universal adversarial vulnerability in CLIP. X-Transfer generates a Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP) capable of deceiving various CLIP encoders and downstream VLMs across different samples, tasks, and domains. We refer to this property as super transferability—a single perturbation achieving cross-data, cross-domain, cross-model, and cross-task adversarial transferability simultaneously. This is achieved through surrogate scaling, a key innovation of our approach. Unlike existing methods that rely on fixed surrogate models, which are computationally intensive to scale, X-Transfer employs an efficient surrogate scaling strategy that dynamically selects a small subset of suitable surrogates from a large search space. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that X-Transfer significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art UAP methods, establishing a new benchmark for adversarial transferability across CLIP models.

paragraphs: CLIP encoders support many downstream tasks and appear within larger vision-language models, making transferable adversarial weaknesses consequential across systems. This is designed to make scaling the surrogate pool efficient while producing a perturbation that transfers beyond the individual models involved in its construction.

Extensive evaluations report that X-Transfer substantially outperforms previous state-of-the-art universal-perturbation methods. The resulting perturbation affects different CLIP encoders and downstream vision-language models in the evaluated settings. The findings highlight a shared vulnerability across uses of CLIP and show that selecting surrogates dynamically can strengthen adversarial transfer across several dimensions at once, rather than improving transfer along only one of them.
summary.tldr: X-Transfer dynamically selects surrogate models to create a universal perturbation that transfers across CLIP-based models, tasks, domains, and samples.

title: X-Transfer Attacks: Towards Super Transferable Adversarial Attacks on CLIP

abstract: Time-series forecasting has gained significant attention in machine learning due to its crucial role in various domains. However, most existing forecasting models rely heavily on point-wise loss functions like Mean Squared Error, which treat each time step independently and neglect the structural dependencies inherent in time series data, making it challenging to capture complex temporal patterns accurately. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Patch-wise Structural (PS) loss, designed to enhance structural alignment by comparing time series at the patch level. Through leveraging local statistical properties, such as correlation, variance, and mean, PS loss captures nuanced structural discrepancies overlooked by traditional point-wise losses. Furthermore, it integrates seamlessly with point-wise loss, simultaneously addressing local structural inconsistencies and individual time-step errors. PS loss establishes a novel benchmark for accurately modeling complex time series data and provides a new perspective on time series loss function design. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PS loss significantly improves the performance of state-of-the-art models across diverse real-world datasets. The data and code are publicly available at: https://github.com/Dilfiraa/PS_Loss.

paragraphs: Forecasting models often train with losses such as mean squared error, which compare predictions and observations one time step at a time. Such comparisons do not directly measure the relationships among nearby values. This paper proposes a patch-wise structural loss that evaluates local segments of a series to capture discrepancies in their temporal structure.

The loss uses local statistical properties, including correlation, variance, and mean. These provide complementary views of whether a predicted patch aligns with the observed patch's structure. By comparing groups of time steps, the objective gives training information about patterns that isolated point comparisons can overlook, while retaining a direct connection to the forecasted values.

The proposed loss can be combined with a point-wise loss, addressing structural mismatch and individual prediction errors together. Extensive experiments report significant improvements for state-of-the-art forecasting models across diverse real-world datasets. The contribution concerns the training objective, offering a way to improve existing models by changing how forecast errors are measured rather than requiring a particular new forecasting architecture.
summary.tldr: Patch-wise structural loss compares local correlation, variance, and mean to improve time-series forecasts alongside conventional point-wise error losses.

title: Patch-wise Structural Loss for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained models is prohibitively expensive in terms of computation and memory costs. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a popular Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method, offers an efficient solution by optimizing only low-rank matrices. Despite recent progress in improving LoRA’s performance, the relationship between the LoRA optimization space and the full parameter space is often overlooked. A solution that appears flat in the loss landscape of the LoRA space may still exhibit sharp directions in the full parameter space, potentially compromising generalization. We introduce Flat-LoRA, which aims to identify a low-rank adaptation situated in a flat region of the full parameter space. Instead of adopting the well-established sharpness-aware minimization approach, which incurs significant computation and memory overheads, we employ a Bayesian expectation loss objective to preserve training efficiency. Further, we design a refined strategy for generating random perturbations to enhance performance and carefully manage memory overhead using random seeds. Experiments across diverse tasks—including mathematical reasoning, coding abilities, dialogue generation, instruction following, and text-to-image generation—demonstrate that Flat-LoRA improves both in-domain and out-of-domain generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/nblt/Flat-LoRA.

paragraphs: LoRA reduces fine-tuning costs by updating low-rank matrices instead of all model parameters. This paper examines a mismatch between that restricted optimization space and the full model. A solution can appear insensitive to changes within the LoRA space while remaining sensitive along directions outside it, potentially weakening generalization.

The method also refines how random perturbations are generated and uses random seeds to manage memory overhead.

Experiments cover mathematical reasoning, coding, dialogue generation, instruction following, and text-to-image generation. The authors report improvements in generalization both within and outside the training domain. The contribution is therefore an efficient adaptation strategy that considers the surrounding full model space when selecting low-rank updates. Its results support the paper’s concern that flatness measured only within the smaller adaptation space can miss directions relevant to generalization.
summary.tldr: Flat-LoRA seeks low-rank updates in flat regions of the full parameter space, improving generalization across the evaluated tasks.

title: Flat-LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation over a Flat Loss Landscape

abstract: Robust reinforcement learning (RL) under the average reward criterion, which seeks to optimize long-term system performance in uncertain environments, remains a largely unexplored area. To address this challenge, we propose a reduction-based framework that transforms robust average reward optimization into the more extensively studied robust discounted reward optimization by employing a specific discount factor. Our framework provides two key advantages. Data Efficiency: We design a model-based reduction algorithm that achieves near-optimal sample complexity, enabling efficient identification of optimal robust policies; Scalability: By bypassing the inherent challenges of scaling up average reward optimization, our framework facilitates the design of scalable, convergent algorithms for robust average reward optimization leveraging function approximation. Our algorithmic design, supported by theoretical and empirical analyses, provides a concrete solution to robust average reward RL with the first data efficiency and scalability guarantees, highlighting the framework’s potential to optimize long-term performance under model uncertainty in practical problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when the goal is strong long-term average performance despite uncertainty about the environment. The challenge is to find policies that remain effective under that uncertainty while keeping learning practical. Robust average-reward optimization has received less attention than its discounted-reward counterpart, leaving fewer established tools for solving it.

The authors introduce a reduction that converts the average-reward problem into a robust discounted-reward problem using a particular discount factor. This makes the better-studied discounted setting useful for the original objective. They build a model-based algorithm around this connection and establish near-optimal sample complexity for identifying optimal robust policies.

The framework also supports scalable, convergent algorithms using function approximation. This matters because data efficiency and the ability to handle larger problems are separate requirements: collecting fewer samples does not by itself make computation manageable. Supported by theoretical and empirical analyses, the paper claims the first guarantees addressing both requirements for robust average-reward reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: A reduction to robust discounted learning provides data-efficiency and scalability guarantees for robust average-reward reinforcement learning.

title: A Reduction Framework for Distributionally Robust Reinforcement Learning under Average Reward

abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) and interpretable machine learning methods help to build trust in model predictions and derived insights, yet also present a perverse incentive for analysts to manipulate XAI metrics to support pre-specified conclusions. This paper introduces the concept of X-hacking, a form of p-hacking applied to XAI metrics such as Shap values. We show how easily an automated machine learning pipeline can be adapted to exploit model multiplicity at scale: searching a set of defensible’ models with similar predictive performance to find a desired explanation. We formulate the trade-off between explanation and accuracy as a multi-objective optimisation problem, and illustrate empirically on familiar real-world datasets that, on average, Bayesian optimisation accelerates X-hacking 3-fold for features susceptible to it, versus random sampling. We show the vulnerability of a dataset to X-hacking can be determined by information redundancy among features. Finally, we suggest possible methods for detection and prevention, and discuss ethical implications for the credibility and reproducibility of XAI.

paragraphs: Explanations of model predictions can appear persuasive even when the analyst selected the model to obtain a preferred explanation. This paper calls that practice X-hacking. It studies how automated machine learning can search among models with similar predictive performance to find one whose explanation metrics, such as SHAP values, support a predetermined conclusion.

The authors formulate the search as a multi-objective optimization problem balancing accuracy and the desired explanation. This exploits model multiplicity: several defensible predictive models can yield different explanations. On the real-world datasets studied, Bayesian optimization accelerates X-hacking by an average factor of three compared with random sampling for features that are susceptible to it.

The study also links a dataset’s vulnerability to information redundancy among its features. This connects the opportunity for explanation manipulation to properties of the data itself. The authors suggest possible detection and prevention methods and discuss credibility and reproducibility. The central finding is that similar predictive accuracy can coexist with explanation differences that an automated search can deliberately exploit.
summary.tldr: Automated model search can exploit equally accurate models to produce preferred explanations, a practice the paper calls X-hacking.

title: X-Hacking: The Threat of Misguided AutoML

abstract: Multimodal representation learning is fundamentally about transforming incomparable modalities into comparable representations. While prior research has primarily focused on explicitly aligning these representations through targeted learning objectives and model architectures, a recent line of work has found that independently trained unimodal models of increasing scale and performance can become implicitly aligned with each other. These findings raise fundamental questions regarding the emergence of aligned representations in multimodal learning. Specifically: (1) when and why does alignment emerge implicitly? and (2) is alignment a reliable indicator of performance? Through a comprehensive empirical investigation, we demonstrate that both the emergence of alignment and its relationship with task performance depend on several critical data characteristics. These include, but are not necessarily limited to, the degree of similarity between the modalities and the balance between redundant and unique information they provide for the task. Our findings suggest that alignment may not be universally beneficial; rather, its impact on performance varies depending on the dataset and task. These insights can help practitioners determine whether increasing alignment between modalities is advantageous or, in some cases, detrimental to achieving optimal performance.

paragraphs: Models trained separately on different modalities can develop similar representations even without an objective that explicitly aligns them. This paper investigates when that implicit alignment emerges and whether stronger alignment reliably signals better task performance. It treats representation similarity and task success as related questions whose connection needs to be tested.

The authors conduct an empirical investigation of how data characteristics affect both phenomena. Two highlighted factors are similarity between modalities and the balance between task-relevant information they share and information unique to each. These factors matter because modalities can overlap substantially while also contributing distinct information needed for a particular task.

The findings show that alignment’s emergence and its relationship to performance depend on these data characteristics. They suggest that stronger alignment is not universally beneficial: its value can change with the dataset and task, and increasing it can sometimes be detrimental. For practitioners, the implication is to assess alignment in relation to the information a task requires, rather than treat similarity between representations as a standalone measure of quality.
summary.tldr: Empirical evidence shows that multimodal alignment and its performance benefits depend on modality similarity and the balance of shared and unique information.

title: Understanding the Emergence of Multimodal Representation Alignment

abstract: We present a novel method for efficiently computing optimal transport maps and Wasserstein barycenters in high-dimensional spaces. Our approach uses conditional normalizing flows to approximate the input distributions as invertible pushforward transformations from a common latent space. This makes it possible to directly solve the primal problem using gradient-based minimization of the transport cost, unlike previous methods that rely on dual formulations and complex adversarial optimization. We show how this approach can be extended to compute Wasserstein barycenters by solving a conditional variance minimization problem. A key advantage of our conditional architecture is that it enables the computation of barycenters for hundreds of input distributions, which was computationally infeasible with previous methods. Our numerical experiments illustrate that our approach yields accurate results across various high-dimensional tasks and compares favorably with previous state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Optimal transport seeks a low-cost way to move one probability distribution into another. A Wasserstein barycenter extends this idea to finding a representative distribution for several inputs. This paper develops a method for computing both in high-dimensional spaces, where the optimization can be computationally demanding.

The method uses conditional normalizing flows to approximate input distributions through invertible transformations of a shared latent space. This representation makes it possible to minimize the transport cost directly with gradients. It provides an alternative to approaches built around dual formulations and complicated adversarial optimization.

For barycenters, the authors extend the approach through a conditional variance minimization problem. They identify the conditional architecture as central to handling hundreds of input distributions, a scale they describe as computationally infeasible for previous methods. Numerical experiments report accurate results on several high-dimensional tasks and favorable comparisons with earlier state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is therefore both an optimization formulation and a way to increase the number of distributions that can be combined.
summary.tldr: Conditional normalizing flows enable direct transport-cost optimization and barycenter computation for hundreds of high-dimensional input distributions.

title: Computing Optimal Transport Maps and Wasserstein Barycenters Using Conditional Normalizing Flows

abstract: Diversity in demonstration selection is critical for enhancing model generalization by enabling broader coverage of structures and concepts. Constructing appropriate demonstration sets remains a key research challenge. This paper introduces the Relevance-Diversity Enhanced Selection (RDES), an innovative approach that leverages reinforcement learning (RL) frameworks to optimize the selection of diverse reference demonstrations for tasks amenable to in-context learning (ICL), particularly text classification and reasoning, in few-shot prompting scenarios. RDES employs frameworks like Q-learning and a PPO-based variant to dynamically identify demonstrations that maximize both diversity (quantified by label distribution) and relevance to the task objective. This strategy ensures a balanced representation of reference data, leading to improved accuracy and generalization. Through extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, including diverse reasoning tasks, and involving 14 closed-source and open-source LLMs, we demonstrate that RDES significantly enhances performance compared to ten established baselines. Our evaluation includes analysis of performance across varying numbers of demonstrations on selected datasets. Furthermore, we investigate incorporating Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, which further boosts predictive performance. The results highlight the potential of RL for adaptive demonstration selection and addressing challenges in ICL.

paragraphs: In-context learning asks a language model to infer a task from examples included in its prompt. The choice of examples matters: relevant demonstrations help explain the task, while diverse demonstrations cover a broader range of structures and concepts. RDES treats the construction of this example set as a reinforcement-learning problem.

The method uses Q-learning and a PPO-based variant to select demonstrations dynamically. Its selection objective combines task relevance with diversity measured through the distribution of labels. This gives the method an explicit way to balance reference examples, connecting the composition of the prompt to the predictive objective.

RDES significantly improves performance relative to ten established baselines. The authors also examine different demonstration counts on selected datasets and find further gains from incorporating chain-of-thought reasoning. Together, the results support adaptive demonstration selection for few-shot classification and reasoning, with the balance between relevance and label diversity serving as the method's organizing principle.
summary.tldr: RDES uses reinforcement learning to select relevant, label-diverse prompt examples, improving few-shot performance across the evaluated language models.

title: Demonstration Selection for In-Context Learning via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Generalizing multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to accommodate variations in problem configurations remains a critical challenge in real-world applications, where even subtle differences in task setups can cause pre-trained policies to fail. To address this, we propose Context-Aware Identity Generation (CAID), a novel framework to enhance MARL performance under the Contextual MARL (CMARL) setting. CAID dynamically generates unique agent identities through the agent identity decoder built on a causal Transformer architecture. These identities provide contextualized representations that align corresponding agents across similar problem variants, facilitating policy reuse and improving sample efficiency. Furthermore, the action regulator in CAID incorporates these agent identities into the action-value space, enabling seamless adaptation to varying contexts. Extensive experiments on CMARL benchmarks demonstrate that CAID significantly outperforms existing approaches by enhancing both sample efficiency and generalization across diverse context variants.

paragraphs: Multi-agent reinforcement learning can struggle when a task’s configuration changes, even if the new setup closely resembles one encountered during training. Policies may fail to transfer across these variations. Context-Aware Identity Generation addresses this problem by giving agents identities that reflect the current context and support correspondence across related task configurations.

A decoder built on a causal Transformer dynamically produces unique agent identities. These representations align corresponding agents across similar problem variants, helping the system reuse policies. An additional action regulator incorporates the generated identities into the action-value space, connecting contextual identity information to the agent’s assessment of available actions.

Experiments on contextual multi-agent reinforcement learning benchmarks report significant improvements in both sample efficiency and generalization over existing approaches. The findings support using context-sensitive identity as part of the policy’s representation. By connecting corresponding agents across variants and carrying that information into action evaluation, the framework makes previously learned behavior more useful when the surrounding task setup changes.
summary.tldr: CAID generates context-aware agent identities to improve policy reuse, sample efficiency, and generalization across multi-agent task variants.

title: Reidentify: Context-Aware Identity Generation for Contextual Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Determining the similarity between dynamical systems remains a long-standing challenge in both machine learning and neuroscience. Recent works based on Koopman operator theory have proven effective in analyzing dynamical similarity by examining discrepancies in the Koopman spectrum. Nevertheless, existing similarity metrics can be severely constrained when systems exhibit complex nonlinear behaviors across multiple temporal scales. In this work, we propose KoopSTD, a dynamical similarity measurement framework that precisely characterizes the underlying dynamics by approximating the Koopman spectrum with explicit timescale decoupling and spectral residual control. We show that KoopSTD maintains invariance under several common representation-space transformations, which ensures robust measurements across different coordinate systems. Our extensive experiments on physical and neural systems validate the effectiveness, scalability, and robustness of KoopSTD compared to existing similarity metrics. We also apply KoopSTD to explore two open-ended research questions in neuroscience and large language models, highlighting its potential to facilitate future scientific and engineering discoveries. Code is available at link.

paragraphs: Comparing dynamical systems means asking whether their behavior over time is similar, even when their representations differ. Methods based on Koopman operator theory compare spectral descriptions of that behavior. However, the paper identifies difficulties when nonlinear systems contain dynamics unfolding across multiple timescales, which can constrain existing similarity measures.

KoopSTD approximates the Koopman spectrum while explicitly separating timescales and controlling spectral residuals. These components aim to characterize the underlying dynamics more accurately. The authors also show that the measure is invariant under several common transformations of the representation space. For those transformations, a change of coordinates does not alter the measured similarity.

Experiments on physical and neural systems support the framework’s effectiveness, scalability, and robustness relative to existing measures. The authors additionally use KoopSTD to investigate two open-ended questions in neuroscience and large language models. Those applications illustrate its potential as a scientific analysis tool, while the stated invariance applies to the examined transformation classes rather than every possible representation change.
summary.tldr: KoopSTD compares dynamical systems through timescale-separated Koopman spectra and remains invariant under several common representation transformations.

title: KoopSTD: Reliable Similarity Analysis between Dynamical Systems via Approximating Koopman Spectrum with Timescale Decoupling

abstract: Recent research has explored that LLM agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, where malicious tasks embedded in tool-retrieved information can redirect the agent to take unauthorized actions. Existing defenses against IPI have significant limitations: either require essential model training resources, lack effectiveness against sophisticated attacks, or harm the normal utilities. We present MELON (Masked re-Execution and TooL comparisON), a novel IPI defense. Our approach builds on the observation that under a successful attack, the agent’s next action becomes less dependent on user tasks and more on malicious tasks. Following this, we design MELON to detect attacks by re-executing the agent’s trajectory with a masked user prompt modified through a masking function. We identify an attack if the actions generated in the original and masked executions are similar. We also include three key designs to reduce the potential false positives and false negatives. Extensive evaluation on the IPI benchmark AgentDojo demonstrates that MELON outperforms SOTA defenses in both attack prevention and utility preservation. Moreover, we show that combining MELON with a SOTA prompt augmentation defense (denoted as MELON-Aug) further improves its performance. We also conduct a detailed ablation study to validate our key designs. Code is available at https://github.com/kaijiezhu11/MELON.

The defense re-executes the agent’s trajectory after applying a masking function to the user prompt. It compares actions from the original and masked executions and flags an attack when those actions are similar. Combining it with a prompt-augmentation defense produces further improvements, and ablations examine its key design choices. The reported evidence supports task-dependence testing as a useful defense signal while explicitly recognizing the importance of avoiding mistaken detections.
summary.tldr: MELON detects indirect prompt injection by comparing agent actions before and after masking the legitimate user task.

title: MELON: Provable Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks in AI Agents

abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose LLM activations into interpretable features, yet existing SAE-based steering methods require contrastive datasets or large activation stores. We introduce CorrSteer, which selects steering features by correlating task outcomes with SAE activations computed during generation, then validates these selections through intervention. This two-stage approach treats correlation as a selection heuristic and intervention as the causal test: features that both correlate with success and improve performance when amplified are retained. Coefficients derive from mean activations on correct samples, yielding a fully automated pipeline without task-specific tuning. On Gemma-2 2B and LLaMA-3.1 8B, CorrSteer achieves +3.3% on MMLU (4k samples) and +27.1% on HarmBench (108 samples), with lower side-effect ratios than fine-tuning despite comparable accuracy. Selected features cluster into interpretable categories: structured-output features for multiple-choice tasks, refusal features for safety, and domain-specific semantics for specialized benchmarks. The method scales to $10^5$ SAE features (16K per layer $\times$ 26 layers for Gemma-2 2B; 32K $\times$ 32 for LLaMA-3.1 8B) via streaming correlation ($O(1)$ in dataset size), requiring no backward passes or activation storage.

CorrSteer identifies useful steering features from activations observed during generation. Its aim is to automate this process without the contrastive datasets or large stored activation collections required by existing approaches.

title: CorrSteer: Generation-Time LLM Steering via Correlated Sparse Autoencoder Features

abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) promote interpretability by grounding predictions in human-understandable concepts. However, existing CBMs typically constrain their task predictor to a single expression whose functional form is set a priori, limiting both predictive accuracy and adaptability to diverse user needs. We propose Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts (M-CBEs), a framework that generalizes existing CBMs along two dimensions: the number of expressions, referred to as experts, employed by the task predictor to map concepts to the task, and the functional form each expression takes, thus exposing an underexplored region of this design space. We investigate this region by instantiating two novel models: Linear M-CBE, which learns a finite set of linear expressions, and Symbolic M-CBE, which leverages symbolic regression to discover expert functions from data subject to user-specified operator vocabularies. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that varying the number of expressions and their functional form provides a robust framework for navigating the accuracy-interpretability trade-off.

paragraphs: Concept Bottleneck Models make predictions through human-understandable concepts, giving users an interpretable intermediate representation. Their final task predictor, however, typically uses one expression with a functional form chosen in advance. This paper argues that the restriction limits both predictive accuracy and the ability to accommodate different users’ interpretability needs.

Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts expands that predictor along two dimensions: how many expressions it uses and what forms those expressions can take. The authors instantiate a linear version that learns a finite collection of linear expressions. They also introduce a symbolic version that discovers expert functions from data through symbolic regression, with users specifying which operators are available.

These choices make the mapping from concepts to predictions a more flexible part of the model design. A user can vary the number of experts and the permitted expression types to explore different balances between accuracy and interpretability. Empirical evaluation supports this framework for navigating that trade-off, rather than fixing the predictor’s structure before considering the task and user requirements.
summary.tldr: Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts varies the number and form of concept-based prediction rules to explore the accuracy-interpretability trade-off.

title: Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts

abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable reasoning capabilities, inherent social biases often cascade throughout the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, leading to continuous "Bias Propagation". Existing debiasing methods primarily focus on static constraints or external interventions, failing to identify and interrupt this propagation once triggered. To address this limitation, we introduce Self-Debias, a progressive framework designed to instill intrinsic self-correction capabilities. Specifically, we reformulate the debiasing process as a strategic resource redistribution problem, treating the model’s output probability mass as a limited resource to be reallocated from biased heuristics to unbiased reasoning paths. Unlike standard preference optimization which applies broad penalties, Self-Debias employs a fine-grained trajectory-level objective subject to dynamic debiasing constraints. This enables the model to selectively revise biased reasoning suffixes while preserving valid contextual prefixes. Furthermore, we integrate an online self-improvement mechanism utilizing consistency filtering to autonomously synthesize supervision signals. With merely 20k annotated samples, Self-Debias activates efficient self-correction, achieving superior debiasing performance while preserving general reasoning capabilities without continuous external oversight.

paragraphs: Social bias can enter a language model’s reasoning and influence the steps that follow. This paper focuses on interrupting that propagation after it begins. Self-Debias trains a model to revise biased reasoning progressively, aiming to preserve useful context while changing the continuation responsible for carrying bias forward.

The framework treats output probability as a limited resource that can be redistributed from biased shortcuts toward unbiased reasoning paths. It uses a fine-grained objective over reasoning trajectories, subject to dynamic debiasing constraints. This supports selective revision of biased suffixes while retaining valid prefixes. An online self-improvement component also generates supervision signals and filters them for consistency.

Using 20,000 annotated samples, the authors report stronger debiasing performance while preserving general reasoning capabilities. They also report self-correction without continuous external oversight. The contribution is a targeted training approach for changing how bias develops within reasoning, rather than applying only broad penalties to outputs. These findings establish reported improvements in debiasing and retained reasoning ability, without implying that every form of social bias has been eliminated.
summary.tldr: Self-Debias trains language models to revise biased reasoning continuations while preserving valid context and general reasoning ability.

title: Self-correcting for Debiasing Large Language Models

abstract: Modern LLM serving systems must sustain high throughput while meeting strict latency SLOs across two distinct inference phases: compute-intensive prefill and memory-bound decode phases. Existing approaches either (1) aggregate both phases on shared GPUs, leading to interference between prefill and decode phases, which degrades Time-Between-Tokens (TBT); or (2) disaggregate the two phases across GPUs, improving latency but wasting resources through duplicated models and KV cache transfers. We present DuetServe, a unified LLM serving framework that achieves disaggregation-level isolation within a single GPU. DuetServe operates in aggregated mode by default and dynamically activates SM-level GPU spatial multiplexing when TBT degradation is predicted. Its key idea is to decouple prefill and decode execution only when needed through fine-grained, adaptive SM partitioning that provides phase isolation only when contention threatens latency service level objectives. DuetServe integrates (1) an attention-aware roofline model to forecast iteration latency, (2) a partitioning optimizer that selects the optimal SM split to maximize throughput under TBT constraints, and (3) an interruption-free execution engine that eliminates CPU–GPU synchronization overhead. Evaluations show that DuetServe improves total throughput by up to 1.3$\times$ while maintaining low generation latency compared to state-of-the-art frameworks.

paragraphs: Language-model serving has two phases with different resource demands. Prefill processes the input and is compute-intensive, while decoding generates successive tokens and is constrained by memory access. Sharing a GPU can let prefill interfere with decoding, increasing the delay between tokens. Separating the phases across GPUs introduces duplicated models and transfers of cached information.

DuetServe normally runs both phases together, but predicts when contention will threaten the required time between tokens. It then partitions the GPU’s streaming multiprocessors to isolate the phases within the same device. An attention-aware performance model forecasts iteration latency, and an optimizer chooses a partition intended to maximize throughput while meeting the latency constraint.

The framework also includes an execution engine that eliminates CPU–GPU synchronization overhead without interrupting execution. Evaluations report up to 1.3× higher total throughput than state-of-the-art serving frameworks while maintaining low generation latency. The main idea is to activate isolation when needed, allowing resource sharing and latency protection to coexist within a single GPU.
summary.tldr: DuetServe adaptively partitions a single GPU to protect token-generation latency while maintaining high serving throughput.

title: DuetServe: Harmonizing Prefill and Decode for LLM Serving via Adaptive GPU Multiplexing

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) possess latent multi-token prediction (MTP) abilities despite being trained only for next-token generation. We introduce ESP (Embedding-Space Probing), a simple and training-free MTP method that probes an LLM using on-the-fly mask tokens drawn from its embedding space, enabling parallel future-token prediction without modifying weights or relying on draft models. ESP constructs a speculative token tree by sampling Top-K candidates from mask-token logits and applies a lightweight pruning rule to retain high-probability continuations. During generation, predictions are verified in parallel, yielding lossless decoding while significantly reducing model calls and increasing token throughput. ESP consistently outperforms existing training-free baselines, improving acceptance length by $7$–$11$% over Lookahead Decoding on LLaMA3 and $7$–$8$% on Qwen3, and increasing throughput by up to $15$–$19$% over the strongest baseline. Finally, we provide theoretical insight and empirical evidence showing that decoder layers naturally align mask-token representations with next-token states, enabling accurate multi-step prediction without retraining or auxiliary models.

paragraphs: Language models trained to predict one token at a time can also contain useful information about several future tokens. Embedding-Space Probing, or ESP, accesses that ability without additional training, weight changes, or a separate draft model. It uses mask tokens constructed on the fly from the model’s embedding space to probe future predictions in parallel.

ESP turns these predictions into a speculative tree of possible continuations. It samples Top-K candidates from the mask-token outputs, then applies a lightweight pruning rule to keep promising branches. The model verifies predictions in parallel during generation. This verification supports lossless decoding while reducing the number of model calls needed to produce tokens.

The reported acceptance-length improvements over Lookahead Decoding are 7–11% on LLaMA3 and 7–8% on Qwen3, with throughput gains reaching 15–19% over the strongest baseline. Theoretical analysis and empirical evidence connect this behavior to decoder layers aligning mask representations with next-token states. The results suggest that existing model representations can support useful multi-step speculation without retraining.
summary.tldr: ESP probes existing model embeddings for parallel future-token predictions, accelerating verified decoding without training or a draft model.

title: Efficient Training-Free Multi-Token Prediction via Embedding-Space Probing

abstract: Fine-tuning Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) on task-specific data is an effective way to improve performance on downstream applications. However, such adaptation often leads to a degradation in generalization on pretrained tasks, a phenomenon known as Catastrophic Forgetting. Existing methods that aim to mitigate this issue either become ineffective when fine-tuning deeper layers of the language decoder or scale poorly with increasing model size. To address these limitations, we propose Model-Dowser, a novel sparse fine-tuning approach for MLLMs. Model-Dowser measures a principled importance score for each model parameter with respect to pretrained generalization (prior to downstream adaptation) by jointly considering weight magnitudes, input activations, and output sensitivities. During fine-tuning, Model-Dowser selectively preserves high-importance parameters and updates the remaining. Comprehensive experiments on two representative MLLMs, LLaVA and NVILA, demonstrate that Model-Dowser effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting and consistently outperforms prior methods, while remaining resource-efficient and scalable to multi-billion-parameter models.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a multimodal language model for a particular task can weaken capabilities acquired during pretraining. This catastrophic forgetting creates a tension between specialization and retaining broad generalization. Existing mitigation methods can lose effectiveness when deeper decoder layers are tuned or become difficult to scale to larger models.

Model-Dowser addresses this with selective parameter updates. Before downstream adaptation, it scores each parameter's importance to pretrained generalization by jointly considering weight magnitude, input activations, and output sensitivity. During fine-tuning, parameters with high importance are preserved while the remaining parameters are updated. The score therefore determines where adaptation is allowed to occur.

Experiments on LLaVA and NVILA show reduced catastrophic forgetting and consistent improvements over prior methods. The approach remains resource-efficient and scales to models with billions of parameters. These findings support using a structured importance estimate to allocate fine-tuning updates, preserving influential parts of the pretrained model while leaving other parameters available to learn the downstream task.
summary.tldr: Model-Dowser reduces forgetting during multimodal fine-tuning by preserving parameters judged important to pretrained generalization.

title: Model-Dowser: Data-Free Importance Probing to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting in Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Publishing a large language model (LLM) benchmark (especially its ground-truth answers) on the Internet risks contaminating future LLMs and enabling evaluation gaming: it may be unintentionally (or intentionally) used to train or select a model, or exploited to overfit and hack leaderboards when labels are accessible. A common mitigation is to keep the benchmark private and let participants submit their models or predictions to the organizers, but this still permits test-set overfitting through feedback loops. To overcome this issue, we propose CapBencher, a way to publish benchmarks without fully disclosing the ground-truth answers, while preserving open evaluation of LLMs. The main idea is to reduce the best possible accuracy, i.e., Bayes accuracy, by injecting randomness to the answers by preparing several logically correct answers, and only include one of them as the solution in the benchmark. Not only does this obscure the ground-truth answers, but it also offers a test for leakage or gaming: since even fully capable models should not surpass the Bayes accuracy, any model that does is a strong signal. We show theoretically and empirically that CapBencher accurately detects test-set overfitting across diverse benchmarks, models, training methodologies, and scenarios.

paragraphs: Public benchmarks can be contaminated by training data or exploited through repeated evaluation feedback. Keeping labels private does not fully prevent overfitting to a test set. CapBencher adds a detectable accuracy ceiling by retaining uncertainty about which valid answer is recorded as the benchmark target.

For each suitable problem, the method prepares several logically correct answers but randomly includes only one as the official solution. This lowers Bayes accuracy for a model without access to that random choice. Performance above the resulting ceiling becomes evidence of leakage or gaming, while the benchmark remains openly evaluable without fully revealing its ground truth.

Theoretical analysis and experiments across benchmarks, models, and training scenarios show effective detection of test-set overfitting. The contribution is an alarm embedded in benchmark design. Its interpretation depends on the randomized-answer construction and the corresponding accuracy bound, rather than treating any unusually strong result on an ordinary benchmark as proof of contamination.
summary.tldr: CapBencher randomizes among valid answers to create an accuracy ceiling whose violation signals benchmark leakage or gaming.

title: CapBencher: Give Your LLM Benchmark a Built-in Alarm for Test-Set Overfitting

abstract: Autonomous Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents often struggle with multi-step tasks due to constrained context windows and static policies that fail to adapt to dynamic environments. To address these limitations, this work proposes the Self-Evolving GUI Agent (SE-GA), a novel framework that integrates hierarchical memory structures with an iterative self-improvement mechanism. At the core of our approach is Test-Time Memory Extension (TTME), which facilitates long-term planning by dynamically retrieving episodic, semantic, and experiential memories to provide salient contexts during inference. To ensure continuous learning, we introduce Memory-Augmented Self-Evolution (MASE), which is a training pipeline that adopts the data collected by TTME to stabilize and enhance the agent’s foundational policy. Extensive evaluations across both offline and online benchmarks demonstrate SE-GA achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching success rates of 89.0% on ScreenSpot and 75.8% on the challenging AndroidControl-High dataset. Furthermore, significant improvements on the AndroidWorld benchmark highlight the superior generalization to dynamic environments.

paragraphs: GUI agents must carry information across multiple actions while adapting to interfaces that can change. Limited context windows make long-term planning difficult, and a fixed policy cannot continually incorporate new experience. SE-GA combines a hierarchical memory system with an iterative training process to address both problems.

During inference, Test-Time Memory Extension retrieves relevant episodic, semantic, and experiential memories. This supplies salient context for the current task without relying only on what remains in the immediate context window. A separate Memory-Augmented Self-Evolution pipeline uses the data collected through this memory-assisted activity to stabilize and improve the agent’s underlying policy.

The evaluations span offline and online benchmarks. SE-GA reports state-of-the-art performance, including success rates of 89.0% on ScreenSpot and 75.8% on AndroidControl-High, alongside significant improvements on AndroidWorld. The AndroidWorld results support better generalization to dynamic environments in the reported evaluation. The overall contribution connects memory retrieval during task execution with policy improvement afterward, so experience serves both immediate planning and subsequent learning.
summary.tldr: SE-GA uses retrieved memories for GUI task planning and turns collected experience into further policy improvements.

title: SE-GA: Memory-Augmented Self-Evolution for GUI Agents

abstract: Mobile Agents requires hybrid-capabilities reasoning, including screen summary, subtask planning, action decision and action function. However, existing agents struggle to achieve both decoupled enhancement and balanced integration of these capabilities. To address these challenges, we propose Channel-of-Mobile-Experts (CoME), a novel agent architecture consisting of four distinct experts, each aligned with a specific reasoning stage, CoME activates the corresponding expert to generate output tokens in each reasoning stage via output-oriented activation. To empower CoME with hybrid-capabilities reasoning, we introduce a progressive training strategy: Expert-FT enables decoupling and enhancement of different experts’ capability; Router-FT aligns expert activation with the different reasoning stage; CoT-FT facilitates seamless collaboration and balanced optimization across multiple capabilities. To mitigate error propagation in hybrid-capabilities reasoning, we propose InfoGain-Driven DPO (Info-DPO), which uses information gain to evaluate the contribution of each intermediate step, thereby guiding CoME toward more informative reasoning. Comprehensive experiments show that CoME outperforms dense mobile agents and MoE methods on both AITZ and AMEX datasets.

To address these challenges, we propose Channel-of-Mobile-Experts (CoME), a novel agent architecture consisting of four distinct experts, each aligned with a specific reasoning stage, CoME activates the corresponding expert to generate output tokens in each reasoning stage via output-oriented activation. To empower CoME with hybrid-capabilities reasoning, we introduce a progressive training strategy: Expert-FT enables decoupling and enhancement of different experts’ capability; Router-FT aligns expert activation with the different reasoning stage; CoT-FT facilitates seamless collaboration and balanced optimization across multiple capabilities. To mitigate error propagation in hybrid-capabilities reasoning, we propose InfoGain-Driven DPO (Info-DPO), which uses information gain to evaluate the contribution of each intermediate step, thereby guiding CoME toward more informative reasoning. Comprehensive experiments show that CoME outperforms dense mobile agents and MoE methods on both AITZ and AMEX datasets.

paragraphs: CoME organizes a mobile agent around four capabilities: summarizing the screen, planning subtasks, deciding actions, and producing action functions. The motivation is that these stages need both specialized improvement and coordinated execution. The architecture assigns each stage its own expert and activates the corresponding expert when generating that stage’s output tokens.

Training proceeds through three phases. Expert-FT develops the individual capabilities separately. Router-FT teaches the system to activate the expert appropriate to each reasoning stage. CoT-FT then trains collaboration across the stages and balances their optimization. This progression gives specialization and integration distinct roles in training, while retaining a single reasoning process that combines their outputs.

The paper also introduces InfoGain-Driven DPO to reduce the spread of errors through intermediate reasoning. It evaluates each step’s contribution using information gain and favors more informative reasoning. Experiments on AITZ and AMEX show improvements over dense mobile agents and mixture-of-experts methods. The results support pairing stage-specific experts with training that explicitly manages both their coordination and the usefulness of intermediate steps.
summary.tldr: CoME trains four stage-specific mobile-agent experts and uses information gain to improve their coordinated reasoning.

title: CoME: Empowering Channel-of-Mobile-Experts with Informative Hybrid-Capabilities Reasoning

abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) offers distribution-free uncertainty quantification for machine learning models, yet its interplay with fairness in downstream decision-making remains underexplored. Moving beyond CP as a standalone operation (procedural fairness), we analyze the holistic decision-making pipeline to evaluate substantive fairness—the equity of downstream outcomes. Theoretically, we derive an upper bound that decomposes prediction-set size disparity into interpretable components, clarifying how label-clustered CP helps control method-driven contributions to unfairness. To facilitate scalable empirical analysis, we introduce an LLM-in-the-loop evaluator that approximates human assessment of substantive fairness across diverse modalities. Our experiments show that label-clustered CP often provides a favorable balance between utility and substantive fairness, while reducing set-size disparities in line with our theory. Finally, we empirically show that equalized set sizes, rather than coverage, strongly correlate with improved substantive fairness, enabling practitioners to design more fair CP systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/layer6ai-labs/llm-in-the-loop-conformal-fairness.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction expresses uncertainty by returning sets of possible answers with statistical coverage guarantees. This paper asks how those sets affect fairness once people or systems use them to make decisions. Its focus is substantive fairness: the equity of downstream outcomes across the complete decision process, beyond the properties of the prediction procedure alone.

The authors derive an upper bound that separates disparities in prediction-set size into interpretable contributions. This analysis explains how label-clustered conformal prediction can help control the portion attributable to the method itself. They also introduce an evaluator that places an LLM within the evaluation process to approximate human judgments of substantive fairness across different modalities.

In the reported experiments, label-clustered conformal prediction often balances usefulness and substantive fairness favorably while reducing set-size disparities. Equalized set sizes correlate strongly with better substantive fairness, more so than coverage does. This is an empirical association rather than a guarantee that matching set sizes produces equitable outcomes, but it identifies a practical property worth evaluating alongside coverage.
summary.tldr: The paper connects conformal prediction to downstream fairness and finds that equalized prediction-set sizes correlate strongly with fairer outcomes.

title: Beyond Procedure: Substantive Fairness in Conformal Prediction

abstract: We introduce ECSEL, an explainable classification method that learns formal expressions in the form of signomial equations, motivated by the observation that many symbolic regression benchmarks admit compact signomial structure. ECSEL directly constructs a structural, closed-form expression that serves as both a classifier and an explanation. On standard symbolic regression benchmarks, our method recovers a larger fraction of target equations than competing state-of-the-art approaches while requiring substantially less computation. Leveraging this efficiency, ECSEL achieves classification accuracy competitive with established machine learning models without sacrificing interpretability. Further, we show that ECSEL satisfies some desirable properties regarding global feature behaviour, decision-boundary analysis, and local feature attributions. Experiments on benchmark datasets and two real-world case studies i.e., e-commerce and fraud detection, demonstrate that the learned equations expose dataset biases, support counterfactual reasoning, and yield actionable insights.

The reported accuracy remains competitive, while the equation exposes aspects of the decision process for direct analysis.
summary.tldr: ECSEL learns compact mathematical classifiers that offer competitive accuracy and directly inspectable explanations.

title: ECSEL: Explainable Classification via Signomial Equation Learning

abstract: Large-scale models are pretrained on massive web-crawled datasets containing documents of mixed quality, making data filtering essential. A popular method is Classifier-based Quality Filtering (CQF), which trains a binary classifier to distinguish between pretraining data and a small, high-quality set. It assigns each pretraining document a quality score defined as the classifier’s score and retains only the top-scoring ones. We provide an in-depth analysis of CQF. We show that while CQF improves downstream task performance, it does not necessarily enhance language modeling on the high-quality set. Importantly, we find that training on CQF-selected data can outperform training directly on the high-quality set, even when the latter is sufficiently large. This finding alone is particularly striking, given the substantial effort and cost recently devoted to augmenting high-quality data. We explain this paradox by the fact that CQF implicitly filters the high-quality dataset as well as the low-quality one. Finally, we introduce an optimization-driven notion of data quality and demonstrate that it can be reliably estimated using small-scale proxy experiments. Altogether, our results both elucidate the mechanisms behind CQF and deepen our understanding of data selection methods widely used in practice.

paragraphs: Classifier-based quality filtering trains a model to distinguish web pretraining documents from a small collection labeled high quality. It then keeps the web documents receiving the highest classifier scores. This paper examines what that procedure actually accomplishes and whether its benefits can be explained simply as finding more documents like the reference collection.

The analysis finds that filtering improves downstream task performance without necessarily improving language modeling on the high-quality set. More strikingly, training on the selected web data can outperform training directly on the high-quality collection, even when that collection is sufficiently large. Thus, the reference set's quality label does not by itself establish that training directly on it is the best choice.

The authors explain this outcome by showing that the classifier implicitly filters both the low-quality and high-quality data. They also introduce a notion of data quality grounded in optimization and show that small proxy experiments can estimate it reliably. These findings clarify why quality filtering can help and connect data value to its role in training.
summary.tldr: Quality filtering can outperform direct training on its high-quality reference set because it implicitly filters both high- and low-quality data.

title: Removing Noise, not Finding Gold: Quality Filtering for Large-Scale Pretraining

abstract: In contemporary deep learning, a prevalent and effective workflow for solving low-data problems is adapting powerful pre-trained foundation models (FMs) to new tasks via parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). However, while empirically effective, the resulting solutions lack generalisation guarantees to certify their accuracy - which may be required for ethical or legal reasons prior to deployment in high-importance applications. In this paper we develop a novel transfer learning approach that is designed to facilitate non-vacuous learning theoretic generalisation guarantees for downstream tasks, even in the low-shot regime. Specifically, we first use upstream tasks to train a distribution over PEFT parameters. We then learn the downstream task by a sample-and-evaluate procedure – sampling plausible PEFTs from the trained diffusion model and selecting the one with the highest likelihood on the downstream data. Crucially, this confines our model hypothesis to a finite set of PEFT samples. In contrast to the typical continuous hypothesis spaces of neural network weights, this facilitates tighter risk certificates. We instantiate our bound and show non-trivial generalization guarantees compared to existing learning approaches which lead to vacuous bounds in the low-shot regime.

paragraphs: Adapting a foundation model with only a few examples can work well empirically while offering weak guarantees about performance on unseen data. This paper designs a transfer-learning procedure around obtaining informative generalization certificates. It focuses on parameter-efficient fine-tuning, where adaptation changes a restricted set of model parameters.

The method first learns a distribution over adaptation parameters from upstream tasks using a diffusion model. For a downstream task, it samples candidate adaptations and selects the one with the highest likelihood on the available examples. This sample-and-evaluate procedure restricts the final choice to a finite collection of candidates.

That finite hypothesis set is central to the theory: it enables tighter risk certificates than the usual continuous space of neural-network weights. The authors instantiate their bound and obtain non-trivial guarantees in a low-shot setting where the compared learning approaches yield vacuous bounds. The contribution links how adaptations are proposed and selected to whether their generalization can be meaningfully certified.
summary.tldr: Sampling a finite set of learned parameter adaptations enables informative generalization guarantees for few-shot transfer learning.

title: Weight-Space Learning for Certifiable Few-shot Transfer Learning

abstract: As Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in complex environments, multi-turn interaction attacks have become a significant security challenge. Existing detection methods typically rely on historical context. However, this retrospective logic struggles to identify deep malicious intents that are split across turns to hide future risks. Inspired by speculative decoding, we propose the Speculative Safety Honeypot (SSH) framework. SSH uses a multi-agent simulation system composed of small LLMs to build an action-level speculate-and-verify workflow. In the speculation stage, SSH predicts future behaviors of the target agent and asynchronously builds a trajectory tree to expose potential risks in advance. In the verification stage, the system uses the target agent’s real actions to calibrate and prune the trajectory tree, effectively reducing false positives. As a plug-and-playable component, SSH provides existing detectors with rich decision redundancy beyond the current interaction slice. By judging risk based on the evolution of the entire trajectory tree rather than a single point in time, the system reduces the reliance on the absolute precision of individual detection components. This improves the defense resilience and the warning lead-time of agent systems against complex temporal attacks.
