paragraphs: Attacks against language-model agents can unfold over several interactions, with malicious intent distributed across turns. A detector that examines only past and current behavior may miss how apparently limited steps could develop into a harmful trajectory. Speculative Safety Honeypot addresses this temporal problem by exploring possible future actions before they occur.

The framework uses multiple small language models to simulate the target agent’s future behavior. It asynchronously builds a branching trajectory tree that exposes potential risks. As the target agent actually acts, a verification stage calibrates and prunes the tree using those observations. This feedback is intended to reduce false positives arising from speculative futures that do not match real behavior.

SSH is designed as an add-on for existing detectors, supplying evidence beyond the current interaction. Risk assessment uses the evolving tree rather than one isolated decision point, reducing dependence on the precision of individual detection components. The abstract reports improved resilience and earlier warnings against complex multi-turn attacks. Its contribution is a proactive, continuously revised view of risk grounded in actual agent actions.
summary.tldr: SSH simulates possible future agent actions and checks them against real behavior to provide earlier, more resilient detection of multi-turn attacks.

title: Speculative Safety Honeypot: Toward Proactive Defense Against Multi-turn Agent Attacks

abstract: Personalizing AI decision support for heterogeneous human decision-makers remains a key challenge. We study a collaboration workflow where AI provides a reduced prediction set via conformal prediction and the human makes the final decision based on the set. We formulate this personalization problem as a contextual bandit, where individual and task features form the context, candidate significance levels $\alpha$ serve as arms, and the optimal prediction-set size varies across contexts. To address large arm spaces and high-dimensional contexts, we introduce the Adaptively Grouped Contextual Bandit (AGCB) framework, which avoids global function approximation by exploiting two Human-AI structural assumptions: continuity and monotonicity. Continuity enables information sharing across nearby contexts and decisions, and drives a data-driven Zooming Mechanism that balances intra-group estimation error against inter-group approximation bias. Monotonicity converts each observation into directional counterfactual information over the $K$ candidate $\alpha$ values, reducing the arm-dependence factor from polynomial to logarithmic in $K$. Together, these mechanisms yield minimax-optimal dependence on the learning horizon $T$ for both cumulative and simple regret objectives. Empirical results confirm that AGCB achieves the strongest overall performance across most heterogeneous, data-scarce settings.

paragraphs: An AI assistant can support a decision by presenting a short list of plausible answers, leaving the final choice to a person. The useful list size can depend on both the person and the task. This paper studies how to personalize that choice when the lists come from conformal prediction.

The authors frame personalization as a contextual bandit: person and task features describe the situation, while candidate significance levels determine the available prediction-set choices. Their Adaptively Grouped Contextual Bandit method shares evidence between nearby situations under a continuity assumption. It adjusts group sizes to balance reliable estimation against the loss of detail from grouping. A monotonicity assumption also lets one observation provide directional information about other candidate choices.

Together, these mechanisms reduce dependence on the number of choices from polynomial to logarithmic. Under the stated structural assumptions, the method achieves minimax-optimal dependence on the learning horizon for both cumulative and final-decision regret. Experiments report the strongest overall performance across most tested settings with heterogeneous users and scarce data, supporting adaptive grouping as a practical personalization strategy.
summary.tldr: AGCB personalizes AI prediction sets by sharing evidence across similar contexts and exploiting continuity and monotonicity assumptions.

title: Adaptively Grouped Contextual Bandits for Heterogeneous Human-AI Decision Making with Conformal Prediction Sets

abstract: The annealing phase is a pivotal convergence stage in LLM pre-training that ultimately determines final model quality. However, effectively selecting training data during this phase remains a key challenge. Current strategies rely on empirical heuristics, such as domain filtering or context extension, which lack a principled grounding in optimization theory. In this work, we characterize the annealing phase through the lens of the loss landscape’s spectral geometry. We argue that optimal convergence requires gradient updates to satisfy heterogeneous constraints across different eigen-directions. Building on this insight, we formulate data selection as a problem of satisfying these directional constraints. To this end, we propose DiReCT (Directionally-Restrained Constrained Training), a novel framework that reformulates sample selection in the annealing stage as a constrained optimization problem. By imposing explicit directional constraints on per-sample gradients based on the spectral properties of the Hessian, DiReCT identifies samples that align with the optimal curvature-aware descent path. Extensive experiments across various model scales demonstrate that DiReCT consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. For future research, code is available at https://github.com/xuyj233/Direct.

title: Towards Efficient LLMs Annealing with Principled Sample Selection

abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have brought substantial gains in the extrapolation capability in computational chemistry. However, most equivariant models are typically built with spherical tensors (STs), while Cartesian tensor formulations remain less developed despite their natural alignment with atomic coordinates and tensorial targets. In this work, we develop a Cartesian framework for irreducible Cartesian tensors (ICTs) by introduce the Cartesian-3j symbol and Cartesian Generalized Clebsch-Gordan Coefficients, which serve as direct analogues of the Wigner-3j symbol and Generalized Clebsch-Gordan coefficients defined for ST coupling. We extend the e3nn library to support ICT product, and use this framework to build Cartesian counterparts of MACE, NequIP, and Allegro, allowing the first controlled comparison where architectures are held fixed and only the tensor basis is changed. Our experiments show that irreducible Cartesian models can achieve accuracy comparable to spherical counterparts, but direct Cartesianization incurs unfavorable compute and memory scaling, motivating dedicated Cartesian architectural choices. Leveraging ICTs and our framework, we introduce TACE-v1-OAM-M and demonstrate that it achieves competitive performance on Matbench Discovery compared to state-of-the-art ST models.

paragraphs: Machine learning interatomic potentials model atomic interactions using representations that respect spatial symmetries. This paper develops mathematical tools that make irreducible Cartesian tensors a more practical foundation for these models.

The authors introduce Cartesian counterparts of established tensor-coupling coefficients and extend e3nn to support the resulting tensor products. They then construct Cartesian versions of MACE, NequIP, and Allegro. Holding the architectures fixed while changing the tensor basis makes it possible to examine the consequences of the representation itself, rather than mixing those effects with architectural changes.

This motivates architectures designed specifically around Cartesian tensors. The proposed TACE-v1-OAM-M achieves competitive results against leading spherical-tensor models on Matbench Discovery. The contribution therefore combines a mathematical framework, a controlled comparison, and evidence that dedicated architectural choices matter for making Cartesian models practical.
summary.tldr: A new Cartesian tensor framework enables controlled comparisons of atomic models and motivates architectures that address the cost of direct Cartesian conversion.

abstract: In this paper we tackle a real world problem, the search of a function to evaluate the merits of beef cattle as meat producers. The independent variables represent a set of live animals� measurements; while the outputs cannot be captured with a single number, since the available experts tend to assess each animal in a relative way, comparing animals with the other partners in the same batch. Therefore, this problem can not be solved by means of regression methods; our approach is to learn the preferences of the experts when they order small groups of animals. Thus, the problem can be reduced to a binary classifi- cation, and can be dealt with a Support Vector Machine (SVM) improved with the use of a feature subset selection (FSS) method. We develop a method based on Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) that employs an adaptation of a metric based method devised for model selection (ADJ). Finally, we discuss the extension of the resulting method to more general settings, and provide a comparison with other possible alternatives.

paragraphs: The application is assessing beef cattle as meat producers from measurements taken on live animals. The available experts judge animals relative to others in the same batch, so their assessments do not supply a single numerical target for each animal. The paper therefore frames the task as learning preferences from orderings of small groups.

The authors reduce this preference-learning problem to binary classification and use a support vector machine. They also select a subset of the available measurements, making feature selection part of the approach. The selection method builds on recursive feature elimination and adapts a metric-based model-selection method called ADJ.

The practical contribution is to align the learning task with the form of expertise actually available: relative judgments among animals. The feature-selection component addresses which measurements should support that learned ordering. The paper compares the resulting method with alternatives and discusses extension to more general settings, presenting the cattle assessment problem as a case study for a broader preference-learning approach.
summary.tldr: The paper combines SVM preference learning with recursive feature selection to learn experts’ relative assessments of beef cattle.

title: Feature subset selection for learning preferences: a case study

abstract: In this paper we show how to boost products of simple base learners. Similarly to trees, we call the base learner as a subroutine but in an iterative rather than recursive fashion. The main advantage of the proposed method is its simplicity and computational efficiency. On benchmark datasets, our boosted products of decision stumps clearly outperform boosted trees, and on the MNIST dataset the algorithm achieves the second best result among no-domain-knowledge algorithms after deep belief nets. As a second contribution, we present an improved base learner for nominal features and show that boosting the product of two of these new subset indicator base learners solves the maximum margin matrix factorization problem used to formalize the collaborative filtering task. On a small benchmark dataset, we get experimental results comparable to the semi-definite-programming-based solution but at a much lower computational cost.

paragraphs: Boosting combines simple classifiers into a stronger predictor. This paper investigates using products of simple learners as the components being boosted. Like tree construction, the approach repeatedly calls a base-learning routine, but it does so iteratively rather than recursively. The authors emphasize the resulting simplicity and computational efficiency.

On the reported benchmark datasets, boosted products of decision stumps outperform boosted trees. The abstract also reports the second-best MNIST result among the no-domain-knowledge algorithms in its comparison, behind deep belief networks. These are empirical findings from the paper's evaluations, illustrating that the product construction can be effective as well as computationally attractive.

A second contribution introduces an improved base learner for nominal features. Boosting products of two such subset-indicator learners solves the maximum-margin matrix factorization problem used to formulate collaborative filtering. On a small benchmark, the method achieves results comparable to a semidefinite-programming solution at much lower computational cost. This connects the same product-based learning idea to both classification and collaborative filtering.
summary.tldr: Boosting products of simple learners offers an efficient alternative to boosted trees and also solves a collaborative-filtering matrix factorization problem.

title: Boosting products of base classifiers

abstract: Pseudo-likelihood and contrastive divergence are two well-known examples of contrastive methods. These algorithms trade off the probability of the correct label with the probabilities of other �nearby� instantiations. In this paper we explore more general types of contrastive objectives, which trade off the probability of the correct label against an arbitrary set of other instantiations. We prove that a large class of contrastive objectives are consistent with maximum likelihood,even for finite amounts of data. This result generalizes asymptotic consistency for pseudo-likelihood. The proof gives significant insight into contrastive objectives, suggesting that they enforce (soft) probability-ratio constraints between pairs of instantiations. Based on this insight, we propose Contrastive Constraint Generation (CCG),an iterative constraint-generation style algorithm that allows us to learn a log-linear model using only MAP inference. We evaluate CCG on a scene classification task, showing that it significantly outperforms pseudo-likelihood,contrastive divergence, and a well-known margin-based method.

In this paper we explore more general types of contrastive objectives, which trade off the probability of the correct label against an arbitrary set of other instantiations. We prove that a large class of contrastive objectives are consistent with maximum likelihood,even for finite amounts of data. This result generalizes asymptotic consistency for pseudo-likelihood. The proof gives significant insight into contrastive objectives, suggesting that they enforce (soft) probability-ratio constraints between pairs of instantiations. Based on this insight, we propose Contrastive Constraint Generation (CCG),an iterative constraint-generation style algorithm that allows us to learn a log-linear model using only MAP inference. We evaluate CCG on a scene classification task, showing that it significantly outperforms pseudo-likelihood,contrastive divergence, and a well-known margin-based method.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning objectives compare the probability of the correct label with probabilities assigned to alternatives. Familiar examples concentrate on nearby alternatives. This paper investigates a broader family of objectives that can compare the correct label against an arbitrary set of other configurations, expanding which comparisons can guide learning.

The authors prove that a large class of these objectives is consistent with maximum likelihood even with finite data. Their proof suggests that contrastive objectives impose soft constraints on probability ratios between pairs of configurations. This interpretation explains the objectives through the relationships they encourage between predictions, and generalizes an earlier asymptotic consistency result for pseudo-likelihood.

Using that insight, the paper introduces Contrastive Constraint Generation. This iterative algorithm learns a log-linear model using only maximum a posteriori inference, which identifies the most probable configuration. On a scene classification task, it significantly outperforms pseudo-likelihood, contrastive divergence, and an established margin-based method. The results connect the broader theoretical view of contrastive objectives to a concrete learning algorithm with favorable task-specific evidence.
summary.tldr: A probability-ratio interpretation of contrastive objectives motivates an algorithm that learns log-linear models using only MAP inference.
